uni-llb-administrative-law.title: Administrative Law
uni-llb-administrative-law.description: Nature and growth of administrative law, rule of law and separation of powers, delegated legislation and its controls, principles of natural justice, judicial review and writs, administrative discretion, tribunals, liability of the State, Lokpal and the Right to Information Act. General education, not legal advice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Nature, scope, rule of law and separation of powers
courses.summary: What administrative law is and why it grew, Dicey's rule of law and its Indian form, separation of powers in the Indian Constitution, droit administratif, and classification of administrative action.
outcomes: Define administrative law and explain the reasons for its growth
State Dicey's three meanings of rule of law and their critique
Explain how separation of powers operates in India
Classify an action as legislative, quasi-judicial, or purely administrative

lessons.title: Meaning, sources and growth of administrative law

scenes.text: Leela applies for a licence to run a tea stall near a railway station. The municipal officer rejects it without reasons.
Which branch of law tells her what powers the officer has and how she can challenge him?

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Ivor Jennings**: the law relating to the administration; it determines the organisation, powers and duties of administrative authorities.
- **K.C. Davis**: the law concerning the powers and procedures of administrative agencies, including especially the law governing judicial review of administrative action.
- **Wade**: the law concerning the powers of government and their control.
Core concerns: **sources of power**, **limits on power**, **procedure**, and **remedies** for those affected.

steps.title: Reasons for growth
steps.body:
1. Shift from **police State** to **welfare State** (Directive Principles in Part IV).
2. Technical and complex problems needing expertise.
3. Inadequacy of legislature (time) and courts (cost, delay, formality).
4. Need for flexibility and experimentation.
5. Preventive measures (licensing, inspection) better than punishment after harm.
Sources in India: the **Constitution**, statutes, delegated legislation, judicial decisions, and administrative instructions (limited).

steps.title: Leela's case mapped
steps.body:
Source of power: State Municipal Act and licensing bye-laws.
Limits: Article 19(1)(g) right to carry on trade, subject to reasonable restrictions (19(6)).
Procedure: natural justice and any statutory requirement to give reasons.
Remedy: statutory appeal if provided; otherwise a writ petition under Article 226.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Equating administrative law with constitutional law: constitutional law deals with the structure of all organs; administrative law focuses on the executive's powers and their control.

activity.prompt: Tick the reasons for the growth of administrative law
items: Rise of the welfare State
Need for technical expertise
Legislature lacks time to legislate on every detail
Courts are slow and formal for many disputes
Need for preventive regulation such as licensing

quiz.q: Who defined administrative law to include judicial review of administrative action as a major concern?
quiz.why: K.C. Davis's definition emphasises powers, procedures and judicial review of agencies.

quiz.q: The main driver of growth of administrative law is
quiz.why: The welfare State vastly increased government functions, needing more administrative power and control.

quiz.q: A writ against a municipal licensing decision is filed under
quiz.why: High Courts issue writs under Article 226 against any authority, including for violation of legal rights.

lessons.title: Rule of law: Dicey and the Indian version

scenes.text: A senior official orders the detention of a journalist without any legal authority.
The journalist's family asks: can the official claim immunity because of his rank?

steps.title: Dicey's three meanings (1885)
steps.body:
1. **Supremacy of law** – absence of arbitrary power; no one punished except for a distinct breach of law established in ordinary courts.
2. **Equality before law** – every person, whatever his rank, is subject to the ordinary law and ordinary courts.
3. **Constitution as the result of ordinary law** – rights in England flow from judicial decisions, not a written constitution.

steps.title: Critique and Indian application
steps.body:
Critique: Dicey confused discretionary with arbitrary power; ignored privileges of the Crown; misread French droit administratif. Modern view: rule of law requires discretion to be controlled, not abolished.
India: rule of law is part of the **basic structure** (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973; Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain, 1975). **Article 14** embodies equality and non-arbitrariness (E.P. Royappa, 1974; Maneka Gandhi, 1978). In ADM Jabalpur (1976) the majority held habeas corpus unavailable during Emergency; this was later expressly overruled in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) and the 44th Amendment made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable.

steps.title: Applying to the journalist
steps.body:
1. Detention needs authority of law (Article 21) and must follow procedure under Article 22.
2. Rank gives no immunity: ordinary courts can examine legality.
3. Remedy: habeas corpus under Article 32 or 226; compensation for illegal detention can also be awarded (Rudul Sah v State of Bihar, 1983).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying rule of law forbids all discretion – it forbids arbitrary, uncontrolled discretion.

activity.prompt: Order the development of rule of law ideas in India
items: Dicey's three meanings (1885)
Kesavananda Bharati: basic structure (1973)
E.P. Royappa: arbitrariness is antithetical to equality (1974)
ADM Jabalpur: Emergency habeas corpus ruling (1976)
Maneka Gandhi: fair, just and reasonable procedure (1978)
Puttaswamy: ADM Jabalpur expressly overruled (2017)

quiz.q: Rule of law is part of the basic structure per
options: Kesavananda Bharati and Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain
quiz.why: Both cases recognised rule of law and related principles as part of the basic structure.

quiz.q: Which case linked arbitrariness with violation of Article 14?
options: E.P. Royappa v State of TN
quiz.why: In Royappa, Bhagwati J said equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies.

quiz.q: ADM Jabalpur was expressly overruled in
quiz.why: The nine-judge bench in Puttaswamy said ADM Jabalpur was seriously flawed and stood overruled.

lessons.title: Separation of powers and droit administratif

scenes.text: A statute allows the minister to frame rules, hear appeals against his own department's orders, and impose penalties.
A student asks: doesn't this breach separation of powers?

steps.title: Montesquieu's doctrine
steps.body: Liberty is lost if the same person or body exercises legislative, executive and judicial powers. Strict form: (1) same persons should not form part of more than one organ; (2) one organ should not control another; (3) one organ should not exercise another's functions.

steps.title: Position in India
steps.body: The Constitution does **not** adopt strict separation, but there is a **functional differentiation** with checks and balances (Ram Jawaya Kapur v State of Punjab, 1955). Examples of overlap: ministers are members of the legislature; the President's ordinance power (Art 123); delegated legislation; legislature punishes for contempt. **Judicial independence** and separation of judiciary from executive (Art 50) are strong. Separation of powers is part of the **basic structure** (Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain, 1975).

steps.title: Droit administratif
steps.body: The French system: administrative disputes go to separate **administrative courts** headed by the **Conseil d'État**, applying special rules. Dicey thought it protected officials; in fact the Conseil d'État developed strong protections for citizens. Disputes over which court has jurisdiction are resolved by the **Tribunal des Conflits**.

steps.title: The minister's powers
steps.body: In India such combination is not per se unconstitutional. Courts test: (1) is delegation within limits (essential legislative function retained)? (2) is the adjudication fair – no bias, hearing given? (3) is there judicial review? A minister hearing an appeal against his own department may raise **departmental bias** concerns (see Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v APSRTC, 1959).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Writing that India follows strict separation of powers like the USA.

activity.prompt: Tick the features showing India does NOT follow strict separation
items: Ministers sit in the legislature
President can issue ordinances
Executive makes delegated legislation
Legislature can punish for contempt of the House

quiz.q: India's position on separation of powers was explained in
options: Ram Jawaya Kapur v State of Punjab
quiz.why: Ram Jawaya Kapur held that India has no rigid separation but a functional differentiation.

quiz.q: The highest French administrative court
quiz.why: The Conseil d'État heads the French administrative courts.

quiz.q: Article 50 directs
quiz.why: Article 50 directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in public services.

lessons.title: Classification of administrative action

scenes.text: A District Collector issues rules on fair-price shops, cancels a dealer's licence after an inquiry, and transfers a clerk.
Each act attracts different controls. How do we classify them?

steps.title: Four categories
steps.body:
1. **Quasi-legislative (rule-making)**: general, prospective rules – e.g., notification of shop timings.
2. **Quasi-judicial**: decision affecting rights after determining facts and applying law, with a **duty to act judicially** – e.g., cancellation of licence after inquiry.
3. **Purely administrative**: policy implementation, discretion, no lis – e.g., transfer of an employee.
4. **Ministerial**: performance of a duty with no discretion – e.g., issuing a certificate once conditions are met.

steps.title: Why classification matters less now
steps.body: Earlier, natural justice applied only to quasi-judicial acts. After **A.K. Kraipak v Union of India (1969)** the line became thin: rules of natural justice apply to administrative inquiries too, since both aim at a just decision. Still, classification helps decide which procedure, which remedy (certiorari vs mandamus) and whether reasons are needed.

steps.title: Classifying the Collector's acts
steps.body:
- Rules on fair-price shops → quasi-legislative (control by Parliament/legislature, courts for ultra vires).
- Licence cancellation → quasi-judicial (notice, hearing, reasons; certiorari).
- Transfer of clerk → administrative (reviewable for mala fides or statutory breach).
- Issuing ration card to eligible person → ministerial (mandamus if refused).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming natural justice never applies to administrative decisions – Kraipak changed that.

activity.prompt: Order the questions to classify an administrative act
items: Is it general and prospective? (if yes, quasi-legislative)
Does it decide rights between parties after finding facts? (quasi-judicial)
Does the authority have discretion on policy? (administrative)
Is there no discretion at all? (ministerial)
Identify the procedural safeguards and remedy that follow

quiz.q: After which case did the quasi-judicial/administrative distinction weaken for natural justice?
options: A.K. Kraipak v Union of India
quiz.why: Kraipak held that natural justice applies to administrative inquiries as well.

quiz.q: Issuing a certificate when all conditions are met is
quiz.why: A ministerial act involves no discretion, only performance of a duty.

quiz.q: Framing general rules is
quiz.why: Rule-making of general, prospective application is quasi-legislative.

questions.q: Ivor Jennings defined administrative law as law relating to
questions.why: Jennings described it as the law relating to the administration.

questions.q: Dicey's second meaning of rule of law is
questions.why: He said every person is subject to the ordinary law and courts.

questions.q: Dicey's main error according to critics was
questions.why: Critics argue modern government needs discretion, which is controllable rather than arbitrary.

questions.q: Compensation for illegal detention was awarded in
options: Rudul Sah v State of Bihar
questions.why: Rudul Sah is a landmark case on compensation for violation of Article 21.

questions.q: 44th Amendment made which Articles non-suspendable in Emergency
questions.why: It amended Article 359 so that Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended.

questions.q: The French tribunal that resolves jurisdiction disputes
questions.why: The Tribunal des Conflits decides whether ordinary or administrative courts have jurisdiction.

questions.q: Separation of powers as basic structure was recognised in
options: Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain
questions.why: Judges in Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain treated separation of powers as part of the basic structure.

questions.q: Transfer of a government employee is typically
questions.why: Transfers involve policy and administrative discretion without a lis.

questions.q: Cancellation of a licence after an inquiry is
questions.why: It decides rights after finding facts and requires acting judicially.

questions.q: Montesquieu's doctrine aims to protect
questions.why: Montesquieu argued that concentration of powers destroys liberty.

questions.q: Departmental bias was examined in
questions.why: Gullapalli quashed a decision where the department secretary effectively heard objections against his own scheme.

questions.q: The welfare-State concept in the Constitution appears mainly in
questions.why: The Directive Principles in Part IV set welfare goals for the State.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Delegated legislation and its control
courses.summary: Meaning and reasons for delegated legislation, conditional legislation, limits of permissible delegation and excessive delegation, sub-delegation, and judicial, legislative and procedural controls.
outcomes: Define delegated legislation and explain why it is necessary
Apply the essential legislative function test from In re Delhi Laws Act
Distinguish conditional legislation from delegated legislation
Apply grounds of judicial review of delegated legislation
Explain laying procedures and publication requirements

lessons.title: Meaning, reasons and forms

scenes.text: Parliament passes a Motor Vehicles law that says 'the Central Government may make rules on safety standards'.
A thousand pages of rules follow, written by ministry officials. Who really made the law?

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Delegated (subordinate) legislation** is law made by an authority other than the legislature, under powers conferred by a parent statute (enabling Act). Salmond: legislation that proceeds from any authority other than the sovereign power and depends for its validity on some superior authority.

steps.title: Reasons
steps.body:
1. Pressure on parliamentary time.
2. Technicality of subject matter.
3. Flexibility – rules can be changed quickly.
4. Experimentation and local conditions.
5. Emergencies.
Forms: **rules**, **regulations**, **bye-laws** (local bodies), **orders**, **notifications**, **schemes**, **directions**.

steps.title: Spotting the hierarchy
steps.body: Constitution → Motor Vehicles Act (parent) → Central Motor Vehicles Rules (delegated) → State notifications on speed limits (further delegated, if permitted). Each layer must be within the one above; a rule conflicting with the Act is void.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating ordinances (Art 123/213) as delegated legislation – they are executive legislation derived directly from the Constitution.

activity.prompt: Tick the reasons for delegated legislation
items: Lack of parliamentary time
Technical subject matter
Need for flexibility
Emergency situations
Local variations

quiz.q: Delegated legislation derives validity from
quiz.why: It is valid only within the powers conferred by the enabling statute.

quiz.q: Bye-laws are usually made by
quiz.why: Municipalities and similar local authorities make bye-laws under their statutes.

quiz.q: An ordinance under Article 123 is
quiz.why: Ordinance power comes directly from the Constitution, not from a parent statute.

lessons.title: Limits: essential legislative function and excessive delegation

scenes.text: An Act lets the Government extend any law in force in a province to Delhi 'with such restrictions and modifications as it thinks fit', even repealing local laws.
Seven judges must decide how far Parliament can hand over its power.

steps.title: In re Delhi Laws Act (1951)
steps.body: The Supreme Court held that the legislature **cannot delegate its essential legislative functions** – determining legislative **policy** and laying it down as a binding rule of conduct. It may delegate subsidiary details. The power to **repeal** existing laws in force in the area was held invalid (excessive delegation), while power to extend laws with modifications not changing policy was upheld.

steps.title: Tests and doctrines
steps.body:
- **Policy and guidelines test**: the Act must lay down policy, standards or guidance (Hamdard Dawakhana v Union of India, 1960 – vague power struck down).
- **Conditional legislation**: the legislature makes the law complete, leaving the executive to decide when/where it applies (Queen v Burah, 1878, Privy Council). Not true delegation.
- **Henry VIII clause**: power to modify the parent Act to remove difficulties – permissible only narrowly, within policy.
- **Sub-delegation**: *delegatus non potest delegare* – permitted only if the parent Act expressly or impliedly authorises it.

steps.title: Testing a clause
steps.body:
Clause: 'The Government may prohibit any advertisement it considers objectionable.'
1. Does the Act state policy? 'Objectionable' is undefined.
2. No standards → uncontrolled discretion.
3. Likely excessive delegation (compare Hamdard Dawakhana).
Redrafted: 'may prohibit advertisements of drugs claiming to cure diseases listed in the Schedule' → valid.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling conditional legislation 'excessive delegation': deciding the date of commencement is not law-making.

activity.prompt: Order the excessive-delegation test
items: Identify the delegating provision
Find the policy declared in the parent Act
Check for standards or guidelines controlling the delegate
Check whether essential functions (policy, repeal) were delegated
Conclude valid delegation, conditional legislation, or excessive delegation

quiz.q: Essential legislative function includes
quiz.why: Determining policy and enacting it as a rule of conduct cannot be delegated.

quiz.q: Queen v Burah concerns
quiz.why: The Privy Council upheld leaving the application of a law to the executive as conditional legislation.

quiz.q: Sub-delegation is valid when
quiz.why: Under delegatus non potest delegare, further delegation needs express or implied authority.

lessons.title: Judicial control of delegated legislation

story.title: The rule that went too far

scenes.text: A rule under a Prisons Act bars prisoners from meeting lawyers entirely.
The parent Act only allows 'regulation of interviews'.

steps.title: Grounds
steps.body:
1. **Parent Act unconstitutional**.
2. **Delegated legislation violates the Constitution** (e.g., Arts 14, 19, 21).
3. **Substantive ultra vires** – beyond the scope of the parent Act.
4. **Procedural ultra vires** – mandatory procedure (consultation, publication) not followed.
5. **Unreasonableness / manifest arbitrariness** – Kruse v Johnson (1898) test for bye-laws; in India, Indian Express Newspapers v Union of India (1985) on grounds of challenge.
6. **Mala fides** (rare for legislation) and conflict with other statutes.

steps.title: The prison rule
steps.body:
1. Act permits 'regulation' – regulation does not include total prohibition.
2. Total bar exceeds the Act → substantive ultra vires.
3. Also violates Article 21 and Article 22(1) right to consult a lawyer.
Result: rule quashed.

steps.title: Effect of 'shall have effect as if enacted in this Act'
steps.body: Such clauses do not immunise rules from review; rules must still be within the Act.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming courts review the wisdom of policy – they review legality, not merits.

activity.prompt: Tick valid grounds to challenge a delegated rule
items: Exceeds power under the parent Act
Violates a fundamental right
Mandatory publication not done
Manifestly arbitrary
Parent Act itself unconstitutional

quiz.q: A rule beyond the parent Act is
quiz.why: Exceeding the scope of the enabling power is substantive ultra vires.

quiz.q: The classic test of unreasonableness of bye-laws
quiz.why: Kruse v Johnson held bye-laws may be struck down if manifestly unjust or oppressive.

quiz.q: Courts reviewing rules examine
quiz.why: Judicial review tests the legality of rules rather than their policy merits.

lessons.title: Legislative and procedural control: laying and publication

scenes.text: A State Government 'notifies' a penal rule but never publishes it in the Gazette.
A trader is prosecuted for breaking it.

steps.title: Legislative control
steps.body:
**Laying** rules before the House:
1. **Simple laying** – for information.
2. **Negative resolution** – rules take effect unless annulled or modified within a period (most common in India; often 30 days in one or more sessions).
3. **Affirmative resolution** – rules take effect only if approved.
**Committee on Subordinate Legislation** (Lok Sabha from 1953; Rajya Sabha too) scrutinises whether rules are within the Act, unusual or unexpected, impose taxes, bar courts, or have retrospective effect without authority.

steps.title: Procedural control
steps.body:
- **Publication**: law must be made known; **Harla v State of Rajasthan (1951)** – an unpublished law cannot bind people.
- **Consultation** of affected interests where the parent Act requires (mandatory if statute so provides).
- **Pre-publication** of draft for objections (e.g., s.23 General Clauses Act procedure where applicable).

steps.title: The trader
steps.body:
1. Penal rule never published in the Gazette.
2. Harla: natural justice requires publication so that people can know the law.
3. Prosecution fails; the rule is not enforceable against him.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating laying as always mandatory for validity – depends on the statute's wording (mandatory or directory).

activity.prompt: Order the life cycle of a rule under a negative-resolution laying clause
items: Parent Act authorises rule-making
Draft rules pre-published for objections if required
Rules finalised and published in the Official Gazette
Rules laid before each House
Period passes without annulment; rules continue in force

quiz.q: Unpublished law cannot bind people per
quiz.why: Harla held that publication is essential before a law can bind.

quiz.q: Most common laying procedure in India
quiz.why: Indian statutes mostly allow the House to annul or modify rules after laying.

quiz.q: Committee on Subordinate Legislation scrutinises
options: Whether rules stay within the Act
quiz.why: It checks that delegated powers are properly exercised within the parent Act.

questions.q: In re Delhi Laws Act struck down delegation of the power to
questions.why: The power to repeal laws in force was held to be excessive delegation.

questions.q: Hamdard Dawakhana is about
questions.why: It struck down a provision giving uncontrolled power without standards.

questions.q: Delegatus non potest delegare means
options: The King can do no wrong
No one judge in own cause
questions.why: The maxim prohibits sub-delegation without authority.

questions.q: Henry VIII clause permits
options: Modifying the parent Act to remove difficulties
questions.why: It allows the executive limited power to modify the Act, narrowly construed.

questions.q: Affirmative resolution means rules
questions.why: The House must approve the rules before they operate.

questions.q: Publication of delegated legislation is required because
questions.why: Harla based publication on the principle that laws must be knowable.

questions.q: Conditional legislation leaves to the executive
options: When and where to apply a complete law
questions.why: The law is complete; only its application depends on executive satisfaction.

questions.q: A rule violating Article 14 is
questions.why: Delegated legislation is subject to fundamental rights like any law.

questions.q: Procedural ultra vires occurs when
questions.why: Failure to follow mandatory steps like consultation invalidates the rule.

questions.q: Committee on Subordinate Legislation in Lok Sabha was set up in
questions.why: The Lok Sabha committee was constituted in 1953.

questions.q: A clause saying rules 'shall have effect as if enacted' makes them
questions.why: Courts hold such clauses do not protect rules that exceed the parent Act.

questions.q: Indian Express Newspapers (1985) concerns
options: Grounds of challenge to subordinate legislation
questions.why: The Court discussed grounds on which subordinate legislation can be questioned.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Principles of natural justice
courses.summary: The rule against bias, the right to a fair hearing and its components, reasoned decisions, exclusions and exceptions, post-decisional hearing, and the effect of violation including the prejudice test.
outcomes: Identify pecuniary, personal and official bias and apply the 'real likelihood' test
List the components of audi alteram partem
Explain when reasons must be given
State the exceptions to natural justice and the post-decisional hearing doctrine
Apply the prejudice test to a breach

lessons.title: Rule against bias (nemo judex in causa sua)

scenes.text: An acting Chief Conservator of Forests sits on a selection board that ranks officers — including himself — for promotion.
He does not vote on his own name but participates in rating his rivals.

steps.title: Kinds of bias
steps.body:
1. **Pecuniary** – any financial interest, however small, disqualifies (Dimes v Grand Junction Canal, 1852: Lord Chancellor held shares in the company).
2. **Personal** – relationship, friendship, hostility.
3. **Official / departmental / policy** – the authority is part of the department whose action is challenged or has pre-committed (Gullapalli Nageswara Rao, 1959).
4. **Subject-matter bias** and **pre-judgment**.

steps.title: Test
steps.body:
Not actual bias but **real likelihood** / **reasonable apprehension** in the mind of a fair-minded informed observer. Ranjit Thakur v Union of India (1987): the test is whether there is a reasonable ground for believing the decision-maker was likely to be biased. Justice must not only be done but **manifestly be seen to be done** (R v Sussex Justices, ex p McCarthy, 1924).
**Doctrine of necessity**: where no other authority can decide, the biased one may (e.g., Election Commission of India v Dr Subramaniam Swamy, 1996 – the CEC to step aside but participate if there is a tie).

steps.title: The selection board — A.K. Kraipak (1969)
steps.body: Facts as in the story. The Supreme Court held that his presence vitiated the selection: he was a candidate; his participation in assessing rivals created a real likelihood of bias even though he did not judge himself. Selection quashed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Requiring proof of actual bias – only a reasonable likelihood is needed.

activity.prompt: Tick situations likely to show disqualifying bias
items: Judge holds shares in a party company
Selection board member is himself a candidate
Inquiry officer is the complainant
Decision-maker is a close relative of a party

quiz.q: Dimes v Grand Junction Canal is an example of
quiz.why: The Lord Chancellor's shareholding in the company disqualified him.

quiz.q: The test for bias in India per Ranjit Thakur
quiz.why: The Court asked whether a reasonable person would apprehend bias.

quiz.q: Doctrine of necessity allows
options: A biased authority to decide when no one else can
quiz.why: Necessity prevents a failure of justice where no alternative decision-maker exists.

lessons.title: Hear the other side (audi alteram partem)

scenes.text: Maneka Gandhi's passport is impounded 'in public interest' with no reasons and no hearing.
The Government argues a prior hearing would defeat the purpose.

steps.title: Components
steps.body:
1. **Notice** – clear, specific charges/proposed action and time to respond.
2. **Disclosure** of adverse material relied on.
3. **Opportunity to present** case and evidence.
4. **Cross-examination** where facts are disputed and witnesses relied on.
5. **Legal representation** – not an absolute right; may be allowed in complex cases or where the other side is legally represented.
6. **Reasoned decision**.
7. **No evidence behind back**.

steps.title: Key cases
steps.body:
- **Ridge v Baldwin (1964, HL)**: a chief constable dismissed without hearing – decision void; revived natural justice in administrative action.
- **Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978)**: procedure under Art 21 must be fair, just and reasonable; audi alteram partem applies to impounding of passports; a **post-decisional hearing** can satisfy fairness where prior hearing is impracticable.
- **Olga Tellis (1985)**: pavement dwellers entitled to notice before eviction.

steps.title: Maneka resolution
steps.body:
1. Impounding affects Art 21 and 19 rights → fair procedure needed.
2. Urgency may justify no prior hearing.
3. The Government's undertaking to give a prompt post-decisional hearing was accepted as compliance.
Lesson: exclusion of hearing is exceptional and must be compensated by an early hearing after action.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Claiming oral hearing is always required – written representation may suffice depending on context.

activity.prompt: Order a fair disciplinary procedure
items: Issue charge-sheet with specific allegations
Supply documents relied upon
Receive written statement of defence
Conduct inquiry with evidence and cross-examination
Furnish inquiry report to the delinquent for comments
Pass reasoned final order

quiz.q: Ridge v Baldwin concerned
options: Dismissal of a chief constable without hearing
quiz.why: The House of Lords held the dismissal void for want of a hearing.

quiz.q: Post-decisional hearing was accepted in
quiz.why: The Government's undertaking to give a hearing after impounding was accepted as fair.

quiz.q: Right to legal representation before tribunals is
quiz.why: Courts allow representation where fairness demands it, such as complex issues or a legally represented opponent.

lessons.title: Reasoned decisions and exceptions

scenes.text: A government employee is dismissed under Article 311(2) proviso (c) in the interest of the security of the State, without inquiry.
Another officer's court-martial confirmation order contains no reasons.

steps.title: Reasons
steps.body: Reasons are the link between material and conclusion. **S.N. Mukherjee v Union of India (1990)**: administrative authorities exercising quasi-judicial functions must record reasons unless the requirement is expressly or impliedly excluded, though the confirming authority of a court-martial was held not required to give reasons under the Army Act scheme. Reasons ensure fairness, enable judicial review, and minimise arbitrariness.

steps.title: Exceptions / exclusion
steps.body:
1. **Statutory exclusion** (express or necessary implication), subject to Art 14 and 21.
2. **Emergency / urgency** – with post-decisional hearing.
3. **Legislative action** – no hearing for general rules.
4. **Confidentiality and national security**.
5. **Impracticability** (huge numbers).
6. **Academic evaluation** (normally no hearing for marks).
7. **Constitutional exclusion**: Art 311(2) second proviso – **Union of India v Tulsiram Patel (1985)** upheld dismissal without inquiry where clauses (a), (b) or (c) apply, subject to judicial review of the satisfaction.

steps.title: Applying
steps.body:
Employee: Article 311(2)(c) – President/Governor satisfied that inquiry is not expedient in the interest of security → inquiry dispensed with (Tulsiram Patel); court may still examine mala fides or irrelevant grounds.
Court-martial officer: under S.N. Mukherjee, no reasons needed at confirmation stage given the Army Act scheme, but the general rule for quasi-judicial authorities is to give reasons.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying exceptions put the action beyond review – courts still test legality and mala fides.

activity.prompt: Tick recognised exceptions to natural justice
items: Legislative (rule-making) action
Genuine emergency with later hearing
National security under Art 311(2)(c)
Express statutory exclusion consistent with the Constitution

quiz.q: Duty to record reasons was discussed in
options: S.N. Mukherjee v Union of India
quiz.why: The Constitution Bench held quasi-judicial authorities ordinarily must record reasons.

quiz.q: Dismissal without inquiry under Art 311(2) proviso was upheld in
options: Union of India v Tulsiram Patel
quiz.why: Tulsiram Patel upheld the constitutional exclusion of inquiry in specified cases.

quiz.q: Natural justice generally does not apply to
quiz.why: Legislative action of general application does not attract an individual hearing.

lessons.title: Effect of violation: void, voidable and the prejudice test

scenes.text: A bank officer is dismissed after an inquiry; one witness statement was not supplied to him, though he had seen it during the inquiry.
Is the dismissal automatically void?

steps.title: Void or voidable?
steps.body: Traditional view: breach of natural justice renders the decision **void** (Ridge v Baldwin). Indian courts generally treat such orders as void, but relief is discretionary under Art 226. Courts now ask whether the breach caused **prejudice**.

steps.title: The prejudice test
steps.body:
**State Bank of Patiala v S.K. Sharma (1996)**: distinguish (1) **no notice/no hearing at all** – order invalid; (2) **violation of a facet** (e.g., a document not supplied) – the court asks whether prejudice was caused. Procedural provisions of a substantive nature are mandatory; others are tested for prejudice.
**Useless formality theory**: where on admitted facts only one conclusion is possible, courts may decline to quash (applied cautiously).

steps.title: The bank officer
steps.body:
1. Hearing was given; only one document not supplied.
2. He had seen and dealt with the statement during inquiry.
3. No prejudice shown → dismissal not set aside on that ground (as in S.K. Sharma reasoning).
If no hearing at all had been given, the dismissal would be invalid without proving prejudice.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Applying the prejudice test to a total denial of hearing.

activity.prompt: Order the analysis after a breach of natural justice
items: Identify which facet was breached
Ask: was there no hearing at all, or a partial lapse?
If partial, ask whether the facet is of a substantive nature
Ask whether actual prejudice resulted
Decide whether to quash and remand for fresh inquiry

quiz.q: Prejudice test was laid down in
options: State Bank of Patiala v S.K. Sharma
quiz.why: S.K. Sharma distinguished total denial from partial violations requiring prejudice.

quiz.q: Total denial of hearing generally
quiz.why: Where no opportunity at all is given, the order is invalid without further inquiry into prejudice.

quiz.q: The 'useless formality' theory applies when
options: Only one conclusion is possible on admitted facts
quiz.why: Courts may decline relief where a hearing could not have changed the inevitable result.

questions.q: Nemo judex in causa sua means
options: No one should be a judge in his own cause
questions.why: It is the rule against bias.

questions.q: 'Justice must be seen to be done' comes from
questions.why: Lord Hewart CJ stated it in R v Sussex Justices, ex p McCarthy.

questions.q: Kraipak quashed selections because
options: A candidate sat on the selection board
questions.why: A candidate's participation in assessing his rivals created a real likelihood of bias.

questions.q: Pavement dwellers' right to notice before eviction
questions.why: Olga Tellis required fair procedure including notice before eviction.

questions.q: Natural justice applies to administrative action per
questions.why: Kraipak extended natural justice to administrative inquiries.

questions.q: Which is NOT part of audi alteram partem?
questions.why: A party has no right to pick the decision-maker; the other three are components of a fair hearing.

questions.q: Reasons enable
questions.why: Recorded reasons allow courts to check legality and rationality.

questions.q: Election Commission v Subramaniam Swamy applied
questions.why: The Court used the doctrine of necessity to allow participation only if required to break a tie.

questions.q: Article 311(2) second proviso clause (c) relates to
questions.why: Clause (c) dispenses with inquiry where it is not expedient in the interest of State security.

questions.q: Official bias was found in
questions.why: The Transport Secretary heard objections to a scheme of his own department.

questions.q: Academic evaluation of answer scripts generally
questions.why: Courts treat academic assessment as outside individual hearing requirements.

questions.q: Legal representation in domestic inquiries is
questions.why: It may be permitted where fairness requires, but is not an absolute right.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Administrative discretion, judicial review and writs
courses.summary: Control of administrative discretion (abuse and non-application), Wednesbury unreasonableness and proportionality, legitimate expectation and promissory estoppel, the five writs, Articles 32 and 226, locus standi and PIL, and 'State' under Article 12.
outcomes: Identify grounds of abuse and failure to exercise discretion
Apply Wednesbury and proportionality tests
Explain legitimate expectation and promissory estoppel
Choose the correct writ for a fact situation
Determine whether a body is 'State' under Article 12

lessons.title: Control of administrative discretion

scenes.text: A transport authority refuses a bus permit to an operator because the local MLA dislikes him.
The officer admits he 'followed instructions from above'.

steps.title: Abuse of discretion
steps.body:
1. **Mala fides** – personal ill-will or improper motive.
2. **Improper purpose** – power used for a purpose other than that for which it was given.
3. **Irrelevant considerations** taken into account or relevant ones ignored.
4. **Unreasonableness** – Wednesbury: so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have come to it (Associated Provincial Picture Houses v Wednesbury Corp, 1948).
5. **Colourable exercise** of power.

steps.title: Failure to exercise discretion
steps.body:
1. **Acting under dictation** of another authority (Commissioner of Police v Gordhandas Bhanji, 1952).
2. **Fettering discretion** by rigid self-imposed rules/policy without considering individual cases.
3. **Sub-delegation** without authority.
4. **Non-application of mind**.

steps.title: Proportionality
steps.body: For fundamental rights (Art 19, 21), Indian courts apply **proportionality**: a legitimate aim, suitable means, necessity (least restrictive), and balance (Om Kumar v Union of India, 2000; Modern Dental College, 2016; Puttaswamy, 2017). For ordinary administrative action, Wednesbury still applies.

steps.title: The bus permit
steps.body:
1. Refusal because MLA dislikes operator → irrelevant consideration and mala fides.
2. Officer followed 'instructions from above' → acting under dictation.
3. Remedy: certiorari to quash and mandamus to reconsider according to law.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Arguing that courts can substitute their own decision – generally they quash and remit.

activity.prompt: Tick the grounds present in the bus permit case
items: Irrelevant consideration
Mala fides
Acting under dictation
Non-application of independent mind

quiz.q: Acting under dictation was condemned in
options: Commissioner of Police v Gordhandas Bhanji
quiz.why: The Commissioner cancelled a licence on the Government's direction rather than his own judgment.

quiz.q: Wednesbury unreasonableness means
options: A decision no reasonable authority could reach
quiz.why: The test sets a high threshold of irrationality.

quiz.q: Proportionality in India was adopted in administrative law in
options: Om Kumar v Union of India
quiz.why: Om Kumar discussed proportionality for action affecting fundamental rights.

lessons.title: Legitimate expectation and promissory estoppel

scenes.text: A State announces a 3-year sales tax exemption for new industries; a company sets up a factory relying on it.
A year later the State withdraws the exemption.

steps.title: Promissory estoppel
steps.body: Where the Government makes a clear **promise** intending it to be acted upon, and the promisee **acts on it to his detriment**, the Government may be held to it, even without consideration and even if not in the form of a contract under Art 299 (**Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v State of UP, 1979**). Limits: it cannot operate against **statute** or compel the Government to act illegally; it yields to **overriding public interest**, which the Government must prove.

steps.title: Legitimate expectation
steps.body: A person may have a reasonable expectation of a benefit or a procedure based on an express promise or a consistent past practice. It usually gives a right to a **hearing** or fair consideration, not necessarily the substantive benefit; it is part of non-arbitrariness under Art 14 (Food Corporation of India v Kamdhenu Cattle Feed, 1993; Union of India v Hindustan Development Corp, 1993).

steps.title: The tax exemption
steps.body:
1. Clear promise ✔; company acted to its detriment ✔.
2. Withdrawal: State must show overriding public interest; mere change of policy is not enough.
3. If exemption was granted by a valid statutory notification and later withdrawn by statute, estoppel cannot override the statute.
Outcome depends on the legal source of the promise and justification shown.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying promissory estoppel can force the State to act against a statute.

activity.prompt: Order the promissory estoppel test
items: Identify a clear and unequivocal promise by the Government
Show the promise was intended to be acted upon
Show the promisee acted on it and altered position
Check that enforcing it would not violate any statute
Ask whether the Government has shown overriding public interest

quiz.q: Promissory estoppel against Government was established in
quiz.why: The Court held the Government bound by its promise to grant tax exemption.

quiz.q: Legitimate expectation ordinarily gives
options: An absolute right to the benefit
A right to fair consideration or hearing
quiz.why: It mainly protects procedural fairness and non-arbitrariness.

quiz.q: Promissory estoppel cannot be used
quiz.why: No estoppel can compel an authority to act contrary to law.

lessons.title: The five writs

scenes.text: A man is held in police lock-up for four days without production before a magistrate.
A university Vice-Chancellor is appointed though he lacks the statutory qualifications.

steps.title: The writs
steps.body:
- **Habeas corpus** ('have the body'): against illegal detention; can be filed by anyone on behalf of the detenu; lies against private persons too.
- **Mandamus** ('we command'): directs a public authority to perform a **public legal duty**; not against the President/Governor personally, a private person, or to enforce a contract generally.
- **Certiorari**: quashes a decision of an inferior court/tribunal/authority for lack or excess of jurisdiction, breach of natural justice, or error of law apparent on the record.
- **Prohibition**: prevents an inferior court/tribunal from proceeding beyond jurisdiction; issued while proceedings are pending.
- **Quo warranto** ('by what authority'): tests the legality of a person's claim to a **public office** of a substantive, statutory character.

steps.title: Matching facts
steps.body:
1. Detention beyond 24 hours without production (Art 22(2)) → **habeas corpus**.
2. Unqualified Vice-Chancellor in a statutory office → **quo warranto** (any person may apply; locus standi relaxed).
3. Municipality refuses to issue a birth certificate to an eligible person → **mandamus**.
4. Tribunal decided a case outside its jurisdiction → **certiorari**.
5. Tribunal about to hear a matter outside its jurisdiction → **prohibition**.

steps.title: Certiorari vs prohibition
steps.body: Prohibition is preventive (before final decision); certiorari is corrective (after decision). Both can be sought together.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Seeking quo warranto against a private office (e.g., club secretary) – it lies only for public offices.

activity.prompt: Order the writs by when they apply to a tribunal's proceeding
items: Prohibition – stop the tribunal before it acts beyond jurisdiction
Certiorari – quash the decision after it is made
Mandamus – direct the authority to reconsider according to law

quiz.q: Writ to test right to hold a public office
quiz.why: Quo warranto asks by what authority a person holds a public office.

quiz.q: Habeas corpus can be issued against
quiz.why: Unlawful detention by anyone, including private persons, can be challenged by habeas corpus.

quiz.q: Mandamus does NOT lie against
quiz.why: Article 361 protects the President and Governors from personal process in courts.

lessons.title: Articles 32 and 226, locus standi, PIL and Article 12

scenes.text: A company challenges a cricket body's cancellation of a broadcasting tender by writ petition.
The body says it is a private society, not 'State'.

steps.title: Articles 32 and 226
steps.body: **Art 32**: right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of **fundamental rights**; itself a fundamental right. **Art 226**: High Courts may issue writs for fundamental rights **and for any other purpose** (legal rights), to any person or authority within their territorial jurisdiction – wider than Art 32. Alternative remedy is a rule of discretion, not a bar; writ still lies for enforcement of fundamental rights, violation of natural justice, lack of jurisdiction, or challenge to vires of an Act (**Whirlpool Corp v Registrar of Trade Marks, 1998**).

steps.title: Locus standi and PIL
steps.body: Traditional rule: only a person aggrieved may petition. **S.P. Gupta v Union of India (1981)** relaxed it: any member of the public acting bona fide may approach the court for persons unable to do so (poverty, disability). Letters may be treated as petitions (epistolary jurisdiction). Courts guard against busybodies and publicity-interest litigation.

steps.title: 'State' under Article 12
steps.body: Includes Government, Parliament, State legislatures, local authorities and **other authorities**. Tests in **Ajay Hasia v Khalid Mujib (1981)** (financial, functional, administrative control). **Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002)**: body is State if it is **financially, functionally and administratively dominated** by Government. **Zee Telefilms v Union of India (2005)**: BCCI is not 'State' under Art 12, but writ under **Art 226** may lie as it performs **public functions**.

steps.title: The cricket body
steps.body:
1. Art 32 petition: following Zee Telefilms, BCCI is not State → Art 32 not maintainable for fundamental rights.
2. Art 226: the body discharges public functions (selecting national teams) → writ may lie for public-law obligations; however, purely contractual tender disputes may be left to civil remedies unless arbitrariness in a public function is shown.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating alternative remedy as an absolute bar to writs.

activity.prompt: Tick the Whirlpool exceptions where a writ lies despite an alternative remedy
items: Enforcement of a fundamental right
Violation of natural justice
Order wholly without jurisdiction
Challenge to the vires of an Act

quiz.q: Which Article lets High Courts issue writs 'for any other purpose'?
quiz.why: Article 226 extends to legal rights beyond fundamental rights.

quiz.q: Relaxation of locus standi for PIL was firmly established in
options: S.P. Gupta v Union of India
quiz.why: S.P. Gupta allowed any public-spirited person to petition for those unable to do so.

quiz.q: BCCI is not 'State' under Article 12 per
options: Zee Telefilms v Union of India
quiz.why: A majority in Zee Telefilms held BCCI not State though Art 226 remedies may lie.

questions.q: Using power for a purpose not authorised is
questions.why: Power must be used only for the purpose for which it was conferred.

questions.q: Rigid policy applied without considering individual cases is
questions.why: An authority must keep its mind open to individual circumstances.

questions.q: Least restrictive means is part of
questions.why: Necessity — choosing the least restrictive measure — is a limb of proportionality.

questions.q: Overriding public interest defeats
questions.why: Motilal Padampat allows the Government to resile only on proving overriding public interest.

questions.q: A preventive writ against a tribunal
questions.why: Prohibition stops proceedings before they are completed.

questions.q: Error of law apparent on the record is a ground for
questions.why: Certiorari corrects such errors by quashing the decision.

questions.q: Arrested person must be produced before a magistrate within
questions.why: Article 22(2) requires production within 24 hours excluding journey time.

questions.q: Financial, functional and administrative domination test
questions.why: The seven-judge bench in Pradeep Kumar Biswas laid down this test.

questions.q: Article 32 is
questions.why: Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court as a fundamental right.

questions.q: Legitimate expectation is linked to
questions.why: Courts treat legitimate expectation as part of fair and non-arbitrary action under Art 14.

questions.q: Writ of mandamus requires
questions.why: Mandamus enforces public duties owed by public authorities.

questions.q: Wednesbury case concerned
questions.why: It concerned a condition banning children from Sunday cinema performances.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Tribunals, liability of the State, Lokpal and Right to Information
courses.summary: Administrative tribunals under Articles 323A/323B and their judicial review, tortious and contractual liability of the State, constitutional tort, the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 and the Right to Information Act, 2005 with timelines and penalty computation.
outcomes: Explain the constitutional status of tribunals after L. Chandra Kumar
Distinguish sovereign and non-sovereign functions in State tort liability
Explain compensation for violation of fundamental rights (constitutional tort)
State the formal requirements of Government contracts under Article 299
Apply RTI timelines, exemptions and compute penalty under s.20

lessons.title: Administrative tribunals

scenes.text: A central government clerk is denied promotion and wants to challenge it.
Should she go to the High Court directly or to a tribunal?

steps.title: Constitutional basis
steps.body: The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted **Article 323A** (administrative tribunals for service matters, by Parliament) and **Article 323B** (tribunals for tax, industrial and labour, land reforms, elections, etc., by appropriate legislature). The **Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985** set up the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) and State tribunals.

steps.title: L. Chandra Kumar v Union of India (1997)
steps.body: Clauses excluding High Court and Supreme Court jurisdiction under Arts 226/227 and 32 were struck down: judicial review is part of the **basic structure**. Tribunals act as courts of **first instance**; their decisions are subject to scrutiny by a **Division Bench of the High Court** under Art 226/227 within whose jurisdiction the tribunal falls. Tribunals cannot hear challenges to the vires of their own parent statute as the final word.

steps.title: Features and criticism
steps.body: Advantages: expertise, speed, less formality, lower cost. Concerns: executive control over appointments, vacancies, independence (Madras Bar Association cases, e.g., 2014, 2020, 2021). Principles of natural justice apply to tribunals.

steps.title: The clerk's route
steps.body:
1. Central government service matter → **CAT** (Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985).
2. After CAT's decision, challenge before a **Division Bench of the High Court** (L. Chandra Kumar).
3. Then Supreme Court under Art 136 if needed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying tribunals' decisions go directly to the Supreme Court only – after L. Chandra Kumar they go to the High Court first.

activity.prompt: Order the forum route for a central service dispute
items: Departmental representation/appeal if provided
Original application before the Central Administrative Tribunal
Writ petition before a Division Bench of the High Court
Special leave petition before the Supreme Court

quiz.q: Articles 323A and 323B were inserted by
quiz.why: The 42nd Amendment of 1976 added Part XIV-A on tribunals.

quiz.q: Judicial review of tribunal decisions lies first with
options: A Division Bench of the High Court
quiz.why: L. Chandra Kumar routed challenges to High Court Division Benches.

quiz.q: Judicial review is part of the basic structure according to
quiz.why: The seven-judge bench held the power of judicial review under Arts 226 and 32 is a basic feature.

lessons.title: Tortious liability of the State and constitutional tort

scenes.text: Police seize a jeweller's gold on suspicion and store it in the police station; a constable absconds with it.
The jeweller sues the State for the loss.

steps.title: Article 300 and history
steps.body:
Art 300: the Union and States may sue and be sued as the Dominion/Provinces could before the Constitution. **P&O Steam Navigation Co v Secretary of State (1861)**: distinction between **sovereign** functions (no liability) and **non-sovereign/commercial** functions (liability).
**State of Rajasthan v Vidyawati (1962)**: State liable for a Government jeep driver's rash driving (non-sovereign).

steps.title: Kasturilal and later dilution
steps.body:
**Kasturi Lal v State of UP (1965)**: State not liable for loss of gold seized by police, as power of arrest and seizure is sovereign. Later cases narrowed this: **N. Nagendra Rao v State of AP (1994)** – sovereign immunity is limited to primary inalienable functions (defence, administration of justice, etc.); the State is liable for negligence of officers in statutory functions like seizure and custody of goods. 
**Constitutional tort**: for violation of Art 21, courts award compensation under Arts 32/226 and sovereign immunity is no defence (**Nilabati Behera v State of Orissa, 1993**, custodial death; also Rudul Sah, 1983; D.K. Basu, 1997).

steps.title: The jeweller today
steps.body:
1. Under Kasturilal, no liability (sovereign function).
2. Under Nagendra Rao, safe custody of seized goods is a statutory duty; negligence → State liable, with a right to recover from the officer.
3. So a modern court is likely to grant damages.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Citing Kasturilal as the current law without noting its dilution.

activity.prompt: Tick the cases that expanded State liability
items: State of Rajasthan v Vidyawati
N. Nagendra Rao v State of AP
Nilabati Behera v State of Orissa
Rudul Sah v State of Bihar

quiz.q: Sovereign immunity for police seizure was upheld in
options: Kasturi Lal v State of UP
quiz.why: Kasturilal held the State not liable because seizure is a sovereign function.

quiz.q: Compensation for custodial death as public-law remedy
quiz.why: Nilabati Behera held sovereign immunity is no defence to constitutional tort.

quiz.q: Rash driving by a Government jeep driver made the State liable in
quiz.why: Vidyawati treated the activity as non-sovereign.

lessons.title: Government contracts and Lokpal

scenes.text: A contractor supplies bricks to a PWD office on an oral order from an engineer; no contract is executed in the President's/Governor's name.
Payment is refused.

steps.title: Article 299
steps.body: Contracts by the Union or a State must be: (1) **expressed to be made by the President/Governor**; (2) **executed** on his behalf; (3) by a person **authorised**. Non-compliance makes the contract **void** and unenforceable against either side (no ratification possible) – but s.70 Indian Contract Act allows recovery for **benefit received** under a lawful non-gratuitous act (State of West Bengal v B.K. Mondal & Sons, 1962). Arbitrary action in contract award or termination is reviewable under Art 14 (Ramana Dayaram Shetty v International Airport Authority, 1979).

steps.title: Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013
steps.body: Establishes the **Lokpal** for the Union (chairperson + up to 8 members, at least half judicial members) and requires States to set up **Lokayuktas**. Jurisdiction over complaints of corruption under the Prevention of Corruption Act against public servants including the Prime Minister (with safeguards), ministers, MPs, and Group A–D officers. Has inquiry and prosecution wings. The ombudsman idea originated in Sweden (1809).

steps.title: The brick supplier
steps.body:
1. No Art 299 contract → void, cannot sue on contract.
2. But the Government used the bricks; supply was not intended to be gratuitous.
3. s.70 Contract Act → recover reasonable value (B.K. Mondal).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying the supplier gets nothing because the contract is void – s.70 provides restitution.

activity.prompt: Tick the requirements of Article 299
items: Contract expressed to be made by the President or Governor
Executed on behalf of the President or Governor
Executed by a person authorised
In the form directed or authorised

quiz.q: A contract not complying with Art 299 is
quiz.why: Courts hold such contracts void and incapable of ratification.

quiz.q: Restitution despite void Govt contract via
quiz.why: B.K. Mondal applied s.70 to allow recovery for benefit enjoyed.

quiz.q: The ombudsman institution originated in
quiz.why: Sweden created the first parliamentary ombudsman in 1809.

lessons.title: Right to Information Act, 2005

story.title: Where is my ration card file?

scenes.text: Rekha files an RTI application on 1 March asking for the status of her ration-card application.
The PIO replies only on 10 May.

steps.title: Key provisions
steps.body:
- **s.2(f)** information; **s.2(h)** public authority; **s.2(j)** right to information.
- **s.4**: proactive disclosure.
- **s.6**: request in writing/electronically to the PIO with fee; no reasons needed.
- **s.7(1)**: decide within **30 days**; **48 hours** if it concerns life or liberty.
- **s.8**: exemptions – sovereignty and security, contempt, legislative privilege, commercial confidence/IP, fiduciary relationship, foreign confidence, endangering life, impeding investigation, Cabinet papers (until decision), personal information without public interest. **s.8(2)**: public interest can override.
- **s.19**: first appeal to senior officer within **30 days**; second appeal to CIC/SIC within **90 days**.
- **s.20**: penalty **₹250 per day** till information is furnished, maximum **₹25,000**.

steps.title: Computing the penalty
steps.body:
Application received 1 March. 30 days → due by **31 March** (1 March excluded: 2 March counted as day 1... day 30 = 31 March).
Reply 10 May. Delay: 1 April – 10 May = 30 (April) + 10 (May) = **40 days**.
Penalty = 40 × ₹250 = **₹10,000** (below the ₹25,000 cap), imposed on the PIO personally if delay was without reasonable cause, after hearing him.
If the delay were 120 days: 120 × 250 = ₹30,000 → capped at **₹25,000**.

steps.title: Cases
steps.body: CBSE v Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011): evaluated answer sheets are information; examinee may inspect. CPIO, Supreme Court v Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019): Office of the CJI is a public authority, subject to s.8 balancing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking the penalty is paid by the department – it is imposed on the PIO personally.

activity.prompt: Order the RTI process
items: Submit application with fee to the PIO
PIO decides within 30 days (48 hours for life/liberty)
If unsatisfied, first appeal within 30 days
First appellate authority decides
Second appeal to Information Commission within 90 days
Commission may impose penalty under s.20

quiz.q: RTI penalty for 60 days' unjustified delay
quiz.why: 60 days multiplied by ₹250 per day equals ₹15,000, within the ₹25,000 cap.

quiz.q: Time limit when information concerns life or liberty
quiz.why: The proviso to s.7(1) requires a reply within 48 hours.

quiz.q: Answer sheets are information per
quiz.why: The Supreme Court held evaluated answer books are information under the Act.

questions.why: Parliament enacted it in 1985 under Article 323A.

questions.q: Tribunals for taxation and industrial disputes are under
questions.why: Article 323B enables tribunals for such listed matters.

questions.why: The 1861 case distinguished sovereign from commercial functions.

questions.q: D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal laid down
questions.why: It prescribed safeguards for arrest and detention to prevent custodial violence.

questions.q: Arbitrary award of Government contracts was struck down in
questions.why: The Court held the State must act non-arbitrarily even in contracts.

questions.why: Section 20 caps the penalty at ₹25,000.

questions.q: RTI delay of 90 days without reasonable cause — penalty
questions.why: 90 × 250 equals ₹22,500, which is below the cap.

questions.why: The 2019 Constitution Bench so held, subject to exemptions.

questions.q: Lokpal's composition includes
options: Chairperson and up to 8 members, half judicial
questions.why: The 2013 Act provides for a chairperson and up to eight members, at least half judicial.

questions.why: Article 300 governs the capacity of the Union and States to sue and be sued.

uni-llb-adr.title: Alternative Dispute Resolution
uni-llb-adr.description: Negotiation, mediation under the Mediation Act 2023, conciliation, Lok Adalats, section 89 CPC and arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, with drafting and simulation labs. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Concept of ADR, Section 89 CPC and Lok Adalats
courses.summary: Why ADR, the spectrum of methods, constitutional basis (Articles 14, 21, 39A), section 89 CPC as read in Afcons, pre-institution mediation in commercial suits, and Lok Adalats and Permanent Lok Adalats under the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987.
outcomes: Place negotiation, mediation, conciliation and arbitration on the ADR spectrum
Apply the Afcons categories of cases unsuitable for ADR
Explain the nature and finality of a Lok Adalat award
Explain mandatory pre-institution mediation under section 12A Commercial Courts Act

lessons.title: The ADR spectrum and its rationale

story.title: Twenty years for a boundary wall

scenes.text: Two neighbours have litigated over a 2-foot strip of land for twenty years, through three courts.
A retired judge asks them to sit together for two hours. They settle. Why didn't this happen earlier?

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
From least to most formal and binding:
- **Negotiation**: parties themselves, no third party.
- **Mediation**: neutral facilitates; no power to decide; settlement voluntary (Mediation Act 2023).
- **Conciliation**: neutral may propose terms of settlement (Part III, A&C Act 1996).
- **Lok Adalat**: conciliatory forum; award deemed a decree.
- **Arbitration**: private adjudication; binding award enforceable as a decree.
Hybrids: med-arb, arb-med, early neutral evaluation, online dispute resolution (ODR).

steps.title: Rationale and constitutional basis
steps.body: Pendency of cases (over 5 crore across courts), cost, delay, preservation of relationships, confidentiality, party autonomy, expertise. Constitutional anchors: Article 21 (speedy justice – Hussainara Khatoon, 1979), Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), Article 14.

steps.title: Choosing a method
steps.body: Neighbours' boundary dispute: relationship matters, facts simple → mediation. Construction contract worth ₹50 crore with technical issues and an arbitration clause → arbitration. Motor accident claim against insurer → Lok Adalat. Partnership with ongoing business → mediation/conciliation.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Calling a mediator's view a 'decision'. A mediator never decides; only arbitrators and judges adjudicate.

quiz.why: An arbitrator adjudicates and the award binds the parties like a decree.

quiz.why: Article 39A directs the State to secure equal justice and free legal aid, the basis of the Legal Services Authorities Act.

lessons.title: Section 89 CPC and court-annexed ADR

scenes.text: In a family property suit, the judge sees elements of settlement and wants to refer the case to ADR.
Can she refer without the parties' consent?

steps.title: Section 89 and Order X Rules 1A–1C
steps.body: Where it appears that elements of a settlement exist, the court shall formulate terms and refer the dispute to arbitration, conciliation, judicial settlement including Lok Adalat, or mediation (inserted 2002, effective 2002). Salem Advocate Bar Association v Union of India (2003, 2005) upheld it and approved model mediation rules.

steps.title: Afcons Infrastructure v Cherian Varkey (2010)
steps.body: The Supreme Court held: the court need not formulate detailed terms – a summary of disputes suffices. Referral to arbitration and conciliation needs consent of parties; reference to mediation, judicial settlement and Lok Adalat does not. Cases normally unsuitable for ADR: representative suits, election disputes, cases involving prosecution for criminal offences, fraud, forgery, coercion, matters needing protection of courts (minors, persons of unsound mind), suits against the government for declaration of title (in some contexts), cases requiring public interest adjudication.

steps.title: Section 12A Commercial Courts Act 2015
steps.body: A commercial suit not contemplating urgent interim relief shall not be instituted unless the plaintiff exhausts **pre-institution mediation**. In Patil Automation v Rakheja Engineers (2022) the Supreme Court held section 12A mandatory; suits filed in breach are to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 (prospectively from 20 August 2022).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking every section 89 reference needs consent. Afcons says mediation and Lok Adalat references can be made without consent.

Allegation of serious fraud and forgery

quiz.why: Arbitration and conciliation need consent because they rest on agreement; mediation and Lok Adalat referrals do not.

quiz.q: Patil Automation (2022) held that pre-institution mediation under section 12A is

quiz.why: The Supreme Court held section 12A mandatory, applying its ruling prospectively from 20 August 2022.

lessons.title: Lok Adalats and Permanent Lok Adalats

scenes.text: On a National Lok Adalat day, lakhs of cases – cheque bounce, motor accidents, electricity bills – are settled in one day across India.
Can a party who settles later appeal?

steps.title: Legal Services Authorities Act 1987
steps.body:
- **Section 19**: Lok Adalats organised by NALSA/State/District/Taluk authorities; jurisdiction over any case pending before a court or a pre-litigation dispute; not over non-compoundable offences.
- **Section 20**: cognizance on reference by court (with consent of parties or where the court is satisfied that the matter is fit); Lok Adalat shall be guided by principles of justice, equity, fair play.
- **Section 21**: award deemed a **decree of a civil court**; **final and binding**; **no appeal** lies; court fee refunded where a pending case is settled.
- If no settlement, case returns to the court.

steps.title: Permanent Lok Adalat (ss. 22A–22E, 2002)
steps.body: For **public utility services** (transport, postal, telecom, power, water, sanitation, hospitals, insurance, education, housing, as notified). Pecuniary limit: **₹1 crore** (raised from ₹10 lakh in 2015). First tries conciliation; if it fails, it **decides the dispute on merits** (where the offence is not involved). Award final, binding and deemed a decree.

steps.title: State of Punjab v Jalour Singh (2008)
steps.body: A Lok Adalat award without consent of both parties is no award; the remedy against a fraudulent or non-consensual award is a writ petition, not an appeal. Lok Adalats cannot decide cases on merits if parties do not settle (except Permanent Lok Adalats).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying an ordinary Lok Adalat may decide on merits. Only a Permanent Lok Adalat can adjudicate when conciliation fails.

quiz.why: Section 21(2) makes the award final with no appeal; a writ is available only in limited cases such as lack of consent.

quiz.why: The limit was raised to ₹1 crore by notification in 2015.

quiz.q: Lok Adalats cannot deal with
quiz.why: Section 19(5) excludes offences not compoundable under any law.

lessons.title: Lab: Negotiation – interests not positions

scenes.text: Two sisters fight over one orange; their mother cuts it in half. One sister eats the fruit and throws the peel; the other uses the peel for a cake and throws the fruit.
If they had asked 'why', each could have had 100%.

steps.title: Principled negotiation (Fisher & Ury, Getting to Yes)
steps.body:
1. Separate the people from the problem.
2. Focus on **interests**, not positions.
3. Invent options for mutual gain.
4. Insist on **objective criteria** (market value, precedent, expert opinion).
Know your **BATNA** (Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement) and the **ZOPA** (zone of possible agreement).

steps.title: Worked ZOPA
steps.body: Tenant will pay up to ₹32,000/month (her BATNA: another flat at ₹32,000). Landlord will accept no less than ₹28,000 (his BATNA: a vacant flat costs him). ZOPA = ₹28,000–₹32,000. Interests: tenant wants stability (3-year lease); landlord wants reliable payment. Option: ₹30,000 with 3-year lock-in and 5% annual escalation.

steps.title: Lawyer's role
steps.body: Prepare the client's BATNA, gather objective data, and draft a clear settlement agreement once a deal is reached.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Revealing your bottom line early. It anchors the other side at your limit.

quiz.q: Buyer's maximum ₹50 lakh, seller's minimum ₹55 lakh. ZOPA?
quiz.why: The seller's minimum exceeds the buyer's maximum, so there is no overlap unless interests or options change.

quiz.why: Fisher and Ury advise looking behind stated positions to the underlying interests.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Arbitration Agreement, Arbitrability and the Tribunal
courses.summary: Scheme of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, essentials of an arbitration agreement (s. 7), separability, reference by courts (s. 8), arbitrability after Vidya Drolia, appointment of arbitrators (s. 11), independence and impartiality (s. 12, Fifth and Seventh Schedules) and unilateral appointments.
outcomes: Draft a valid arbitration clause with seat, rules and number of arbitrators
Apply the Vidya Drolia fourfold test of non-arbitrability
Explain the scope of court review under sections 8 and 11 after 2015
Identify ineligibility of arbitrators under the Seventh Schedule

lessons.title: The arbitration agreement

scenes.text: Two companies never signed a contract, but exchanged emails agreeing that 'disputes shall be settled by arbitration in Mumbai'.
Is that a valid arbitration agreement?

steps.title: Section 7
steps.body: An agreement to submit to arbitration all or certain disputes which have arisen or may arise in respect of a defined legal relationship, contractual or not. It may be a clause in a contract or a separate agreement. Must be **in writing**: a signed document, an exchange of letters, telex, telegrams or other means of telecommunication **including electronic communication** (2015 amendment), or an exchange of statements of claim and defence where existence is alleged by one and not denied by the other. Reference in a contract to a document containing an arbitration clause incorporates it if the reference makes it part of the contract.

steps.title: Essentials and separability
steps.body: Essentials (K.K. Modi v K.N. Modi, 1998; Jagdish Chander v Ramesh Chander, 2007): intention to be bound by the decision of a private tribunal, after hearing both sides, decision final and binding. Words like 'may be referred to arbitration if parties agree' show no present intention – not an arbitration agreement. **Separability** (s. 16(1)): the clause is independent of the main contract; invalidity of the contract does not automatically invalidate the clause.

steps.title: Model clause
steps.body: 'Any dispute arising out of or in connection with this contract, including any question regarding its existence, validity or termination, shall be referred to and finally resolved by arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 by a sole arbitrator appointed by mutual agreement. The seat of arbitration shall be Mumbai. The language shall be English. The law governing this clause shall be the law of India.'

steps.title: Stamping
steps.body: In re: Interplay between Arbitration Agreements under the A&C Act and the Indian Stamp Act (7-judge bench, 2023): unstamped or insufficiently stamped agreements are not void; stamping objections are for the tribunal, not a ground to refuse reference.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking a signed contract is essential. Email exchanges can satisfy section 7(4)(b).

activity.prompt: Valid arbitration agreement?

items.text: 'Disputes shall be finally resolved by arbitration seated in Delhi'
'Parties may, if they both agree later, go to arbitration'
Arbitration clause agreed by exchange of emails
Oral agreement to arbitrate made over the phone
Clause in an unstamped contract

quiz.q: Under section 7, an arbitration agreement must be
options: In writing, which includes electronic communication
quiz.why: Section 7(3)–(4) require writing and, since 2015, include electronic communication.

quiz.q: 'May be referred to arbitration' with a requirement of further consent was held not an arbitration agreement in
quiz.why: The court held such words show only a possibility of future agreement, not a present binding intention.

quiz.q: Effect of an unstamped arbitration agreement after the 2023 seven-judge ruling
options: Not void; stamping issue for the tribunal
Must be stamped before reference by court
quiz.why: The Court overruled N.N. Global (2023, 5-judge) and held non-stamping is a curable defect.

lessons.title: Arbitrability and reference by courts

scenes.text: A commercial lease has an arbitration clause. The landlord wants eviction; the tenant says eviction can only be ordered by the Rent Controller.
Which disputes cannot go to arbitration?

steps.title: Vidya Drolia v Durga Trading Corp (2020)
Typically non-arbitrable
steps.body: Criminal offences, matrimonial status (divorce), guardianship, insolvency/winding up (in rem), testamentary matters, trust disputes under the Trusts Act (Vimal Kishor Shah, 2016), rent-control tenancy, consumer disputes before consumer fora at the consumer's option (Emaar MGF v Aftab Singh, 2018).

steps.title: Sections 8 and 11 after 2015
steps.body: Section 8: a judicial authority **shall** refer parties to arbitration if a party applies not later than the first statement on the substance, unless it finds that **prima facie no valid arbitration agreement exists**. Section 11(6A): the court confines itself to examining existence of an arbitration agreement (the provision has been omitted by the 2019 amendment, not yet notified on this point; courts follow a limited 'prima facie' review – SBI General Insurance v Krish Spinning, 2024).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying all fraud allegations make a dispute non-arbitrable. Only serious fraud of the kind Ayyasamy and Vidya Drolia describe does.

activity.prompt: Arbitrable or not (Vidya Drolia)?

Divorce petition
Winding up of a company
Lease dispute under the Transfer of Property Act
Eviction under a State rent control Act
Breach of warranty claim between two companies

quiz.q: Vidya Drolia held tenancy disputes under the Transfer of Property Act are
quiz.why: They involve rights in personam; only disputes covered by rent control legislation are excluded.

quiz.q: Under section 8, the application to refer must be made
options: Not later than the first statement on the substance of the dispute
quiz.why: Section 8(1) requires the application before or along with the first statement on the substance.

quiz.q: Which is an action in rem and non-arbitrable?
quiz.why: Insolvency affects creditors at large and requires centralised adjudication.

lessons.title: Constituting the tribunal and arbitrator neutrality

scenes.text: A government contract says disputes will be decided by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Engineer of the employer.
The contractor objects. Can one side choose the arbitrator alone?

steps.title: Appointment (ss. 10–11)
steps.body: Parties are free to determine the number of arbitrators, but not an even number; failing agreement, a sole arbitrator (s. 10). Appointment procedure by agreement; failing that, each party appoints one and the two appoint the presiding arbitrator. If a party fails within 30 days, the **Supreme Court** (international commercial arbitration) or **High Court** (domestic) or its designated institution appoints (s. 11(4)–(6)).

steps.title: Independence and impartiality (s. 12)
steps.body: Prospective arbitrators must disclose circumstances giving justifiable doubts as to independence or impartiality (**Fifth Schedule** grounds; Sixth Schedule form). **Section 12(5)** read with the **Seventh Schedule**: persons with listed relationships (employee, consultant, advisor of a party, etc.) are **ineligible**, unless parties, after disputes arise, waive by an **express agreement in writing**.

steps.title: Unilateral appointments
steps.body: TRF Ltd v Energo Engineering (2017): a person ineligible to be an arbitrator cannot nominate one. **Perkins Eastman v HSCC (2019)**: a party with an interest cannot unilaterally appoint a sole arbitrator. **Central Organisation for Railway Electrification v ECI-SPIC-SMO-MCML (JV) (Constitution Bench, 2024)**: unilateral appointment clauses for sole arbitrators violate equality (Art. 14 for public sector) and s. 18; a clause forcing a party to choose from a curated panel of the other side's nominees is invalid (applied prospectively).

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Chief Engineer is the employer's employee → ineligible under Seventh Schedule; also cannot appoint a sole arbitrator (TRF, Perkins). Contractor should apply under s. 11(6) to the High Court for appointment of an independent arbitrator.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Treating conduct (participating) as waiver of s. 12(5) ineligibility. The proviso needs an express written agreement after disputes arise (Bharat Broadband v United Telecoms, 2019).
