options: No, the number must not be even
quiz.why: Section 10(1) prohibits an even number of arbitrators.

quiz.q: Perkins Eastman (2019) held
options: Unilateral appointment of a sole arbitrator by an interested party is invalid
quiz.why: A party with an interest in the outcome cannot have exclusive power to appoint a sole arbitrator.

quiz.q: Waiver of Seventh Schedule ineligibility requires
options: Express written agreement after disputes arise
quiz.why: The proviso to section 12(5) requires an express agreement in writing subsequent to disputes.

lessons.title: Lab: Draft and audit an arbitration clause

scenes.text: A startup's vendor contract says: 'Disputes may be resolved by arbitration at Delhi or Mumbai by two arbitrators appointed by the Vendor.'
Fix it.

steps.title: Audit
steps.body: Defects: (1) 'may' – weak intention; (2) two venues – unclear seat; (3) two arbitrators – even number (s. 10); (4) appointment by Vendor alone – Perkins/CORE problem; (5) no rules or language; (6) no carve-out for interim relief.

steps.title: Redrafted clause
steps.body:
'1. Any dispute arising out of or in connection with this Agreement shall be finally resolved by arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
2. The tribunal shall consist of three arbitrators: each party shall appoint one arbitrator within 30 days of the notice under section 21, and the two arbitrators shall appoint the presiding arbitrator.
3. The seat of arbitration shall be New Delhi, and courts at New Delhi shall have exclusive supervisory jurisdiction.
4. The language shall be English.
5. Nothing prevents a party from seeking interim relief under section 9.'

steps.title: Seat vs venue
steps.body: BGS SGS Soma JV v NHPC (2019): designation of a 'venue' without contrary indicia is the 'seat', conferring exclusive jurisdiction on courts there.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Naming two cities. Pick one seat to avoid satellite litigation.

quiz.why: A balanced appointment mechanism avoids challenges under Perkins and CORE and section 11 litigation.

quiz.why: Section 9 lets a party approach the court for interim measures before, during or after proceedings (subject to s. 9(3)).

courses.title: Unit 3 · Arbitral Proceedings, Interim Measures and the Award
courses.summary: Kompetenz-kompetenz (s. 16), interim measures by court (s. 9) and tribunal (s. 17), conduct of proceedings (ss. 18–27), time limits (ss. 23(4), 29A, 29B), form and contents of the award (s. 31), interest and costs, and correction of awards (s. 33).
outcomes: Explain the tribunal's power to rule on its own jurisdiction
Compare interim relief under sections 9 and 17
Compute the time limit for making an award under section 29A
List the formal requirements of a valid award and compute post-award interest

lessons.title: Jurisdiction of the tribunal and interim measures

scenes.text: An employer threatens to encash a ₹5 crore bank guarantee. The contractor has just sent an arbitration notice.
The tribunal is not yet formed. Where can the contractor get urgent relief?

steps.title: Section 16 – kompetenz-kompetenz
steps.body: The tribunal may rule on its own jurisdiction, including objections on the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement. Plea of lack of jurisdiction must be raised not later than the statement of defence; plea of exceeding scope as soon as the matter arises. If the tribunal rejects the plea, it continues and makes the award; the party may challenge under section 34 (no immediate appeal). If it accepts the plea, an appeal lies under section 37(2)(a).

steps.title: Interim measures
steps.body:
- **Section 9 (court)**: before, during or after award (but before enforcement): preservation, interim custody, securing amount in dispute, injunction, receiver. If granted before commencement, arbitration must start within **90 days**. Once the tribunal is constituted, the court shall not entertain a s. 9 application unless the remedy under s. 17 is inefficacious (s. 9(3)).
- **Section 17 (tribunal)**: same powers as the court; orders enforceable as if orders of court (2015 amendment). Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings v Future Retail (2021): orders of an emergency arbitrator in institutional arbitration seated in India are enforceable under s. 17(2).

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Contractor: s. 9 application to the court at the seat to restrain encashment. Note: courts rarely injunct encashment of unconditional bank guarantees except for egregious fraud or irretrievable injustice (U.P. State Sugar Corp v Sumac International, 1997). If granted, arbitration must commence within 90 days.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking a party can appeal immediately when the tribunal upholds its own jurisdiction. The remedy is a section 34 challenge after the award.

activity.prompt: Section 9 (court) or section 17 (tribunal) – or both?

items.text: Interim relief before notice of arbitration
Injunction during proceedings where tribunal remedy is efficacious
Relief after the award but before enforcement
Order to preserve goods during hearings

quiz.q: After a court grants interim relief under section 9 before arbitration starts, proceedings must commence within
quiz.why: Section 9(2) requires commencement within 90 days or such time as the court fixes.

quiz.q: If the tribunal rejects a jurisdiction objection, the aggrieved party
options: Challenges the final award under s. 34
quiz.why: Section 16(5)–(6) direct the tribunal to continue, with a challenge only under section 34.

quiz.q: Amazon v Future Retail (2021) concerned
quiz.why: The Supreme Court held emergency arbitrator awards are orders under section 17(1), enforceable under s. 17(2).

lessons.title: Conduct of proceedings and time limits

scenes.text: Arbitrations used to take as long as court cases, with hearings adjourned for years.
The 2015 and 2019 amendments added hard deadlines. How do they work?

steps.title: Core procedure
steps.body:
- **Section 18**: parties treated with equality and given a full opportunity to present their case.
- **Section 19**: tribunal not bound by CPC or Evidence Act; parties free to agree procedure.
- **Section 20**: parties free to agree the place (seat).
- **Section 23**: statement of claim and defence; **s. 23(4)** – to be completed within **6 months** from the arbitrators' receipt of notice of appointment.
- **Section 24**: oral hearings or documents only; hearings day-to-day as far as possible.
- **Section 25**: default – claimant's failure terminates; respondent's failure → proceedings continue.
- **Section 26**: tribunal-appointed expert; **s. 27**: court assistance in taking evidence.

steps.title: Section 29A and 29B
steps.body: Award in domestic arbitrations (and in international commercial arbitration, 'endeavour') within **12 months from completion of pleadings** under s. 23(4). Parties may extend by consent for a further **6 months**. Thereafter only the **court** may extend on sufficient cause; mandate terminates otherwise. Where delay is attributable to the tribunal, the court may reduce fees by up to **5%** for each month of delay. **Section 29B fast-track**: on written agreement, sole arbitrator, documents-only, award within **6 months**.

steps.title: Worked timeline
steps.body: Arbitrator receives notice of appointment on 1 January 2026. Pleadings must be completed within 6 months → by 1 July 2026 (say completed 30 June 2026). Award due within 12 months → by 30 June 2027. Parties extend by consent 6 months → 30 December 2027. Beyond that, court extension under s. 29A(4).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Counting the 12 months from the date of reference. Since 2019 it runs from completion of pleadings.

activity.prompt: Order the domestic arbitration timeline
items: Notice invoking arbitration (s. 21)
Constitution of tribunal
Pleadings within 6 months (s. 23(4))
Hearings and evidence
Award within 12 months of pleadings (s. 29A)
Optional 6-month extension by consent, then court

quiz.q: Pleadings completed on 15 March 2026. Award deadline under section 29A without extension?
quiz.why: The award is due within 12 months from completion of pleadings, i.e. by 15 March 2027.

quiz.q: Fast-track arbitration under section 29B must conclude within
quiz.why: Section 29B requires the award within six months of the tribunal entering on reference.

quiz.q: Section 18 requires
quiz.why: Equality and full opportunity are the core procedural guarantees of arbitration.

lessons.title: The award: form, interest, costs and correction

scenes.text: A tribunal awards ₹1 crore to the claimant but says nothing about post-award interest.
Will the money grow until paid?

steps.title: Section 31
steps.body:
- In writing and **signed** by the members (majority suffices, with reasons for omitted signatures).
- **Reasons** must be stated unless parties agreed otherwise or it is an award on agreed terms (s. 30).
- State **date and place** (seat) of arbitration.
- Signed copy delivered to each party.
- **Interest**: tribunal may award pre-award interest at reasonable rate (s. 31(7)(a)); post-award, unless the award directs otherwise, the sum carries interest at **2% higher than the current rate of interest prevalent** on the date of award (s. 31(7)(b), 2015) – current rate as defined in the Interest Act 1978.
- **Costs** (s. 31A): 'loser pays' as general rule, considering conduct, partial success, frivolous claims.

steps.title: Correction and additional award (s. 33)
steps.body: Within **30 days** of receipt: correct computation, clerical or typographical errors; give interpretation of a specific point (if agreed); make an additional award on claims presented but omitted. Tribunal may correct on its own within 30 days of the award.

steps.title: Worked interest
steps.body: Award ₹1,00,00,000 on 1 April 2026 silent on post-award interest; assume the current rate is 9% p.a. Statutory post-award rate = 9% + 2% = 11% p.a. If paid on 1 April 2027, simple interest = 1,00,00,000 × 11% = ₹11,00,000; total ₹1,11,00,000.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying arbitrators must give reasons in every case. Parties can dispense with reasons, and consent awards need none.

activity.prompt: Order the structure of a reasoned award
items: Parties, arbitration agreement and constitution of tribunal
Procedural history
Issues framed
Evidence and submissions on each issue
Findings with reasons
Operative directions: amount, interest, costs, date, seat, signatures

quiz.q: Post-award interest where the award is silent is
options: 2% above the current rate of interest
quiz.why: Section 31(7)(b) as amended in 2015 provides 2% higher than the current rate prevalent on the date of award.

quiz.q: Time limit to request correction of an award
quiz.why: Section 33(1) allows 30 days from receipt of the award, unless another period is agreed.

quiz.q: An award on agreed terms is made under section
quiz.why: Section 30(2) lets the tribunal record a settlement as an arbitral award on agreed terms.

lessons.title: Lab: Mock arbitration – procedural order no. 1

scenes.text: A sole arbitrator holds a video conference with counsel for a supplier and a buyer.
She must issue Procedural Order No. 1 fixing the roadmap.

steps.title: Contents of PO1
steps.body: Seat and venue; language; applicable procedural rules; timetable for pleadings, document production, witness statements, expert reports; hearing dates; mode (virtual/physical); fees and deposits (Fourth Schedule or agreed); confidentiality (s. 42A); communications protocol; record of disclosure under s. 12.

steps.title: Sample PO1 extract

courses.title: Unit 4 · Setting Aside, Enforcement, Appeals and Foreign Awards
courses.summary: Grounds and limitation for setting aside under section 34, public policy after Ssangyong, modification after Gayatri Balasamy, enforcement and stay under section 36, appeals under section 37, international commercial arbitration, BALCO, and enforcement of New York Convention awards under Part II.
outcomes: List section 34 grounds and compute the limitation period
Explain the narrowed public policy ground and patent illegality
Explain the effect of filing a section 34 petition on enforcement
Apply section 48 refusal grounds to a foreign award

lessons.title: Setting aside an award under section 34

scenes.text: A State corporation receives an adverse award on 10 January 2026 and believes the arbitrator misread the contract.
Can it ask the court to re-decide the case?

steps.title: Grounds (s. 34(2))
steps.body:
(a) The applicant **establishes on the basis of the record of the tribunal** that: (i) a party was under some incapacity; (ii) the agreement is invalid; (iii) no proper notice of appointment or proceedings, or otherwise unable to present its case; (iv) award deals with disputes beyond the scope of submission; (v) composition of tribunal or procedure not in accordance with agreement/Part I.
(b) The court finds that: (i) subject matter not arbitrable; (ii) award is in conflict with the **public policy of India** – only if induced by fraud or corruption or in violation of s. 75/81, in contravention of the **fundamental policy of Indian law**, or in conflict with the **most basic notions of morality or justice** (Explanation 1, 2015). No review on merits (Explanation 2).
**s. 34(2A)**: domestic (non-international) awards may also be set aside for **patent illegality** appearing on the face of the award – but not merely for erroneous application of law or re-appreciation of evidence.

steps.title: Cases
steps.body:
- ONGC v Saw Pipes (2003) – expansive 'patent illegality'; ONGC v Western Geco (2014) and Associate Builders (2015) – broad public policy; legislatively narrowed in 2015.
- **Ssangyong Engineering v NHAI (2019)**: 'fundamental policy' and 'most basic notions of justice' are narrow; a new contract unilaterally created by the tribunal shocks the conscience.
- **Gayatri Balasamy v ISG Novasoft (Constitution Bench, 2025)**: courts under s. 34 have a limited power to modify awards – severing invalid parts, correcting clerical/computational errors, and modifying post-award interest in some cases – but cannot review merits.

steps.title: Limitation (s. 34(3))
steps.body: **3 months** from receipt of the award (or disposal of a s. 33 request), extendable by the court by a further **30 days** on sufficient cause, 'but not thereafter'. Section 5 of the Limitation Act does not apply (Popular Construction, 2001). Petition to be disposed within one year (s. 34(6)); prior notice to other party (s. 34(5)).

steps.title: Worked limitation
steps.body: Award received 10 January 2026. Three months → 10 April 2026. Additional 30 days on sufficient cause → 10 May 2026. A petition filed on 20 May 2026 is barred absolutely.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Arguing that the arbitrator 'misread evidence'. That is a review on merits, excluded by Explanation 2.

activity.prompt: Valid section 34 ground or impermissible merits review?

items.text: Party not given notice of hearings
Tribunal preferred one witness over another
Award decides a dispute not referred
Award induced by corruption of the arbitrator
Court would have interpreted a clause differently

quiz.why: Three months to 1 June 2026, plus a maximum of 30 days, ending about 1 July 2026.

options: Domestic awards (not international commercial arbitration seated in India)
quiz.why: Section 34(2A) applies only to arbitrations other than international commercial arbitrations.

quiz.q: Gayatri Balasamy (2025) held that courts under section 34
options: Have limited power to modify, e.g. severance and clerical errors
quiz.why: The Constitution Bench recognised a narrow power to modify while barring merits review.

lessons.title: Enforcement and appeals (sections 36 and 37)

story.title: Is filing a challenge enough to stop payment?

scenes.text: The losing party files a section 34 petition and tells the winner: 'Now you must wait.'
Since 2015, is that true?

steps.title: Section 36
steps.body: Once the time for s. 34 has expired, the award is enforced under the CPC as if it were a decree. **Filing a s. 34 petition does not by itself stay the award** (s. 36(2), 2015); a separate stay application is needed. For money awards, stay is granted on conditions such as deposit, with regard to CPC provisions (Order XLI Rule 5). The 2021 proviso: unconditional stay where the agreement or award was induced by fraud or corruption (prima facie). BCCI v Kochi Cricket (2018) and Hindustan Construction Co v Union of India (2019) – amended s. 36 applies to pending s. 34 petitions; s. 87 struck down.

steps.title: Section 37 appeals
steps.body: Appeals lie only from orders: refusing to refer under s. 8; granting/refusing s. 9 measures; setting aside or refusing to set aside under s. 34; tribunal orders accepting a s. 16 plea; granting/refusing s. 17 measures. **No second appeal**, but SLP under Article 136 remains. Commercial Courts Act s. 13(1A) for commercial disputes.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Winner may file execution once 3 months pass. Loser seeks stay; court orders stay on deposit of 50% of the awarded amount within 4 weeks, which the winner may withdraw on furnishing security.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking an appeal lies against an order appointing an arbitrator under s. 11. It does not under s. 37.

Order appointing an arbitrator under s. 11

Tribunal rejecting a jurisdiction plea
Tribunal accepting a jurisdiction plea

options: Does not by itself stay the award
quiz.why: Section 36(2) requires a separate stay application and the court may impose conditions.

quiz.q: A second appeal from a section 37 order
options: Is barred, though SLP under Art. 136 is available
quiz.why: Section 37(3) bars second appeals while preserving the Supreme Court's Article 136 jurisdiction.

quiz.q: Hindustan Construction Co (2019) struck down section
quiz.why: Section 87, inserted in 2019 to revive automatic stay for older cases, was held arbitrary.

lessons.title: International commercial arbitration and foreign awards

scenes.text: A Korean supplier wins a SIAC award seated in Singapore against an Indian buyer.
Can the Indian buyer challenge it in Delhi under section 34?

steps.title: Definitions and BALCO
steps.body: **International commercial arbitration** (s. 2(1)(f)): commercial relationship where at least one party is a foreign national/resident, a foreign body corporate, a company with central management abroad, or a foreign government. **Part I** applies where the place of arbitration is in India (s. 2(2)), with ss. 9, 27, 37(1)(b) available for foreign-seated arbitrations unless excluded (2015 proviso). **BALCO v Kaiser Aluminium (2012)** overruled Bhatia International (2002): Part I does not apply to foreign-seated arbitrations (prospectively for agreements after 6 September 2012). PASL Wind Solutions v GE Power (2021): two Indian parties may choose a foreign seat.

steps.title: Part II – New York Convention awards
steps.body: India enforces awards made in a Convention country notified as reciprocating (commercial reservation and reciprocity reservation). Procedure: application with original/certified award and agreement (s. 47). Refusal only on **section 48** grounds: incapacity, invalid agreement, lack of notice/inability to present case, beyond scope, irregular composition/procedure, award not yet binding or set aside at the seat; or non-arbitrability or public policy of India (narrow: fraud/corruption, fundamental policy, basic notions of morality/justice; no merits review). Once enforceable, deemed a decree (s. 49); appeal only from refusal (s. 50). Vijay Karia v Prysmian Cavi (2020): courts must be very slow to refuse enforcement.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Singapore-seated award: Part I s. 34 not available (BALCO); challenge only at the seat (Singapore courts). In India the buyer can only resist enforcement under s. 48 – e.g. if it never received notice. Singapore is a notified Convention country, so enforcement proceeds in the High Court with commercial division jurisdiction.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Applying 'patent illegality' to foreign awards. It applies only to domestic awards under s. 34(2A).

activity.prompt: Ground to refuse enforcement under section 48?

quiz.why: The Supreme Court held nothing in the Act or public policy prevents Indian parties from choosing a foreign seat.

steps.title: Structure

1. Cause title: In the High Court/Commercial Court at the seat; Petition under section 34.
2. Synopsis and list of dates.
3. Facts: contract, clause, disputes, tribunal, award date and receipt date.
4. Limitation statement (within 3 months).
5. Grounds.
6. Prayer: set aside the award (or the severable portion), costs.
7. Interim application under s. 36(2) for stay.
8. Notice under s. 34(5) to the respondent with affidavit of service.

steps.title: Grounds drafted
steps.body:
'A. Because the tribunal decided the claim for loss of profit on a methodology never pleaded nor put to the petitioner, the petitioner was unable to present its case (s. 34(2)(a)(iii)).
B. Because the award, by adopting a formula outside the record, is in conflict with the most basic notions of justice (Ssangyong).
C. Because the award on this head is severable, it may be set aside to that extent (Gayatri Balasamy).'

steps.title: Record-based
steps.body: Since 2019, grounds in s. 34(2)(a) must be established on the basis of the arbitral record; avoid adding new evidence.

steps.title: Common mistake

courses.title: Unit 5 · Mediation Act 2023, Conciliation, ODR, Revision & Exam
courses.summary: The Mediation Act 2023 (pre-litigation mediation, mediators, time limits, mediated settlement agreements and their challenge, community mediation), conciliation under Part III of the 1996 Act, online dispute resolution, a mediation simulation and a cumulative exam.
outcomes: Describe the stages and time limits of mediation under the Mediation Act 2023
Explain the enforceability and grounds of challenge of a mediated settlement agreement
Contrast mediation and conciliation
Conduct a structured mediation using the joint and private session model

lessons.title: The Mediation Act 2023

scenes.text: A homebuyer and a builder disagree over delayed possession.
Under the new Mediation Act, they try mediation before filing anything. What happens if they settle?

steps.title: Key features
steps.body:
- Applies to mediations in India where parties are Indian or (in commercial disputes) at least one party is foreign, or government-related as notified.
- **Pre-litigation mediation** is **voluntary** (s. 5), subject to other laws that make it mandatory (e.g. s. 12A Commercial Courts Act).
- **First Schedule**: disputes not fit for mediation – e.g. criminal offences (except compoundable ones, as permitted), claims against minors/persons of unsound mind, disputes affecting third parties' rights, tax collection, proceedings before NGT and CCI, etc.
- **Time limit** (s. 18): **120 days** from first appearance, extendable by up to **60 days** by consent.
- Party may withdraw after the first two sessions (s. 18 read with s. 24).

steps.title: Mediated Settlement Agreement (MSA)
steps.body: Signed in writing by parties and authenticated by the mediator (s. 19). **Final, binding and enforceable** in accordance with the CPC as if it were a judgment or decree (s. 27). Challenge (s. 28) within **90 days** of receipt (extendable by 90 days) only on: **fraud, corruption, impersonation**, or mediation in a dispute not fit for mediation.

steps.title: Institutions
steps.body: Mediation Council of India (s. 31) regulates mediators and mediation service providers; online mediation permitted (s. 30); **community mediation** (s. 43) for disputes likely to affect peace and harmony among residents of a locality, with a panel of three mediators. Confidentiality and privilege protected (s. 22–23).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking an MSA can be challenged on merits like an award. Section 28 grounds are limited to fraud, corruption, impersonation and non-mediable subject matter.

activity.prompt: Order a pre-litigation mediation under the 2023 Act
items: Party approaches a mediation service provider or court-annexed centre
Mediator appointed and discloses conflicts
First joint session within the 120-day window begins
Joint and private sessions
Mediated settlement agreement signed and authenticated
Registration (optional) and enforcement as a decree

quiz.q: A mediated settlement agreement can be challenged on
options: Fraud, corruption, impersonation or non-mediable subject
quiz.why: Section 28 lists only these limited grounds, protecting finality.

quiz.q: Pre-litigation mediation under section 5 of the Mediation Act is
options: Voluntary, unless another law mandates it
quiz.why: Parliament made it voluntary in the final Act, while keeping s. 12A Commercial Courts Act mandatory.

lessons.title: Conciliation and online dispute resolution

scenes.text: An infrastructure company and a PSU appoint a conciliator under their contract.
The conciliator proposes terms. Both sign. Is it binding?

steps.title: Part III (ss. 61–81)
steps.body: Commencement when the other party accepts the invitation (s. 62). Conciliator assists parties independently and impartially, guided by objectivity, fairness and justice (s. 67), and may make proposals for settlement. **Settlement agreement** signed by parties has the same status and effect as an arbitral award on agreed terms under s. 30 (s. 74). Confidentiality (s. 75); no arbitral or judicial proceedings during conciliation, except to preserve rights (s. 77); conciliator cannot act as arbitrator or witness in the same dispute (s. 80); evidence of proposals inadmissible (s. 81). The Mediation Act 2023 omits ss. 61–81 for future proceedings and treats conciliation as mediation (see s. 61 amendments).

steps.title: ODR
steps.body: Online dispute resolution uses technology for negotiation, mediation and arbitration; NITI Aayog's ODR Policy Plan (2021); Mediation Act s. 30 recognises online mediation; s. 7 of the 1996 Act accepts electronic communication; virtual hearings widely used since 2020. Issues: digital divide, identity verification, data security, confidentiality.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Conciliation settlement signed by both: enforceable as an arbitral award on agreed terms (s. 74 read with s. 36). Note: after the Mediation Act 2023, new conciliations are to be conducted as mediations; check the transitional position for pending matters.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Letting the conciliator later act as the arbitrator in the same dispute. Section 80 prohibits it unless parties agree otherwise.

activity.prompt: Mediation, conciliation or arbitration feature?

items.text: Neutral facilitates; no proposals required
Neutral may propose terms of settlement
Neutral decides and issues a binding award
Settlement has the status of an award on agreed terms (s. 74)
Settlement challengeable only for fraud, corruption, impersonation

quiz.q: A conciliation settlement has the status of
options: An arbitral award on agreed terms
quiz.why: Section 74 equates it with an award on agreed terms under section 30.

quiz.q: Can a conciliator act as arbitrator in the same dispute?
quiz.why: Section 80 bars it to preserve candour in conciliation, subject to party agreement.

quiz.q: Online mediation is recognised in the Mediation Act 2023 under section
quiz.why: Section 30 allows online mediation, including pre-litigation mediation, using secure electronic means.

lessons.title: Lab: Mediation simulation – the family business

scenes.text: Two brothers co-own a 40-year-old sweet shop. The elder wants to sell; the younger wants to expand. They have stopped talking.
You are the mediator.

steps.title: Stages
steps.body:
1. **Opening statement**: introduce, explain process, confidentiality, voluntariness, ground rules.
2. **Parties' statements**: each speaks without interruption.
3. **Joint discussion**: identify issues and interests.
4. **Private sessions (caucus)**: explore interests, BATNA, reality-test, keep confidences unless permitted.
5. **Option generation and negotiation**.
6. **Agreement**: draft clear, specific, implementable terms.

steps.title: Interests and options
steps.body:
Elder: needs money for daughter's education and retirement. Younger: wants to keep the family brand and expand. Options: younger buys elder's share in instalments at a valuer-fixed price; elder keeps a 10% royalty on brand for 5 years; elder retains honorary chair role; bank loan for the buy-out.
Draft term: 'B2 shall pay B1 ₹60,00,000, being the value fixed by the agreed valuer, in 24 equal monthly instalments of ₹2,50,000 commencing 1 January 2027.' (24 × 2,50,000 = 60,00,000.)

steps.title: Mediator skills
steps.body: Active listening, reframing ('You want to be respected for building the shop' instead of 'He's greedy'), open questions, summarising, reality-testing.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Disclosing caucus information to the other side without consent – this breaches confidentiality and trust.

lessons.title: Lab: Article 14 – is the classification reasonable?

story.title: The scheme for some, not all

scenes.text: A state announces a free-laptop scheme only for students of government colleges in rural districts. A student from an urban government college challenges it.
The state says rural students need more help. Is this valid classification?

steps.title: Equality before the law and equal protection
steps.body: Article 14 forbids arbitrary state action. The state may classify if there is an **intelligible differentia** distinguishing those grouped from others and the differentia has a **rational nexus** with the object of the law (State of West Bengal v Anwar Ali Sarkar and later cases). In E.P. Royappa (1974) the Supreme Court said arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body:
- Differentia: rural district colleges versus urban ones
- Object: reduce the digital divide
- Nexus: rural students have less access, so the nexus is plausible

The court would probably uphold it unless the classification is arbitrary or unevenly applied.

steps.title: Structure your answer
steps.body: State the rule, state the test, apply each limb, conclude.

activity.prompt: Order the Article 14 test
items: Identify the classification made by the law
Ask whether there is an intelligible differentia
Ask whether the differentia has a rational nexus with the object
Check for manifest arbitrariness
Conclude whether the law is valid

lessons.title: Lab: Article 19 and the limits of free speech

scenes.text: A government orders a social media post criticising a minister to be removed under a law that punishes offensive messages.
The poster argues the law is too vague. In 2015 the Supreme Court dealt with a similar law.

steps.title: Freedoms and restrictions
steps.body:
Article 19(1)(a) protects speech and expression; 19(1)(b) to (g) protect assembly, association, movement, residence and profession. Reasonable restrictions are permitted only on the grounds listed in 19(2) to 19(6). For speech these include sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence.

In Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015) the Court struck down section 66A of the IT Act as vague and over-broad, distinguishing discussion, advocacy and incitement.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: A restriction must fall within a listed ground. Embarrassing the government is not a ground.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Read the task once fully. Note what 'done' looks like, then work step by step. If you get stuck, use the hint — then try again without it.

steps.title: From A.K. Gopalan to Maneka Gandhi
steps.body: Article 21: no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. In **Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978)** the Court held the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable, and Articles 14, 19 and 21 are linked. Since then Article 21 has covered the right to live with dignity, privacy, a clean environment, speedy trial, legal aid and more. **K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017)** held privacy to be a fundamental right. Article 21A gives free and compulsory education to children from 6 to 14.

story.title: The amendment that tried to oust the courts

scenes.text: Parliament passes a constitutional amendment saying no court may question certain laws. A citizen files a petition.
Which court, which article, and which writ?

steps.title: Writs and basic structure
steps.body:
Under Article 32 the Supreme Court and under Article 226 the High Courts issue writs: **habeas corpus** (produce the detained person), **mandamus** (command to perform a public duty), **certiorari** (quash a decision of a lower body), **prohibition** (stop proceedings) and **quo warranto** (by what authority an office is held).

In **Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973)** the Court held that Parliament's power under Article 368 does not allow it to alter the basic structure, which includes judicial review, supremacy of the Constitution and the rule of law. Minerva Mills (1980) reinforced this.

steps.title: Three kinds of jurisdiction
steps.body:
- **Subject matter**: civil courts hear all suits of a civil nature unless barred (section 9)
- **Pecuniary**: the value of the suit decides which court tries it, fixed by state law
- **Territorial**: the suit is filed where the defendant resides or carries on business, or where the cause of action arises (section 20)

Immovable property suits are filed where the property lies (sections 16 to 18).

steps.title: Pleadings
steps.body:
A suit starts with a **plaint** (Order VII): court name, plaintiff and defendant details, facts constituting the cause of action, jurisdiction, valuation and court fee, limitation, reliefs claimed and verification. The defendant files a **written statement** (Order VIII) within 30 days, extendable up to 90 days, admitting or denying each allegation specifically, with any set-off or counterclaim.

An Order VII Rule 11 application seeks rejection of a plaint, for example where no cause of action is disclosed or the suit is barred by law.

steps.title: Barriers to repeat litigation
steps.body:
- **Res sub judice (section 10)**: a later suit on the same matter in issue between the same parties is stayed while the earlier suit is pending
- **Res judicata (section 11)**: a matter already finally decided between the same parties cannot be tried again

**Interim relief**: under Order XXXIX the court may grant a temporary injunction to preserve the position if the plaintiff shows a prima facie case, balance of convenience and irreparable injury.

steps.title: After judgment

Remedies: first appeal on facts and law (section 96); second appeal only on a substantial question of law (section 100); review by the same court (section 114, Order XLVII); revision by the High Court (section 115). **Execution** is under Order XXI: attachment and sale of property, arrest and detention, garnishee orders or delivery of possession. Limitation Act, 1963 sets time limits for suits and appeals.

steps.title: How to answer

rounds.q: What are the essentials of a valid contract under the Indian Contract Act?
rounds.model: Section 10 says agreements are contracts if made by free consent of competent parties for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and not expressly declared void. Writing and registration are needed only where a particular law requires them. I would test each element against the facts, for example capacity of a minor or coercion.
followups: What is the effect of a minor's agreement?

rounds.q: Explain the difference between strict liability and absolute liability.
rounds.model: Strict liability from Rylands v Fletcher applies to escape of a dangerous thing but allows exceptions such as act of God. In M.C. Mehta the Supreme Court evolved absolute liability for hazardous enterprises with no exceptions and compensation linked to the enterprise's capacity.
followups: Which case involved the oleum gas leak?

rounds.q: A police officer refuses to register an FIR for a cognizable offence. What can the complainant do under the BNSS?
points: send information to the superintendent of police
rounds.model: The complainant can send the information in writing to the Superintendent of Police, and if still not acted upon can approach a magistrate to direct investigation. The complainant may also use a zero FIR at any station or give information electronically. I would document the refusal and advise accordingly.

rounds.q: Which writ would you seek to challenge an order of a tribunal that exceeded its jurisdiction, and why?
rounds.model: Certiorari under Article 226 or 32 allows the High Court or Supreme Court to quash an order that is without jurisdiction or against natural justice. I would also check alternative remedies.

rounds.q: Why law, and what area do you want to practise in?

story.title: The client who wants to lie

scenes.text: A client asks you to submit a document you know is backdated.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Professional ethics
steps.body: Advocates owe duties to the court first, then to the client. They must not mislead the court, fabricate evidence or breach confidentiality except as the law allows. The Bar Council of India Rules set standards of professional conduct.

steps.title: Approach
steps.body: Show calm, principle and a practical alternative.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

rounds.q: Your client wants you to file a backdated document. What do you do?
rounds.model: I would refuse, explaining that filing a backdated document misleads the court, may be forgery, and risks the client's case and my licence. I would offer lawful alternatives, such as explaining the real chronology. If the client insists, I would withdraw from the matter.
followups: What if the client says everyone does it?

rounds.q: You discover a senior's citation is wrong the night before arguments. What do you do?
rounds.model: I would verify the citation carefully, then tell the senior privately with the correct authority and a one-line note, so the court is not misled. It protects the client and the senior's credibility.
followups: How would you phrase it politely?

rounds.q: How would you explain a 3-year limitation period to a worried client?
rounds.model: I would say: you generally have three years from the date your right to sue arose, but the exact date depends on the case, so please bring all documents this week so we can calculate it and file in time. I would avoid jargon and confirm the date in writing.
followups: What if the period has just expired?

rounds.q: Describe a time you worked under pressure on a deadline.
rounds.model: In a moot preparation our co-researcher left a week before submission. I divided the remaining issues, set daily checkpoints and proofread citations. We submitted on time and I learned to plan buffers.

rounds.q: Where do you see yourself in five years?
rounds.model: I want to be a confident litigator who drafts well, argues effectively and handles matters independently, while continuing to learn from seniors and serve clients ethically.
followups: Which skill do you most need to build?

lessons.title: Company as a separate legal person

scenes.text: Aron Salomon converts his shoe business into a company, holding almost all shares himself and taking secured debentures.
The company fails. Unsecured creditors say Salomon and the company are the same person.

steps.title: Definition and features
steps.body:
**s.2(20)**: 'company' means a company incorporated under the 2013 Act or any previous company law.
Features: (1) **separate legal entity**; (2) **limited liability** (by shares or guarantee) or unlimited; (3) **perpetual succession** – members may come and go; (4) **common seal** (now optional after 2015 amendment); (5) **separate property**; (6) **transferability of shares** (restricted in private companies); (7) capacity to **sue and be sued**.

steps.title: Salomon v A. Salomon & Co Ltd (1897, HL)
steps.body: Once validly incorporated, a company is a distinct person from its members, even if one person holds nearly all shares. Salomon as secured debenture-holder was entitled to be paid first. Indian application: **Lee v Lee's Air Farming (1961, PC)** – a controlling director could also be an employee of his company; **Bacha F. Guzdar v CIT (1955, SC)** – shareholders do not own company property.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body:
Company assets ₹10 lakh; Salomon's secured debentures ₹10 lakh; unsecured creditors ₹7 lakh.
1. Secured creditor paid first from secured assets → ₹10 lakh to Salomon.
2. Nothing left for unsecured creditors.
3. Salomon is not personally liable – shareholders' liability is limited to unpaid share value (his shares were fully paid).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying shareholders own the company's assets – they own shares, the company owns the assets.

quiz.q: Salomon's case established
quiz.why: The House of Lords held the company was a distinct person from Salomon.

quiz.q: Shareholders do not own company property per
quiz.why: The Supreme Court held a shareholder has no interest in the company's property as such.

quiz.why: The company's existence does not depend on who its members are.

lessons.title: Lifting the corporate veil

scenes.text: Horne, bound by a non-compete covenant, sets up a company run by his wife to solicit his ex-employer's customers.
The ex-employer asks the court to look behind the company.

steps.title: Judicial grounds
steps.body:
1. **Fraud or improper conduct / sham** – Gilford Motor Co v Horne (1933): company was a 'mere cloak'; injunction against both.
2. **Evasion of law / taxes** – Dinshaw Maneckjee Petit (Bombay HC 1927): company formed only to avoid tax.
3. **Enemy character** – Daimler Co v Continental Tyre (1916).
4. **Agency or single economic unit** (applied cautiously).
5. **Public interest** – LIC v Escorts (1986, SC): veil may be lifted where statute requires or for fraud, evasion of taxes or welfare legislation.
6. **Vodafone International v Union of India (2012)**: veil lifting only if the structure is a sham or tax avoidance device.

steps.title: Statutory grounds (2013 Act examples)
steps.body:
- **s.7(7)**: incorporation by furnishing false information – Tribunal may order removal of name or make members liable without limit.
- **s.34–35**: misstatement in prospectus.
- **s.339**: fraudulent conduct of business on winding up – personal liability.
- **s.447**: punishment for fraud.
- Officer in default provisions (s.2(60)).

steps.title: Gilford v Horne
steps.body:
1. Horne bound personally by covenant.
2. Company formed to evade the covenant → sham.
3. Court ignored the corporate form and restrained both Horne and the company.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating veil-lifting as routine – it is an exception to Salomon.

activity.prompt: Tick recognised grounds for lifting the corporate veil
items: Company used to commit fraud
Company formed to evade tax
Determining enemy character in wartime
Statutory provisions on fraudulent trading

quiz.q: Gilford Motor Co v Horne involved
options: A company used to evade a non-compete covenant
quiz.why: The company was a cloak for Horne's breach of covenant.

quiz.q: Enemy character case
quiz.why: The House of Lords looked at the German controllers to determine enemy character.

quiz.q: Fraudulent conduct of business on winding up is in
quiz.why: Section 339 imposes personal liability on persons knowingly party to fraudulent trading.

lessons.title: Kinds of companies

scenes.text: A solo software developer, a family of five, a listed manufacturer, and an NGO each want to incorporate.
Which type suits each?

steps.title: By members and access
steps.body:
- **Private company** (s.2(68)): restricts transfer of shares; members limited to **200** (excluding employees/ex-employees); prohibits invitation to public to subscribe. Minimum 2 members, 2 directors.
- **Public company** (s.2(71)): not private; minimum **7 members**, **3 directors**. A subsidiary of a public company is deemed public.
- **One Person Company (OPC)** (s.2(62)): one member, natural person and Indian citizen (resident rules apply); must nominate a nominee.
- **Small company** (s.2(85)): private company with paid-up capital and turnover below limits notified (currently up to ₹4 crore paid-up and ₹40 crore turnover, as amended in 2022).

steps.title: Other classifications
steps.body:
- By liability: **limited by shares**, **limited by guarantee**, **unlimited**.
- **Section 8 company**: for charitable objects; profits applied to objects; no dividend.
- **Holding and subsidiary** (s.2(46), s.2(87)): control of composition of board or more than one-half of total voting power.
- **Government company** (s.2(45)): ≥51% paid-up capital held by Central/State Governments.
- **Foreign company** (s.2(42)), **listed company** (s.2(52)), **associate company** (s.2(6)).

steps.title: Matching
steps.body:
Solo developer → OPC.
Family of five → private limited company (two directors minimum).
Listed manufacturer → public company (7 members, 3 directors; listing compliance).
NGO → Section 8 company (licence from Central Government).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying a private company can have 50 members max – the 2013 Act raised it to 200.

activity.prompt: Order minimum directors from fewest to most
items: One Person Company – 1 director
Private company – 2 directors
Public company – 3 directors

quiz.q: Maximum members of a private company
quiz.why: Section 2(68) limits members to 200, excluding employees.

quiz.q: A Government company requires Government shareholding of at least
quiz.why: Section 2(45) defines it as one where Governments hold not less than 51% of paid-up share capital.

quiz.q: Section 8 companies may
quiz.why: They must apply profits to their objects and are prohibited from paying dividends.

lessons.title: Promoters, pre-incorporation contracts and incorporation

scenes.text: A promoter signs a 5-year office lease 'for and on behalf of XYZ Pvt Ltd (proposed)' a month before incorporation.
After incorporation the company refuses to pay rent. Who is liable?

steps.title: Promoters
steps.body: A **promoter** (s.2(69)) is a person named as such in a prospectus or annual return, or who has control over the company's affairs, or on whose advice the board is accustomed to act (professional advisers excepted). Promoters stand in a **fiduciary position**: they must not make secret profits and must disclose interests (Erlanger v New Sombrero Phosphate, 1878).

steps.title: Pre-incorporation contracts
steps.body: A company cannot contract before it exists, nor ratify such a contract (Kelner v Baxter, 1866: promoters personally liable). In India, the **Specific Relief Act, 1963 ss.15(h) and 19(e)** allow the company to enforce, and to be bound by, a pre-incorporation contract if it was **warranted by the terms of incorporation** and the company **accepted** it after incorporation and communicated acceptance.

steps.title: Incorporation steps (s.7)
steps.body:
1. Reserve name (RUN / SPICe+ Part A).
2. Draft memorandum and articles.
3. File SPICe+ with declarations, subscribers' and directors' details, registered office proof.
4. Registrar issues **certificate of incorporation** with **CIN**; it is **conclusive evidence** of incorporation.
5. Commencement of business declaration within 180 days (s.10A) for companies having share capital.

steps.title: The lease
steps.body:
1. Company not in existence when signed → cannot be party.
2. Common law: promoter personally liable (Kelner v Baxter).
3. Indian position: if the lease was warranted by the company's objects and the company adopted it after incorporation, it would be enforceable by and against the company (SRA ss.15(h), 19(e)). Since the company refuses, the promoter remains liable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying a company can 'ratify' a pre-incorporation contract – ratification needs an existing principal; Indian law uses adoption/acceptance under the SRA.

activity.prompt: Order incorporation steps
items: Reserve the company name
Draft memorandum and articles
File incorporation form with declarations and documents
Registrar issues certificate of incorporation with CIN
File declaration for commencement of business within 180 days

quiz.q: Promoters are personally liable on pre-incorporation contracts per
quiz.why: In Kelner v Baxter the promoters who signed for a non-existent company were held personally liable.

quiz.q: Certificate of incorporation is
quiz.why: Section 7(7) context and settled law treat it as conclusive of registration.

quiz.q: Commencement of business declaration time limit
quiz.why: Section 10A requires filing within 180 days of incorporation.

questions.why: The Privy Council recognised two separate persons: Lee and his company.

questions.why: The Companies (Amendment) Act, 2015 made the common seal optional.

questions.why: Section 3 requires seven persons to form a public company.

options: A natural person and Indian citizen
questions.why: The rules require an OPC member to be a natural person and Indian citizen.

questions.q: Veil may be lifted for tax evasion, as in
questions.why: The company was a device to avoid tax and was disregarded.

questions.q: LIC v Escorts (1986) addressed
questions.why: The Court listed situations where the veil may be pierced.

questions.q: Subsidiary of a public company is
questions.why: Section 2(71) proviso deems such a subsidiary to be a public company.

questions.q: Promoter's secret profit case
questions.why: Erlanger required promoters to disclose profits to an independent board.

questions.q: Indian law allowing enforcement of pre-incorporation contracts
questions.why: These provisions let a company enforce and be bound by adopted pre-incorporation contracts.

options: More than one-half of total voting power or board composition
questions.why: Section 2(87) defines subsidiary by control of board composition or majority voting power.

options: Structure is a sham or tax-avoidance device
questions.why: The Court respected genuine corporate structures absent sham.

questions.why: Members undertake to contribute up to the guaranteed amount on winding up.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Memorandum, articles, key doctrines and prospectus
courses.summary: Contents and alteration of the memorandum, the doctrine of ultra vires, articles of association and their binding effect, constructive notice and indoor management, and the law on prospectus and liability for misstatements.
outcomes: List the clauses of a memorandum under s.4
Apply the ultra vires doctrine (Ashbury)
Explain the binding effect of articles under s.10
Apply constructive notice and the Turquand rule with its exceptions
Identify civil and criminal liability for prospectus misstatements (ss.34–35)

lessons.title: Memorandum of association and ultra vires

scenes.text: Ashbury Railway Carriage Co, formed to make and sell railway carriages, contracts to finance construction of a railway in Belgium.
Shareholders even approve it. Later the company repudiates the contract.

steps.title: Clauses (s.4)
steps.body:
1. **Name clause** (ending 'Limited' or 'Private Limited').
2. **Registered office clause** (State).
3. **Objects clause**.
4. **Liability clause**.
5. **Capital clause** (for companies with share capital).
6. **Subscription/association clause**; for OPC, **nominee** clause.
Alteration: s.13 – special resolution; change of registered office between States needs Central Government (Regional Director) approval; change of name needs Central Government approval (delegated to Registrar).

steps.title: Doctrine of ultra vires
steps.body: An act beyond the objects clause is **ultra vires** and **void ab initio**; it cannot be ratified even by all shareholders (**Ashbury Railway Carriage & Iron Co v Riche, 1875, HL**). Consequences: injunction by members; directors personally liable; property acquired ultra vires may be held by the company; the other party may claim restitution in equity. Indian acceptance: **A. Lakshmanaswami Mudaliar v LIC (1963)** – donation of company funds outside objects was ultra vires.

steps.title: Ashbury applied
steps.body:
1. Objects: make and sell carriages.
2. Financing railway construction – not in objects, not incidental.
3. Act ultra vires → void; shareholder approval cannot cure it.
Modern drafting: broad objects clauses reduce ultra vires disputes, but the doctrine survives in India.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing acts ultra vires the company (void) with acts ultra vires directors (ratifiable by members).

activity.prompt: Tick the clauses of a memorandum
items: Name clause
Registered office clause
Objects clause
Liability clause
Capital clause

quiz.q: An act ultra vires the company is
quiz.why: Ashbury held such acts void ab initio and incapable of ratification.

quiz.q: Alteration of objects clause requires
quiz.why: Section 13 requires a special resolution to alter the memorandum.

quiz.q: Indian case applying ultra vires to donations
quiz.why: The Supreme Court held a donation outside objects to be ultra vires.

lessons.title: Articles of association and their binding effect

scenes.text: A company's articles say Eley shall be its solicitor for life. He also becomes a member.
The company appoints another solicitor. Eley sues on the articles.

steps.title: Articles (s.5)
steps.body: Articles contain regulations for the internal management – shares, transfer, meetings, directors, dividends, accounts. Model articles in **Table F** (company limited by shares) of Schedule I apply where not excluded. **Entrenchment** provisions (s.5(3)) can make alteration conditional on more restrictive procedures. Alteration: **special resolution** (s.14); must be bona fide for the benefit of the company as a whole (Allen v Gold Reefs of West Africa, 1900) and cannot override the Act or memorandum.

steps.title: Binding effect (s.10)
steps.body: Memorandum and articles bind the company and members as if signed by each member – a contract between company and members **in their capacity as members**. They do not bind the company to outsiders: **Eley v Positive Government Security Life Assurance (1876)** – Eley could not enforce the solicitor clause because it concerned him as an outsider, not as a member.

steps.title: Applying to Eley
steps.body:
1. Right claimed: employment as solicitor – an outsider right.
2. s.10 contract covers membership rights only.
3. Eley fails on the articles; he needs a separate contract to sue.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming articles can override the memorandum – the memorandum prevails.

activity.prompt: Tick matters usually dealt with in the articles
items: Transfer and transmission of shares
Calling and conduct of general meetings
Appointment and powers of directors
Declaration of dividends

quiz.q: Articles bind the company and members
quiz.why: Section 10 creates a statutory contract concerning membership rights.

quiz.q: Eley's case shows that articles
options: Do not give outsiders enforceable rights
quiz.why: Eley could not enforce an outsider right contained in the articles.

quiz.q: Alteration of articles must be
options: Bona fide for the benefit of the company as a whole
quiz.why: Allen v Gold Reefs set the bona fide benefit test.

lessons.title: Constructive notice and indoor management

scenes.text: A company's articles allow directors to borrow on bonds if authorised by a general meeting resolution. Directors issue a bond to Turquand without such a resolution.
Turquand sues on the bond.

steps.title: Constructive notice
steps.body: Anyone dealing with a company is deemed to know the contents of its **public documents** (memorandum, articles) filed with the Registrar. So outsiders cannot plead ignorance of limits in them. (The 2013 Act does not expressly abolish it; courts still apply it, though its practical force is reduced by online filings.)

steps.title: Indoor management (Royal British Bank v Turquand, 1856)
steps.body:
An outsider acting in **good faith** need not inquire into **internal proceedings**; he may assume internal requirements (e.g., resolutions, quorum) were complied with. Exceptions:
1. **Knowledge of irregularity** (Howard v Patent Ivory, 1888).
2. **Negligence / suspicious circumstances** – failure to inquire when put on inquiry (Anand Bihari Lal v Dinshaw & Co, 1942).
3. **Forgery** – void (Ruben v Great Fingall Consolidated, 1906).
4. Acts beyond the apparent authority of the officer, where no representation.

steps.title: Turquand succeeds
steps.body:
1. Articles (public) allowed borrowing with a resolution → Turquand had constructive notice that a resolution was needed.
2. Whether a resolution was passed is an internal matter → he could assume it.
3. He acted in good faith → company bound.
If the bond had been forged by the secretary, Turquand would lose (Ruben).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating indoor management as protecting insiders – directors with knowledge cannot rely on it.

activity.prompt: Order the analysis when an outsider deals with a company
items: Check public documents for the limit (constructive notice)
Is the requirement internal (resolution, quorum)?
Did the outsider act in good faith without knowledge of irregularity?
Were there suspicious circumstances or forgery?
Decide if the company is bound

quiz.q: Indoor management protects
quiz.why: The Turquand rule protects bona fide outsiders from internal irregularities.

quiz.q: Forgery is an exception per
quiz.why: A forged document is a nullity and binds no one.

quiz.q: Constructive notice covers
options: Public documents like memorandum and articles
quiz.why: Outsiders are deemed to know the registered public documents.

lessons.title: Prospectus and liability for misstatements

scenes.text: A prospectus claims a firm's plant 'is operating at full capacity' when it has been shut for three months.
Investors who subscribed lose 40% when the truth emerges.

steps.title: Prospectus
steps.body: **s.2(70)**: any document described or issued as a prospectus inviting offers from the public for subscription or purchase of securities, including a **red herring prospectus** (s.32; lacks price/quantity details), **shelf prospectus** (s.31) and **abridged prospectus**. Contents under s.26 and SEBI (ICDR) Regulations. **Deemed prospectus** (s.25): offer for sale through an issuing house.

steps.title: Liability
steps.body:
- **Criminal (s.34)**: an untrue or misleading statement, or inclusion/omission likely to mislead → every person authorising issue liable under **s.447** (fraud), unless he proves the statement was immaterial or he believed it true with reasonable grounds, or the omission was necessary.
- **Civil (s.35)**: subscribers who suffer loss can claim compensation from directors, persons named as directors, promoters, persons authorising issue, and experts. Defences: withdrawal of consent before issue, issue without knowledge and prompt public notice.
- **Fraudulent inducement (s.36)**.
- Common law: rescission for misrepresentation; deceit (Derry v Peek, 1889, required fraud).

steps.title: The rosy IPO
steps.body:
1. 'Operating at full capacity' is untrue and material.
2. Investors relied and lost → civil claim under s.35 against directors and promoters.
3. Those who authorised issue face s.34 read with s.447 unless they prove reasonable belief.
4. A director who withdrew consent before issue has a defence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking literal truth is enough – a true statement misleading by omission also counts (R v Kylsant, 1932).

activity.prompt: Tick persons who can be civilly liable under s.35
items: Directors at the time of issue
Persons named as directors with consent
Promoters
Persons who authorised the issue
Experts whose statements were included

quiz.q: Criminal liability for misstatement in prospectus
quiz.why: Section 34 makes misstatement punishable under s.447.

quiz.q: A prospectus without price and quantity details is
quiz.why: Section 32 describes the red herring prospectus.

quiz.q: Misleading by omission was held punishable in
quiz.why: Lord Kylsant was convicted for a prospectus that was literally true but misleading.

questions.why: Section 4 lists the objects clause in the memorandum.

questions.q: Model articles for a company limited by shares
questions.why: Schedule I Table F contains the model articles for share-limited companies.

questions.q: Entrenchment provisions are under
questions.why: Section 5(3) allows articles to contain entrenchment provisions.

questions.q: Shift of registered office from one State to another requires approval of
questions.why: Section 13(4) requires Central Government approval for inter-State shift.

questions.q: Royal British Bank v Turquand laid down
questions.why: Turquand protects outsiders from internal irregularities.

questions.q: Knowledge of irregularity exception case
questions.why: Directors who knew of the irregularity could not rely on the rule.

questions.q: Shelf prospectus is in
questions.why: Section 31 permits shelf prospectus for multiple issues.

questions.q: Deemed prospectus arises in
options: Offer for sale through an issuing house
questions.why: Section 25 treats a document of offer for sale as a prospectus.

questions.why: The House of Lords held deceit requires knowing or reckless falsity.

questions.q: Allen v Gold Reefs is about
questions.why: It set the bona fide for the benefit of the company test.

questions.q: An act ultra vires directors but within the company's objects
questions.why: Members may ratify acts within the company's powers but beyond directors' authority.

questions.why: Section 34 makes persons liable under s.447.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Share capital, debentures, charges and dividends
courses.summary: Kinds of share capital, further issue (rights, preferential, ESOP, bonus), buy-back with worked limits, transfer and transmission, debentures and registration of charges, and declaration and payment of dividends with computations.
outcomes: Distinguish equity and preference shares and their rights
Explain rights issue, bonus issue and sources of bonus
Compute buy-back limits under s.68
State the time limits for registering charges
Compute dividend and apply ss.123–127 timelines

lessons.title: Kinds of shares and further issue (ss.43, 55, 62, 63)

scenes.text: A listed company needs ₹50 crore and wants to give existing shareholders the first chance.
It also wants to reward shareholders by capitalising reserves.

steps.title: Kinds (s.43)
steps.body:
- **Equity shares** – with voting rights, or with differential rights as to dividend/voting.
- **Preference shares** – preferential right to fixed dividend and to repayment of capital on winding up.
**s.55**: no irredeemable preference shares; redeemable within **20 years** (up to 30 years for infrastructure projects, with annual redemption of at least 10% after the 21st year); redemption out of profits or fresh issue; Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) created when out of profits.

steps.title: Further issue (s.62) and bonus (s.63)
steps.body:
- **Rights issue** (s.62(1)(a)): offer to existing equity holders in proportion; open for 15–30 days; renounceable unless articles say otherwise.
- **ESOP** (s.62(1)(b)): by special resolution.
- **Preferential/other persons** (s.62(1)(c)): special resolution, valuation report.
- **Bonus** (s.63): out of **free reserves**, **securities premium**, or **CRR**; **not** out of revaluation reserves; must be authorised by articles and recommended by board, approved in general meeting; cannot be issued in lieu of dividend; partly paid shares must be made fully paid.

steps.title: A bonus computation
steps.body:
Paid-up capital: 1 crore equity shares of ₹10 = ₹10 crore. Free reserves ₹25 crore. Bonus 1:2 (one bonus share for every two held) → 50 lakh shares × ₹10 = **₹5 crore** capitalised from free reserves.
After bonus: paid-up capital = ₹15 crore; free reserves = 25 − 5 = **₹20 crore**. Total equity unchanged.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using revaluation reserve for bonus – prohibited by s.63(1) Explanation.

activity.prompt: Tick permitted sources for issuing bonus shares
items: Free reserves
Securities premium account
Capital redemption reserve account

quiz.q: Irredeemable preference shares under the 2013 Act are
quiz.why: Section 55(1) bars issue of irredeemable preference shares.

quiz.q: Bonus of 1:4 on 80 lakh shares of ₹10 capitalises
quiz.why: One bonus for four held gives 20 lakh shares, and 20 lakh × ₹10 equals ₹2 crore.

quiz.q: ESOP issue requires
quiz.why: Section 62(1)(b) requires a special resolution for employee stock options.

lessons.title: Buy-back of securities (s.68–70)

scenes.text: A company with paid-up equity of ₹50 crore and free reserves of ₹30 crore wants to buy back shares.
How much can the board approve alone, and how much needs shareholders?

steps.title: Conditions under s.68
steps.body:
1. Authorised by the **articles**.
2. **Board resolution** if buy-back ≤ **10%** of total paid-up equity capital + free reserves; otherwise **special resolution** up to **25%**.
3. For equity shares, buy-back in a financial year cannot exceed **25% of total paid-up equity capital** (in number).
4. Post buy-back **debt-equity ratio ≤ 2:1** (secured and unsecured debt ≤ twice paid-up capital + free reserves).
5. Shares must be **fully paid-up**.
6. Completed within **one year** of the resolution; no fresh buy-back within one year of the previous one.
Sources: free reserves, securities premium, or proceeds of a different kind of shares/securities.

steps.title: Computing limits
steps.body:
Paid-up equity = ₹50 crore; free reserves = ₹30 crore; base = ₹80 crore.
- Board limit (10%) = 0.10 × 80 = **₹8 crore**.
- Special resolution limit (25%) = 0.25 × 80 = **₹20 crore**.
Debt check: suppose debt after buy-back = ₹110 crore; post buy-back capital + free reserves for ₹20 crore buy-back ≈ 80 − 20 = ₹60 crore; 2 × 60 = 120 ≥ 110 ✔ (allowed).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the separate 25%-of-equity-shares-in-a-year cap and the debt-equity test.

activity.prompt: Order the steps for a buy-back above 10%
items: Check articles authorise buy-back
Board approves proposal and explanatory statement
Shareholders pass special resolution
File letter of offer and declaration of solvency
Complete buy-back and extinguish shares within 7 days of completion
File return of buy-back with the Registrar

quiz.q: Paid-up equity ₹40 cr, free reserves ₹20 cr — board-only limit
quiz.why: Ten per cent of ₹60 crore is ₹6 crore.

quiz.q: Maximum post buy-back debt-equity ratio
quiz.why: Section 68(2)(d) caps the ratio at two to one.

quiz.q: Minimum gap between two buy-backs
quiz.why: Section 68(2) proviso bars a buy-back within one year of the previous offer.

lessons.title: Transfer, transmission, debentures and charges

scenes.text: A bank lends ₹5 crore to a company secured by a charge on its machinery, but the charge is not registered with the Registrar.
The company goes into liquidation.

steps.title: Transfer and transmission (s.56)
steps.body: **Transfer** = voluntary act of a member (instrument of transfer, stamped, within prescribed time; dematerialised shares via depository). **Transmission** = by operation of law (death, insolvency). Private company articles restrict transfer; public company shares are freely transferable (s.58 appeals to Tribunal on refusal).

steps.title: Debentures (s.71)
steps.body: Instruments of debt; may be secured or unsecured; convertible (special resolution) or non-convertible; **no voting rights**. Debenture trustee required for public issue to more than 500 persons. **Debenture Redemption Reserve** as prescribed.

steps.title: Charges (s.77)
steps.body: Every company creating a charge must register it with the Registrar within **30 days** of creation; Registrar may allow up to **60 days** with additional fees (and beyond that within a further window as amended). An **unregistered charge is void against the liquidator and creditors** (s.77(3)), but the debt itself remains payable as an unsecured debt.

steps.title: The bank
steps.body:
1. Charge not registered → void against liquidator and other creditors.
2. Bank ranks as **unsecured creditor** for ₹5 crore.
3. Lesson: register within 30 days; file satisfaction (s.82) on repayment.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying non-registration makes the loan void – only the security fails.

activity.prompt: Order the life of a charge
items: Company creates charge in favour of lender
File particulars with Registrar within 30 days
Registrar issues certificate of registration
Loan repaid
Company files satisfaction of charge

quiz.q: Ordinary time to register a charge
quiz.why: Section 77(1) requires registration within 30 days of creation.

quiz.q: An unregistered charge is void against
quiz.why: Section 77(3) makes it unenforceable against the liquidator and creditors.

quiz.q: Debenture-holders generally have
quiz.why: Section 71(2) prohibits debentures carrying voting rights.

lessons.title: Dividends (ss.123–127)

scenes.text: A company with a loss this year wants to pay a dividend from last year's reserves.
Shareholders ask when it must be paid and what happens if unclaimed.

steps.title: Sources (s.123)
steps.body: Dividend only out of: (a) **current year profits** after providing **depreciation**; (b) **accumulated profits** of previous years (after depreciation) transferred to free reserves, per prescribed rules; (c) money provided by Government for dividend under guarantee. **Not out of capital**. Board may declare **interim dividend**. If current-year loss, interim dividend rate is capped at the average rate of the preceding three years. Previous losses and depreciation must be set off before declaring dividend out of current profits.

steps.title: Payment timelines
steps.body:
- Deposit dividend in a separate bank account within **5 days** of declaration.
- Pay within **30 days** of declaration (s.127) – failure is an offence.
- Unpaid amount → **Unpaid Dividend Account** within **7 days** after expiry of 30 days (s.124).
- After **7 years** unclaimed → **Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF)** (s.125), along with the shares (s.124(6)).

steps.title: A dividend computation
steps.body:
Paid-up capital: 1 crore equity shares of ₹10 = ₹10 crore. Profit after depreciation and tax: ₹6 crore. Board recommends dividend of 20% (on face value).
Dividend per share = 20% × ₹10 = **₹2**. Total = 1 crore × ₹2 = **₹2 crore** ≤ ₹6 crore ✔.
Shareholder with 1,500 shares receives 1,500 × 2 = **₹3,000** (before any tax deducted at source).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Computing dividend on market price – dividend % is on face value.
