courses.title: Unit 4 · Directors, meetings and corporate social responsibility
courses.summary: Board composition, appointment, duties and disqualification of directors, independent and women directors, removal; general meetings, notice, quorum and resolutions; board meetings; and CSR under s.135 with computations.
outcomes: State minimum/maximum directors and board composition requirements
List the statutory duties of directors under s.166
Compute AGM deadlines, notice periods and quorum
Distinguish ordinary and special resolutions
Determine CSR applicability and compute the 2% spend

lessons.title: Board composition and appointment (ss.149–152, 164)

scenes.text: A newly listed company has 9 directors, all men, and only 2 are independent.
The compliance officer flags problems.

steps.title: Numbers and composition (s.149)
steps.body:
- Minimum: **3** (public), **2** (private), **1** (OPC). Maximum **15**, more by special resolution.
- At least **one director resident in India** (stayed ≥182 days in the previous calendar year).
- **Woman director**: at least one in every listed company and in prescribed public companies.
- **Independent directors**: listed companies at least **one-third** of total directors; prescribed public companies at least two. Term up to 5 consecutive years, max two terms; cooling-off of 3 years.
- **DIN** is required (s.152).

steps.title: Disqualification (s.164)
steps.body: Unsound mind declared by court; undischarged insolvent; convicted with imprisonment ≥6 months (and within 5 years of expiry); order of disqualification by court/Tribunal; unpaid calls for 6 months; director of a company that has not filed financial statements/annual returns for **3 consecutive financial years** or failed to repay deposits/debentures for a year (disqualified for 5 years from other companies).

steps.title: Fixing the board
steps.body:
9 directors → independent directors needed = ⌈9/3⌉ = **3**; it has 2 → appoint one more independent director (or reduce board size suitably).
No woman director → must appoint at least one.
Check at least one resident director.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Counting nominee directors as independent – they are not independent under s.149(6).

activity.prompt: Tick the board requirements for a listed company
items: At least one-third independent directors
At least one woman director
At least one director resident in India
Each director holds a DIN

quiz.q: A listed board of 12 needs at least how many independent directors?
quiz.why: One-third of 12 is 4.

quiz.q: Maximum directors without special resolution
quiz.why: Section 149(1) caps at fifteen unless a special resolution allows more.

quiz.q: Independent director maximum consecutive terms
options: Two terms of up to 5 years
quiz.why: Section 149(10)-(11) allows two consecutive terms of up to five years each.

lessons.title: Duties, liability and removal of directors (ss.166, 169, 184, 188)

scenes.text: A director's family firm wins a supply contract from the company without disclosure.
Shareholders want to remove him before his term ends.

steps.title: Duties (s.166)
steps.body:
1. Act in accordance with the **articles**.
2. Act in **good faith** to promote the objects for the benefit of members as a whole and in the best interests of the company, employees, shareholders, community and environment.
3. Exercise **due and reasonable care, skill and diligence** and independent judgment.
4. Not be involved in situations of **conflict of interest**.
5. Not make **undue gain**; if so, pay an equal amount to the company.
6. Not **assign** his office.
Penalty for breach under s.166(7).

steps.title: Interest and related party transactions
steps.body:
- **s.184**: disclose interest at the first board meeting of the year and whenever it changes; interested director must not participate.
- **s.188**: related party transactions (sale/purchase of goods, services, leasing etc.) need board consent and, above thresholds, members' **ordinary resolution**; exemptions for ordinary-course, arm's-length transactions.
- **Removal (s.169)**: by **ordinary resolution** after **special notice** (s.115) and a reasonable opportunity of being heard; not applicable to directors appointed by the Tribunal under s.242. Independent director re-appointed for a second term can be removed only by special resolution.

steps.title: The undisclosed contract
steps.body:
1. Breach of s.184 (no disclosure) and possibly s.188 (RPT without approval).
2. Breach of s.166(4) (conflict) and (5) (undue gain).
3. Contract voidable at the option of the board under s.188(3) if not ratified within 3 months.
4. Removal: special notice of 14 days, director heard, ordinary resolution.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying a special resolution is required to remove a director – ordinary resolution with special notice suffices.

activity.prompt: Order the removal of a director
items: Member gives special notice at least 14 days before the meeting
Company sends notice to the director and members
Director may make written representation
Director is heard at the general meeting
Members pass an ordinary resolution
File Form with Registrar

quiz.q: Directors' duties are codified in
quiz.why: Section 166 lists directors' statutory duties.

quiz.q: Removal of a director requires
quiz.why: Section 169 provides removal by ordinary resolution with special notice and hearing.

quiz.q: Undisclosed RPT not ratified within three months is
quiz.why: Section 188(3) makes it voidable at the board's option.

lessons.title: General meetings and resolutions (ss.96–114)

scenes.text: A public company's financial year ends on 31 March 2026; it last held an AGM on 15 July 2025.
It has 3,200 members. What are the AGM deadline and quorum?

steps.title: AGM (s.96)
steps.body: Every company other than an OPC must hold an AGM each year. **First AGM** within **9 months** of the close of the first financial year; thereafter within **6 months** of the close of the financial year, and **not more than 15 months** between two AGMs. Registrar may extend by up to 3 months (not for the first AGM). Held during business hours on a working day at the registered office or within the same city/town.

steps.title: Notice, quorum, resolutions
steps.body:
- **Notice**: at least **21 clear days** (s.101); shorter notice with consent of members (for AGM, 95% of members entitled to vote).
- **Quorum** (s.103), public company: **5** members if ≤1,000 members; **15** if >1,000 up to 5,000; **30** if >5,000. Private company: **2**.
- **Ordinary resolution** (s.114(1)): votes in favour exceed votes against.
- **Special resolution** (s.114(2)): votes in favour at least **three times** votes against, with intention specified in notice.
- **EGM** (s.100): board may call; members holding 1/10 of paid-up voting capital can requisition.

steps.title: Computing for the company
steps.body:
1. FY ends 31 March 2026 → 6-month deadline = **30 September 2026**.
2. 15-month gap from 15 July 2025 → **15 October 2026**.
3. Earlier of the two governs → **30 September 2026**.
4. 3,200 members → quorum **15** members personally present.
5. Special resolution: 900 for, 280 against → 900 ≥ 3 × 280 = 840 ✔ passed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Counting proxies for quorum – quorum requires members personally present.

activity.prompt: Order the AGM process
items: Board approves financial statements and notice
Send notice at least 21 clear days before
Hold meeting with quorum present
Transact ordinary and special business
Prepare minutes within 30 days
File resolutions and annual return with Registrar

quiz.q: Quorum for a public company with 800 members
quiz.why: Section 103 requires five members personally present where members do not exceed 1,000.

quiz.q: Special resolution: 600 for, 210 against — passed?
quiz.why: Three times 210 is 630, and 600 is less than 630, so it fails.

quiz.q: Maximum gap between two AGMs
quiz.why: Section 96(1) forbids more than fifteen months between two AGMs.

lessons.title: Board meetings and CSR (ss.173, 135)

scenes.text: A company's net profits (computed under s.198) for the last three years are ₹4 crore, ₹6 crore and ₹8 crore; turnover ₹600 crore; net worth ₹300 crore.
Does CSR apply, and how much must be spent?

steps.title: Board meetings (s.173)
steps.body: First board meeting within **30 days** of incorporation; thereafter at least **four** meetings a year with **not more than 120 days** between two consecutive meetings. Notice at least **7 days**. Quorum (s.174): **one-third of total strength or two directors, whichever is higher**. Video-conferencing permitted.

steps.title: CSR (s.135)
steps.body:
Applies to a company having, in the **immediately preceding financial year**: net worth ≥ **₹500 crore**, or turnover ≥ **₹1,000 crore**, or net profit ≥ **₹5 crore**.
- CSR Committee of the board (not needed where CSR obligation ≤ ₹50 lakh; board performs functions).
- Spend at least **2% of average net profits of the three immediately preceding financial years**.
- Activities from **Schedule VII** (hunger, education, health, environment, etc.).
- Unspent amount: transfer to Schedule VII fund within 6 months, or to **Unspent CSR Account** within 30 days for ongoing projects.

steps.title: Computing CSR
steps.body:
1. Applicability: last year's net profit ₹8 crore ≥ ₹5 crore → **CSR applies** (turnover and net worth thresholds not met, but one is enough).
2. Average net profit = (4 + 6 + 8) ÷ 3 = 18 ÷ 3 = **₹6 crore**.
3. 2% × ₹6 crore = **₹12 lakh**.
4. Obligation ≤ ₹50 lakh → CSR Committee not mandatory; the board discharges functions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using only last year's profit to compute 2% – the base is the three-year average.

activity.prompt: Tick any ONE condition that triggers CSR (in the preceding FY)
items: Net worth of ₹500 crore or more
Turnover of ₹1,000 crore or more
Net profit of ₹5 crore or more

quiz.q: Average net profits ₹15 cr, ₹21 cr, ₹27 cr — CSR spend
quiz.why: The average is ₹21 crore and 2% of that is ₹42 lakh.

quiz.q: Maximum gap between two board meetings
quiz.why: Section 173(1) allows not more than one hundred and twenty days between meetings.

quiz.q: Board meeting quorum for a board of 9
quiz.why: One-third of 9 is 3, which is higher than two.

questions.q: Minimum directors in a private company
questions.why: Section 149(1)(a) requires two directors for a private company.

questions.q: Resident director must have stayed in India at least
questions.why: Section 149(3) requires stay of at least 182 days in the previous calendar year.

questions.q: Non-filing of returns for 3 consecutive years leads to
questions.why: Directors of such a company are disqualified for five years from other companies.

questions.q: Duty to avoid conflict of interest is in
questions.why: Section 166(4) bars directors from conflict situations.

questions.q: Special notice is required at least
questions.why: Section 115 requires special notice at least 14 days before the meeting.

questions.q: First AGM must be held within
options: 9 months of the first FY end
questions.why: Section 96(1) proviso allows nine months for the first AGM.

questions.q: FY ends 31 March 2027 — AGM deadline (absent extension)
questions.why: Six months from 31 March is 30 September, subject to the 15-month gap rule.

questions.q: Quorum for a public company with 6,000 members
questions.why: Above 5,000 members, s.103 requires thirty members present.

questions.q: Special resolution requires votes in favour
questions.why: Section 114(2) requires votes for to be at least three times votes against.

questions.q: Notice of board meeting
questions.why: Section 173(3) requires at least seven days' notice.

questions.q: CSR spend basis
options: 2% of average net profits of 3 preceding years
questions.why: Section 135(5) uses average net profits of the three immediately preceding years.

questions.q: Unspent CSR on ongoing projects goes to Unspent CSR Account within
questions.why: Section 135(6) requires transfer within thirty days from the end of the financial year.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Majority rule, oppression and mismanagement, restructuring, winding up and insolvency
courses.summary: The rule in Foss v Harbottle and its exceptions, oppression and mismanagement remedies with eligibility computations, class actions, compromises and mergers, winding up by the Tribunal, and the corporate insolvency resolution process under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.
outcomes: State the rule in Foss v Harbottle and its exceptions
Compute eligibility to apply under s.244
List grounds for winding up by the Tribunal under s.271
Explain triggers, timelines and moratorium in CIRP under the IBC
Apply the CoC voting threshold and liquidation waterfall basics

lessons.title: Majority rule and its exceptions

story.title: Directors who sold land to themselves

scenes.text: Directors of a park company sold their own land to the company at an inflated price.
Two minority shareholders sue the directors on the company's behalf.

steps.title: Foss v Harbottle (1843)
steps.body: Where a wrong is done to the company, the **proper plaintiff is the company** itself, and if the majority can ratify the act, courts will not interfere at the instance of a minority. Rationale: separate personality, majority rule, avoidance of multiple suits.

steps.title: Exceptions
steps.body:
1. **Ultra vires or illegal acts**.
2. **Fraud on the minority** where wrongdoers are in control (Menier v Hooper's Telegraph, 1874; Cook v Deeks, 1916).
3. Acts requiring a **special majority** passed by simple majority.
4. Infringement of **personal rights** of members (e.g., voting – Pender v Lushington, 1877).
5. **Oppression and mismanagement** – statutory remedies (ss.241–244).
6. **Class action** (s.245).

steps.title: The park company
steps.body:
1. Wrong was to the company → company is the proper plaintiff (Foss).
2. Wrongdoers (directors) control the company → they will not sue themselves.
3. Fraud on minority exception may be argued; today the minority would more likely petition the NCLT under s.241 for mismanagement or use a class action under s.245.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Applying Foss to infringement of a member's personal right – personal rights can always be enforced.

activity.prompt: Tick exceptions to the rule in Foss v Harbottle
items: Ultra vires acts
Fraud on the minority by those in control
Special resolution matters passed by simple majority
Infringement of a member's personal rights

quiz.q: Under Foss v Harbottle the proper plaintiff for a wrong to the company is
quiz.why: The company as a separate person must sue for wrongs done to it.

quiz.q: Fraud on the minority was found in
quiz.why: Directors diverted a company contract to themselves, which the majority could not ratify.

quiz.q: Class action is provided in
quiz.why: Section 245 allows members or depositors to bring class action suits.

lessons.title: Oppression and mismanagement (ss.241–244)

scenes.text: A group holding 18% of shares complains when the board removes the executive chairman they nominated.
They petition the Tribunal alleging oppression.

steps.title: Grounds (s.241)
steps.body: A member may apply to the **NCLT** if the company's affairs are conducted in a manner **prejudicial to public interest**, or **prejudicial or oppressive** to him or other members, or prejudicial to the company's interests; or a material change in management/control makes it likely the affairs will be so conducted. Oppression = conduct that is burdensome, harsh and wrongful, lacking probity and fair dealing (Shanti Prasad Jain v Kalinga Tubes, 1965).

steps.title: Eligibility (s.244) and powers (s.242)
steps.body:
Company with share capital: **not less than 100 members or one-tenth of total members, whichever is less**, OR members holding **not less than one-tenth of the issued share capital** (calls paid). Without share capital: **one-fifth of total members**. Tribunal may **waive** these requirements.
s.242 powers: regulate conduct, purchase of shares by others, reduce capital, terminate or modify agreements, remove directors, recover undue gains, etc.
**Tata Consultancy Services v Cyrus Investments (2021)**: removal of an executive chairman is not by itself oppression; the Tribunal must find conduct making it just and equitable to wind up, yet the winding up would unfairly prejudice members.

steps.title: Eligibility computation
steps.body:
Company: 2,500 members; issued capital ₹100 crore.
- Member route: 1/10 of 2,500 = 250; 100 is less → need **100 members**.
- Capital route: 1/10 of ₹100 crore = **₹10 crore** of issued capital.
Petitioners holding 18% (₹18 crore) qualify under the capital route.
Merits: following Tata v Cyrus, mere removal of a nominee chairman is unlikely to establish oppression without a pattern of lack of probity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Requiring both the member and capital thresholds – either suffices.

activity.prompt: Order an oppression petition
items: Check eligibility under s.244 (or seek waiver)
Identify specific acts of oppression/mismanagement
File petition under s.241 before the NCLT
Seek interim relief under s.242(4)
Tribunal hears and passes orders under s.242
Appeal to NCLAT if aggrieved

quiz.q: Company with 600 members — member-route eligibility
quiz.why: One-tenth of 600 is 60, which is less than 100, so 60 members suffice.

quiz.q: Tata v Cyrus Investments held that removal of an executive chairman
quiz.why: The Supreme Court held removal alone did not meet the oppression standard.

quiz.q: Oppression definition 'lack of probity and fair dealing' is from
options: Shanti Prasad Jain v Kalinga Tubes
quiz.why: The Supreme Court described oppression in these terms in Kalinga Tubes.

lessons.title: Compromises, mergers and winding up by the Tribunal

scenes.text: Two group companies plan to merge; another subsidiary has not filed returns for five years.
Which procedures apply?

steps.title: Compromise and merger (ss.230–232)
steps.body: Application to NCLT; meetings of creditors/members as directed; approval by **majority in number representing three-fourths in value** of creditors or members (present and voting); notices to regulators; Tribunal sanction. **Fast-track merger** (s.233) for small companies and holding–wholly-owned subsidiary, approved by Regional Director.

steps.title: Winding up by Tribunal (s.271)
steps.body:
Grounds: (a) **special resolution** to be wound up by the Tribunal; (b) acted against sovereignty, integrity, security, friendly relations, public order, decency or morality; (c) on Registrar's/authorised person's application, affairs conducted **fraudulently** or for unlawful purpose, or persons guilty of fraud/misconduct; (d) **default in filing** financial statements or annual returns for **five consecutive financial years**; (e) **just and equitable**.
Inability to pay debts is now handled under the **IBC**; voluntary liquidation is under **s.59 IBC**.

steps.title: The two cases
steps.body:
Merger: board approvals → NCLT application → meetings (¾ in value + majority in number) → regulatory notices → sanction → file order with Registrar.
Defaulting subsidiary: five consecutive years' non-filing → s.271(d) ground; alternatively Registrar may strike off under s.248 if not carrying on business.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Citing 'inability to pay debts' as a s.271 ground after 2016 – it moved to the IBC.

activity.prompt: Tick grounds for winding up by the Tribunal under s.271
items: Special resolution of the company
Acts against sovereignty and integrity of India
Fraudulent conduct of affairs
Default in filing returns for five consecutive years
Just and equitable ground

quiz.q: Approval threshold for a scheme under s.230
options: Majority in number and three-fourths in value
quiz.why: Section 230(6) requires majority in persons representing three-fourths in value.

quiz.q: Fast-track merger is approved by
quiz.why: Section 233 schemes are confirmed by the Central Government acting through the Regional Director.

quiz.q: Voluntary liquidation now proceeds under
quiz.why: The IBC moved voluntary liquidation of corporate persons to section 59.

lessons.title: Corporate insolvency resolution under the IBC, 2016

scenes.text: A bank's ₹40 crore term loan to a steel company is in default since January 2026.
The bank files under the IBC. What happens next and how long can it take?

steps.title: Initiation
steps.body:
- **s.7**: financial creditor files with NCLT.
- **s.9**: operational creditor, after a **demand notice** (s.8) and **10 days** without payment or notice of dispute.
- **s.10**: corporate debtor itself.
Minimum default: **₹1 crore** (notification of March 2020). NCLT admits if default is proved (Innoventive Industries v ICICI Bank, 2017). Constitutional validity upheld in **Swiss Ribbons v Union of India (2019)**.

steps.title: Process and timelines
steps.body:
1. Admission → **moratorium** (s.14): no suits, execution, recovery or transfer of assets.
2. **Interim Resolution Professional** appointed; public announcement; claims collected.
3. **Committee of Creditors** (financial creditors) formed; RP confirmed.
4. Resolution plans invited; CoC approves by **≥ 66% voting share**.
5. NCLT approves plan (s.31).
Time: **180 days**, extendable once by **90 days**; outer limit **330 days** including litigation (s.12, as amended 2019). If no plan → **liquidation** (s.33), distribution by **waterfall** (s.53): insolvency costs → workmen's dues (24 months) and secured creditors (relinquishing security) → employees' dues (12 months) → unsecured financial creditors → Government dues and remaining secured creditors → others → shareholders.

steps.title: The bank's case in numbers
steps.body:
Default ₹40 crore ≥ ₹1 crore ✔ → s.7 petition.
CoC voting shares: Bank A 45%, Bank B 25%, Bank C 30%. Plan supported by A and B = 45 + 25 = **70% ≥ 66%** → approved. If only A and C (75%) → also approved. A alone (45%) → fails.
Timeline: admitted on 1 March 2026 → 180 days → about end of August 2026; with 90-day extension → about end of November 2026; outer limit 330 days → late January 2027.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying operational creditors vote in the CoC – the CoC normally comprises financial creditors only.

activity.prompt: Order the CIRP stages
items: Default of ₹1 crore or more
Application under s.7, s.9 or s.10
NCLT admits; moratorium begins
IRP appointed and public announcement made
Committee of Creditors constituted
Resolution plan approved by 66% of CoC
NCLT approves plan (or orders liquidation)

quiz.q: CoC approval threshold for a resolution plan
quiz.why: Section 30(4) requires at least 66% of the voting share of financial creditors.

quiz.q: Outer time limit for CIRP including litigation
quiz.why: The 2019 amendment to s.12 set a mandatory outer limit of 330 days.

quiz.q: Moratorium is under
quiz.why: Section 14 imposes the moratorium on admission.

questions.q: Pender v Lushington concerned
questions.why: A member could sue for refusal of his votes, a personal right.

questions.q: Company without share capital — eligibility under s.244
questions.why: Section 244(1)(b) requires one-fifth of total members.

questions.q: Issued capital ₹50 crore — capital-route threshold
questions.why: One-tenth of ₹50 crore is ₹5 crore.

questions.q: Who can waive s.244 requirements?
questions.why: The proviso to s.244(1) lets the Tribunal waive the requirements.

questions.q: Demand notice period for operational creditor
questions.why: Section 9 allows filing if no payment or dispute within ten days of demand notice.

questions.q: IBC constitutionality was upheld in
options: Swiss Ribbons v Union of India
questions.why: The Supreme Court upheld the Code in Swiss Ribbons (2019).

questions.q: Minimum default for CIRP since 2020
questions.why: The March 2020 notification raised the threshold to ₹1 crore.

questions.q: CoC shares 40%, 20%, 25%, 15%: plan backed by first two only
questions.why: Forty plus twenty is 60%, below the 66% requirement.

questions.q: First in the liquidation waterfall
questions.why: Section 53 places these costs at the top.

questions.q: Default in filing returns for five years is a ground under
questions.why: Section 271 lists five consecutive years' default as a ground.

questions.q: Admission standard for s.7 petitions per Innoventive
questions.why: The NCLT must admit once a financial debt default is shown.

questions.q: Rule that majority can ratify wrongs to company comes from
questions.why: Foss v Harbottle established majority rule and the proper plaintiff principle.

uni-llb-constitutional-law.title: Constitutional Law I & II
uni-llb-constitutional-law.description: The Constitution of India unit by unit: Preamble and nature, citizenship and 'State', Fundamental Rights and writs, Directive Principles and Duties, the Union and State organs, federal relations, emergency and the basic structure doctrine. General education, not legal advice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB (3-year and 5-year) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Foundations: Preamble, Nature, Citizenship and 'State'
courses.summary: How the Constitution was made, what the Preamble says and how courts use it, whether India is federal or quasi-federal, who is a citizen under Articles 5–11 and the Citizenship Act 1955, and which bodies count as 'State' under Article 12.
outcomes: Explain the making of the Constitution and its main sources
Interpret the Preamble and state its legal status after Kesavananda Bharati
Classify Indian federalism using unitary and federal features
Apply Articles 5–11 and the modes of acquiring citizenship
Use the Ajay Hasia tests to decide whether a body is 'State' under Article 12

lessons.title: Making of the Constitution and its salient features

story.title: Two years, eleven months, eighteen days

scenes.text: The Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946. Dr B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.
The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 (now Constitution Day) and came fully into force on 26 January 1950.

steps.title: Sources
steps.body:
Much of the structure was borrowed from the **Government of India Act 1935** (federal scheme, emergency provisions, public service commissions). Other sources:
- UK: parliamentary government, rule of law, cabinet system, writs
- USA: fundamental rights, judicial review, independent judiciary
- Ireland: Directive Principles of State Policy
- Canada: federation with a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Union
- Australia: Concurrent List, joint sitting
- Weimar Germany: suspension of rights during emergency

steps.title: Salient features
steps.body:
- Lengthiest written constitution
- Blend of rigidity and flexibility (Article 368 has three kinds of procedures)
- Parliamentary form of government at Union and State level
- Federal system with unitary bias
- Fundamental Rights (Part III), DPSP (Part IV), Fundamental Duties (Part IVA)
- Integrated, independent judiciary with judicial review
- Universal adult franchise (voting age lowered from 21 to 18 by the 61st Amendment, 1988)
- Single citizenship

steps.title: Original vs today
steps.body: The original text had a Preamble, 395 Articles in 22 Parts and 8 Schedules. Today there are 12 Schedules; Article numbers are still nominally 395 because new Articles are inserted with letters (e.g. 21A, 243A).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that the Constitution came into force on 26 November 1949: only some provisions (citizenship, elections, provisional Parliament – Article 394) came into force then.
- Calling the Constitution 'borrowed': the framers adapted sources to Indian needs, an answer should say so.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: For a 'salient features' question, give each feature an Article number and one line of significance; that alone lifts an answer from average to good.

activity.prompt: Match each feature with its main source

quiz.q: The Constitution of India came fully into force on
quiz.why: Adopted on 26 November 1949, it commenced as a whole on 26 January 1950 under Article 394.

quiz.q: Directive Principles were inspired mainly by the Constitution of
quiz.why: Part IV draws on the Directive Principles of Social Policy in the Irish Constitution of 1937.

quiz.why: Dr Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, while Dr Rajendra Prasad presided over the Constituent Assembly.

lessons.title: The Preamble: text, meaning and legal status

story.title: Is the Preamble part of the Constitution?

scenes.text: In Re Berubari (1960) the Supreme Court said the Preamble is a key to the minds of the makers but not part of the Constitution.
In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) a 13-judge Bench held that it IS part of the Constitution and can be amended, but not so as to destroy the basic structure.

steps.title: Key words
steps.body:
WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA → source of authority is the people.
- **Sovereign**: no external authority over India
- **Socialist** and **Secular**: added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976 (with 'integrity')
- **Democratic Republic**: elected head of State
- Objectives: **Justice** (social, economic, political), **Liberty** (of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), **Equality** (of status and opportunity), **Fraternity** (dignity of the individual, unity and integrity of the Nation)

steps.title: How courts use it
steps.body:
1. Where an Article is ambiguous, the Preamble guides interpretation.
2. It is not a source of power and not of limitations by itself.
3. In S.R. Bommai (1994) secularism was held to be part of the basic structure.
4. In LIC v Consumer Education & Research Centre (1995) the Court read the Preamble's socio-economic justice into Article 21 analysis.

steps.title: Only amendment
steps.body: The Preamble has been amended once: the 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'and integrity'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Preamble is enforceable in a court: it is not justiciable on its own.
- Citing Berubari as current law on its status: it was overruled on that point by Kesavananda Bharati.

activity.prompt: Put the Preamble's content in its actual order
items: We, the people of India
Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic
Justice, social, economic and political
Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship
Equality of status and of opportunity
Fraternity assuring dignity and unity and integrity of the Nation

quiz.q: Which case held the Preamble to be part of the Constitution?
quiz.why: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) departed from Berubari and treated the Preamble as part of the Constitution.

quiz.q: 'Secular' was added to the Preamble by the
quiz.why: The 42nd Amendment, 1976, inserted the words socialist, secular and integrity.

quiz.q: The source of authority named in the Preamble is
quiz.why: It begins 'We, the people of India', locating sovereignty in the people.

quiz.q: The Preamble is
options: Not enforceable on its own but an aid to interpretation
quiz.why: Courts use it to resolve ambiguity, but it neither grants power nor is enforceable by itself.

lessons.title: Nature of the Indian federation

scenes.text: K.C. Wheare called India 'quasi-federal'. Granville Austin called it 'cooperative federalism'.
In S.R. Bommai (1994) the Supreme Court held federalism to be a basic feature of the Constitution.

steps.title: Federal features
steps.body:
- Written, supreme constitution
- Division of powers: Seventh Schedule (Union, State, Concurrent Lists)
- Bicameral Parliament with Rajya Sabha representing States
- Independent judiciary to decide Centre–State disputes (Article 131)
- Rigid amendment for federal provisions (ratification by half the States under Article 368(2) proviso)

steps.title: Unitary features
steps.body:
- Article 1: 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States' – States cannot secede
- Parliament can alter State boundaries (Article 3) by simple law
- Residuary power with the Union (Article 248)
- Emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360)
- Governor appointed by the President
- Single citizenship, all-India services, integrated judiciary
- Union law prevails over State law in the Concurrent List (Article 254)

steps.title: Answering a 10-mark question
steps.body:
1. Define federation (two levels of government, each supreme in its sphere).
2. List federal features with Articles.
3. List unitary features with Articles.
4. Cite Wheare, Austin and State of West Bengal v Union of India (1962), where the Court said the Constitution is not a traditional federation.
5. Conclude with Bommai: federalism is basic structure, so the Centre's powers must be used within limits.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The word 'federation' does not appear in the Constitution; Article 1 says 'Union of States'. Do not quote a non-existent 'federal' Article.

activity.prompt: Sort each provision

items.text: Seventh Schedule division of subjects
Residuary powers with Parliament (Art. 248)
Supreme Court's original jurisdiction in Centre–State disputes (Art. 131)
Governor appointed by the President
Parliament can create new States by ordinary law (Art. 3)
Rajya Sabha representing States

quiz.q: Article 1 describes India as
quiz.why: Article 1 deliberately uses 'Union of States' to show the federation is indestructible.

quiz.q: Residuary legislative power lies with
quiz.why: Article 248 and Entry 97 of List I give residuary power to Parliament.

quiz.q: Federalism was declared a basic feature in
quiz.why: The nine-judge Bench in S.R. Bommai (1994) treated federalism and secularism as basic features.

quiz.q: Who described the Indian Constitution as 'quasi-federal'?
quiz.why: K.C. Wheare used the phrase quasi-federal because of the strong unitary features.

lessons.title: Citizenship and the meaning of 'State' (Article 12)

story.title: Can you file a writ against a cricket board?

scenes.text: In Zee Telefilms v Union of India (2005) the Supreme Court held that BCCI is not 'State' under Article 12.
But the Court added that a writ under Article 226 can still lie because BCCI performs public functions.

steps.title: Citizenship at commencement (Articles 5–11)
steps.body:
- Art. 5: domicile in India plus birth in India, or a parent born in India, or ordinary residence for 5 years before 26 January 1950
- Art. 6: migrants from Pakistan before 19 July 1948 (and after, if registered)
- Art. 7: persons who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 are not citizens, unless they returned under a permit for resettlement
- Art. 8: persons of Indian origin residing abroad (registration)
- Art. 9: voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship ends Indian citizenship
- Art. 11: Parliament may regulate citizenship by law → Citizenship Act 1955

steps.title: Citizenship Act 1955
steps.body:
Acquisition: birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory.
Loss: renunciation, termination (on voluntarily acquiring another citizenship), deprivation (e.g. fraud, disloyalty).
India does not allow dual citizenship; Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) is a status, not citizenship.

steps.title: Article 12 – 'State'
steps.body:
Includes the Government and Parliament of India, Government and Legislature of each State, and all local or other authorities within India or under the control of the Government of India.

Ajay Hasia v Khalid Mujib (1981) tests for an 'instrumentality or agency':
1. Entire share capital held by Government
2. Financial assistance meeting almost all expenditure
3. Monopoly status conferred or protected by State
4. Deep and pervasive State control
5. Functions of public importance closely related to governmental functions
6. Transfer of a government department to the body

Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002): the question is whether the body is financially, functionally and administratively dominated by Government.

steps.title: Applying the tests
steps.body:
ONGC and LIC: statutory corporations under pervasive control → State (Sukhdev Singh, 1975).
CSIR: held State in Pradeep Kumar Biswas.
BCCI: no deep and pervasive control, not State (Zee Telefilms), though amenable to Article 226.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating any one Ajay Hasia factor as decisive; courts look at the cumulative picture.
- Forgetting that Article 226 reaches 'any person or authority', which is wider than 'State' in Article 12.

activity.prompt: Tick the factors you would check to argue a company is 'State' under Article 12
items: Who holds the share capital
Whether government funds nearly all its expenditure
Whether it enjoys State-conferred monopoly
Whether control is deep and pervasive
Whether its functions are governmental in nature
Whether a government department was transferred to it

quiz.q: The six tests for 'instrumentality or agency' were laid down in
quiz.why: Ajay Hasia v Khalid Mujib (1981) set out the six indicative tests.

quiz.q: BCCI was held to be
options: Not State, but writs under Article 226 may lie
quiz.why: Zee Telefilms held BCCI is not State, while noting its public functions allow Article 226 review.

quiz.q: Voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship after commencement leads to loss of Indian citizenship under
quiz.why: Article 9 for the transitional period and termination under the Citizenship Act 1955 thereafter.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a mode of acquiring citizenship under the 1955 Act?
options: Marriage to an OCI cardholder automatically
quiz.why: There is no automatic citizenship by marrying an OCI cardholder; registration has its own conditions.

questions.q: The Preamble was amended by
questions.why: The 42nd Amendment of 1976 is the only amendment to the Preamble.

questions.q: Article 12 defines
questions.why: Article 12 defines 'State' for Part III.

questions.why: Article 5 covers domiciled persons at the commencement of the Constitution.

questions.q: Which provision enables Parliament to make law on citizenship?
questions.why: Article 11 empowers Parliament, under which the Citizenship Act 1955 was enacted.

questions.q: Re Berubari is known for holding that the Preamble
options: Is not part of the Constitution
questions.why: Berubari (1960) said the Preamble is not part of the Constitution, later departed from in Kesavananda.

questions.q: Concurrent List as a concept was taken mainly from
questions.why: The Australian Constitution inspired the concurrent field of legislation.

questions.q: The test of 'financially, functionally and administratively dominated' was stated in
questions.why: Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002) restated the Article 12 test in those terms.

questions.q: Which is a unitary feature?
questions.why: A single citizenship for the whole country is a unitary feature.

questions.q: Article 394 relates to
options: Commencement of certain provisions on 26 November 1949 and the rest on 26 January 1950
questions.why: Article 394 fixes the commencement of the Constitution in two stages.

questions.q: Writ jurisdiction under Article 226 extends to
options: Any person or authority, including in suitable cases private bodies performing public duties
questions.why: Article 226 speaks of 'any person or authority', wider than Article 12.

questions.q: Who called the Indian system 'cooperative federalism'?
questions.why: Granville Austin used the phrase cooperative federalism.

questions.q: Statutory corporations like ONGC and LIC were held to be State in
questions.why: A Constitution Bench in Sukhdev Singh held such statutory corporations to be authorities under Article 12.

questions.q: Federal provisions of the Constitution are amended with
options: Special majority plus ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures
questions.why: The proviso to Article 368(2) requires ratification by half the States for federal matters.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Article 13 and the Right to Equality (Articles 14–18)
courses.summary: Judicial review under Article 13 and the doctrines of severability and eclipse; equality before law and reasonable classification; the arbitrariness doctrine; Articles 15 and 16 on discrimination and reservations including Indra Sawhney; abolition of untouchability and titles.
outcomes: Apply Article 13 with the doctrines of severability, eclipse and waiver
Test a law with the twin test of reasonable classification
Explain the new doctrine of arbitrariness from Royappa to Shayara Bano
State the law on reservations: Indra Sawhney, the 50% rule, creamy layer and EWS
Explain Articles 17 and 18

lessons.title: Article 13: 'law', judicial review and the doctrines

story.title: A pre-1950 law that suddenly became unconstitutional

scenes.text: A 1939 State law let the government take over motor transport, which clashed with the freedom of trade after 1950.
In Bhikaji Narain Dhakras (1955) the Court held the law was only eclipsed; once the 1951 Amendment removed the conflict, it revived.

steps.title: The text
steps.body:
- Art. 13(1): pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Part III are void to the extent of inconsistency.
- Art. 13(2): the State shall not make any law that takes away or abridges Part III rights; any such law is void to that extent.
- Art. 13(3): 'law' includes ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, custom or usage having the force of law.
- Art. 13(4) (24th Amendment, 1971): nothing in Art. 13 applies to a constitutional amendment under Art. 368.

steps.title: Doctrines
steps.body:
**Severability** (R.M.D.C. v Union of India, 1957): only the offending part is struck down if it can be separated and the rest can stand on its own.
**Eclipse** (Bhikaji Narain, 1955): a pre-constitutional law inconsistent with Part III is dormant, not dead; it revives if the obstacle is removed. Deep Chand (1959) held that a post-constitutional law violating Part III is void from inception, so eclipse does not normally apply to it.
**Waiver** (Basheshar Nath v CIT, 1959): a citizen cannot waive a Fundamental Right.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A State Act of 2010 has 20 sections; section 7 permits arrest without any reason being recorded and violates Article 21; the rest regulate licensing.
Step 1: Is s.7 'law' under 13(3)? Yes, a statute.
Step 2: Does it abridge Part III? Yes.
Step 3: Severable? The licensing scheme works without s.7, so only s.7 is void.
Step 4: Eclipse? No, it is post-constitutional, so it is void from inception and will not revive by itself.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying eclipse to post-1950 laws as a general rule.
- Forgetting personal-law questions: whether uncodified personal law is 'law' under Art. 13 has been debated (State of Bombay v Narasu Appa Mali, 1952 said no); state this carefully.

activity.prompt: Which doctrine fits each situation?

items.text: Only one clause of a statute is unconstitutional and can be cut out
A 1940 law conflicts with Part III until a later amendment removes the conflict
An employee signs away his right to equality in a contract
A rule's offending proviso is struck down while the rule survives

quiz.q: Fundamental Rights cannot be waived – which case?
quiz.why: Basheshar Nath v CIT (1959) held that Fundamental Rights are not for an individual to waive.

quiz.q: Article 13(4) was inserted by the
quiz.why: The 24th Amendment, 1971, added Art. 13(4) after Golaknath to exclude amendments from Art. 13.

quiz.q: Doctrine of eclipse primarily applies to
quiz.why: Bhikaji Narain applied eclipse to existing laws; post-constitutional violating laws are void ab initio.

quiz.q: 'Custom or usage having the force of law' is
options: Included in the definition of law in Art. 13(3)
quiz.why: Art. 13(3)(a) expressly includes custom or usage having the force of law.

lessons.title: Article 14: reasonable classification and arbitrariness

scenes.text: West Bengal allowed the government to send any case it chose to a Special Court with a shorter procedure.
In State of West Bengal v Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) the Court struck it down: there was no rational basis for picking cases.

steps.title: Two limbs
steps.body:
'The State shall not deny to any person **equality before the law** or the **equal protection of the laws** within the territory of India.'
- Equality before law: negative concept from British rule of law (Dicey) – no one is above the law.
- Equal protection: positive concept from the 14th Amendment of the US Constitution – like should be treated alike.
Article 14 applies to 'any person', including non-citizens and companies.

steps.title: Twin test (Ram Krishna Dalmia, 1958)
steps.body:
Classification is allowed, class legislation is not. A classification is valid only if:
1. It is founded on an **intelligible differentia** that distinguishes those grouped together from those left out; and
2. The differentia has a **rational nexus** with the object of the law.
Example: a lower tax rate for small-scale industries (differentia: size) to promote small business (nexus) – valid.

steps.title: New doctrine: arbitrariness
steps.body:
E.P. Royappa v State of Tamil Nadu (1974): 'equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies'.
Maneka Gandhi (1978): Art. 14 strikes at arbitrariness in State action and ensures fairness.
Shayara Bano (2017): instant triple talaq struck down; manifest arbitrariness can invalidate legislation too.
Navtej Singh Johar (2018) and Joseph Shine (2018) also used manifest arbitrariness.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A State reserves all forest-guard posts for persons over 6 feet tall.
Differentia: height – intelligible.
Nexus: does height relate to guarding forests? Weakly; a court may find no rational nexus, and the rule may also be manifestly arbitrary. A minimum physical standard tied to job tasks is more defensible.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Article 14 forbids all classification.
- Applying only the twin test and forgetting arbitrariness, or vice versa – a good answer applies both.

activity.prompt: Arrange the steps of testing a law under Article 14
items: Identify the class created by the law
Find the differentia separating the class
Ask whether the differentia is intelligible
Identify the object of the law
Check rational nexus between differentia and object
Check whether the law is manifestly arbitrary

quiz.q: The twin test of classification is associated with
quiz.why: Ram Krishna Dalmia v Justice Tendolkar (1958) consolidated the intelligible differentia and rational nexus test.

quiz.q: 'Equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies' was said in
quiz.why: Justice Bhagwati in E.P. Royappa (1974) launched the arbitrariness doctrine.

quiz.q: Article 14 is available to
quiz.why: Article 14 uses the word 'person', so non-citizens and juristic persons are protected.

quiz.q: Instant triple talaq was invalidated in
quiz.why: Shayara Bano v Union of India (2017) held talaq-e-biddat invalid, with opinions relying on manifest arbitrariness.

lessons.title: Articles 15 and 16: non-discrimination and reservations

scenes.text: The Union government notified 27% reservation for socially and educationally backward classes in central government jobs, based on the Mandal Commission.
A nine-judge Bench in Indra Sawhney (1992) upheld it with limits: creamy layer exclusion and a normal ceiling of 50%.

steps.title: Article 15
steps.body:
15(1): no discrimination by the State on grounds **only** of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them.
15(2): access to shops, hotels, wells, public places.
15(3): special provisions for women and children.
15(4) (1st Amendment, 1951, after State of Madras v Champakam Dorairajan): special provisions for SEBCs, SCs and STs.
15(5) (93rd Amendment, 2005): reservation in educational institutions including private unaided ones (minority institutions excepted) – upheld in Pramati Educational Trust (2014).
15(6) (103rd Amendment, 2019): up to 10% for economically weaker sections (EWS).

steps.title: Article 16
steps.body:
16(1)–(2): equality of opportunity in public employment.
16(3): Parliament may prescribe residence requirements.
16(4): reservation for backward classes not adequately represented.
16(4A): reservation in promotion for SC/ST (77th Amendment) with consequential seniority (85th).
16(4B): carry-forward of unfilled vacancies, not counted toward the 50% in the year (81st).
16(6): EWS up to 10%.
M. Nagaraj (2006) and Jarnail Singh (2018) dealt with promotion reservation conditions; Jarnail Singh held quantifiable data on backwardness of SC/ST is not required.

steps.title: Indra Sawhney holdings
steps.body:
- Caste can be a criterion for identifying backward classes
- Creamy layer of OBCs to be excluded
- Reservations should normally not exceed 50% save in extraordinary situations
- No reservation in promotions under 16(4) (later altered by 16(4A))
Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upheld EWS reservation by 3:2.

steps.title: Worked numeric
steps.body:
A recruitment has 200 posts. SC 15%, ST 7.5%, OBC 27%, EWS 10%.
SC = 0.15 × 200 = 30; ST = 0.075 × 200 = 15; OBC = 0.27 × 200 = 54; EWS = 0.10 × 200 = 20.
Total reserved = 30 + 15 + 54 + 20 = 119, i.e. 59.5%. Open category = 200 − 119 = 81.
(SC+ST+OBC alone = 99 posts = 49.5%, within the Indra Sawhney ceiling; Janhit Abhiyan held the EWS quota is outside that ceiling.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling 50% an absolute constitutional rule: Indra Sawhney allowed exceptions in extraordinary cases.
- Mixing up Art. 15 (any State action incl. education) and Art. 16 (public employment only).

activity.prompt: Which clause supports each measure?

items.text: Seats for women in a State scheme
OBC quota in a private unaided engineering college
Reservation for SC officers in promotion
Free education scheme only for girls

quiz.q: Creamy layer exclusion was laid down in
quiz.why: Indra Sawhney (1992) required exclusion of the creamy layer among OBCs.

quiz.q: Art. 15(4) was inserted in response to
quiz.why: Champakam Dorairajan (1951) struck down a caste-based admissions order, prompting the 1st Amendment.

quiz.q: EWS reservation was upheld in
options: Janhit Abhiyan v Union of India
quiz.why: In 2022 a five-judge Bench upheld the 103rd Amendment by majority 3:2.

quiz.q: With 200 posts and SC 15%, ST 7.5%, OBC 27%, how many posts are reserved for these three groups?
quiz.why: 30 + 15 + 54 = 99 posts, which is 49.5% of 200.

lessons.title: Articles 17 and 18: untouchability and titles

scenes.text: A village group stops Dalit families from entering a public temple.
Article 17 makes untouchability an offence 'in any form', enforced through the Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989.

steps.title: Article 17
steps.body:
'Untouchability' is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden; enforcement of any disability arising from it is an offence punishable by law.
The right is enforceable against private persons too, not only the State. The word is not defined in the Constitution; courts read it in its historical sense of caste-based exclusion (Devarajiah v Padmanna, 1958).

steps.title: Article 18
steps.body:
- No title, except military or academic distinction, shall be conferred by the State.
- Citizens shall not accept titles from foreign States.
- Balaji Raghavan v Union of India (1996): Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not 'titles' under Art. 18, but must not be used as suffixes or prefixes to names.

steps.title: Why horizontal application matters
steps.body: Most Fundamental Rights bind only the State. Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24 also operate against private persons, which is why a private employer or a village panchayat practising untouchability can be prosecuted.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not write that national awards are prohibited titles: Balaji Raghavan upheld them with the naming restriction.

activity.prompt: Tick the Fundamental Rights that apply against private persons
items: Article 15(2) access to shops and public places
Article 17 abolition of untouchability
Article 23 prohibition of forced labour
Article 24 prohibition of child labour in hazardous employment

quiz.why: Balaji Raghavan (1996) held national awards are not titles under Article 18.

quiz.q: Article 17

quiz.q: The statute that implements Article 17 originally as the Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955 is now called
quiz.why: The 1955 Act was renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976.

questions.why: Art. 13(3) gives the inclusive definition of law.

options: British concept of rule of law
questions.why: It reflects Dicey's rule of law; equal protection is from the US.

questions.why: Deep Chand v State of UP (1959) held such laws void from inception.

options: Religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth
questions.why: These five grounds are listed; residence is not among them.

questions.q: Maximum EWS reservation permitted is
questions.why: Arts. 15(6) and 16(6) allow up to 10%.

options: Used manifest arbitrariness to read down Section 377 IPC
questions.why: The Court read down s.377 IPC for consensual adult acts, relying partly on manifest arbitrariness.

Article 18 permits the State to confer

questions.why: The Constitution Bench in Pramati upheld Art. 15(5).
