courses.title: Unit 3 · Freedoms, Life and Personal Liberty (Articles 19–22)
courses.summary: The six freedoms of Article 19 and the reasonable restrictions in clauses (2)–(6); protection in respect of conviction under Article 20; the expansion of Article 21 from Gopalan to Maneka Gandhi and Puttaswamy; Article 21A; and safeguards against arrest and preventive detention in Article 22.
outcomes: List the Article 19(1) freedoms and match each with its restriction clause
Apply the test of reasonableness and proportionality to a restriction
Explain ex post facto law, double jeopardy and self-incrimination under Article 20
Trace the expansion of Article 21 with leading cases
Distinguish punitive arrest from preventive detention under Article 22

lessons.title: Article 19: six freedoms and reasonable restrictions

scenes.text: Two young women were arrested in 2012 over a Facebook post questioning a city shutdown.
In Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015) the Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act as vague and not covered by Article 19(2).

steps.title: Freedoms (citizens only)
steps.body:
19(1)(a) speech and expression → restriction 19(2)
19(1)(b) assemble peaceably without arms → 19(3)
19(1)(c) form associations, unions or co-operative societies → 19(4)
19(1)(d) move freely throughout India → 19(5)
19(1)(e) reside and settle anywhere → 19(5)
19(1)(g) practise any profession, occupation, trade or business → 19(6)
(19(1)(f) property was deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978; property is now a constitutional right under Art. 300A.)

steps.title: Grounds under Art. 19(2)
steps.body:
Sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to an offence.
The list is exhaustive: restrictions on speech cannot be justified on other grounds such as 'public interest' generally (Sakal Papers, 1962).

steps.title: Testing reasonableness
steps.body:
State of Madras v V.G. Row (1952): look at the nature of the right, purpose of the restriction, extent and urgency of the evil, proportionality.
Modern courts apply **proportionality** (Modern Dental College, 2016; Puttaswamy, 2017; Anuradha Bhasin, 2020): legitimate aim, rational connection, necessity (least restrictive measure), balancing.
Anuradha Bhasin (2020): indefinite internet suspension is impermissible; orders must be published and reviewed.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A State bans all protest marches in a city for one year 'to keep traffic smooth'.
1. Right: 19(1)(b) and (a).
2. Ground: 19(3) allows restrictions in the interests of sovereignty and integrity or public order.
3. Traffic smoothness can relate to public order, but a city-wide one-year ban is not the least restrictive measure.
4. Likely unreasonable and disproportionate; designated sites and timings would be a lesser alternative.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Art. 19 is available to companies or foreigners: it is available to citizens (shareholders may sometimes challenge, as in Bennett Coleman, 1973).
- Treating press freedom as a separate Article: it is part of 19(1)(a) (Romesh Thappar, 1950).

activity.prompt: Match the freedom with its restriction clause

items.text: Freedom of speech and expression
Right to assemble peaceably
Right to carry on a trade or business
Freedom of the press

quiz.q: Section 66A of the IT Act was struck down in
quiz.why: Shreya Singhal (2015) found s.66A vague, overbroad and outside Art. 19(2).

quiz.q: The right to property was removed from Part III by the
quiz.why: The 44th Amendment deleted Arts. 19(1)(f) and 31 and created Art. 300A.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a ground in Art. 19(2)?
quiz.why: Art. 19(2) lists specific grounds and general public interest is not among them.

quiz.q: Indefinite suspension of internet was held impermissible in
quiz.why: Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020) required proportionality and periodic review.

lessons.title: Article 20: protection in respect of conviction

story.title: A new offence, an old act

scenes.text: A law made in 2025 makes a certain sale an offence and says it applies to sales since 2020.
Article 20(1) bars conviction for an act that was not an offence when committed.

steps.title: Three protections
steps.body:
20(1) **No ex post facto criminal law**: no conviction except for violation of law in force at the time of the act, and no penalty greater than that in force then. Civil or tax laws may be retrospective. A beneficial change can benefit the accused (Rattan Lal v State of Punjab, 1965).
20(2) **Double jeopardy**: no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. It requires both prior prosecution and punishment by a court (Maqbool Hussain, 1953: confiscation by customs authorities is not prosecution).
20(3) **Self-incrimination**: no person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.

steps.title: Self-incrimination in practice
steps.body:
Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961): specimen handwriting, signatures, fingerprints are not 'testimonial compulsion'.
Selvi v State of Karnataka (2010): involuntary narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping violate Art. 20(3) and Art. 21.
Nandini Satpathy (1978): protection extends to police interrogation of a person accused.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
X is dismissed from service after a departmental inquiry for bribery and then prosecuted in court for the same act.
Is Art. 20(2) violated? No. A departmental inquiry is not 'prosecution and punishment' by a court; only the criminal trial is prosecution.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying 20(1) to procedural changes: it covers conviction and penalty, not procedure or forum.
- Forgetting Art. 20 rights cannot be suspended even during an emergency (44th Amendment amended Art. 359).

activity.prompt: Does Article 20 protect the accused here?

items.text: Compelled narco-analysis test
Taking fingerprints for comparison
Second prosecution after conviction for the same offence
Departmental dismissal followed by criminal trial
Retrospective increase of punishment for an offence

quiz.q: Involuntary narco-analysis was held unconstitutional in
quiz.why: Selvi (2010) held compulsory narco-analysis violates Arts. 20(3) and 21.

quiz.q: Article 20(2) requires
options: Prosecution and punishment by a court earlier
quiz.why: Double jeopardy under 20(2) applies when there was earlier prosecution and punishment for the same offence.

quiz.q: Can Art. 20 be suspended during a national emergency?
quiz.why: After the 44th Amendment, Art. 359 cannot suspend Articles 20 and 21.

lessons.title: Article 21: from Gopalan to Puttaswamy

scenes.text: In 1977 Maneka Gandhi's passport was impounded 'in public interest' with no hearing and no reasons.
The Court held the procedure under Art. 21 must be 'right, just and fair', not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive.

steps.title: Text and the turn
steps.body:
'No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.'
A.K. Gopalan (1950): any procedure enacted by law is enough; Articles 19, 21 and 22 are separate compartments.
Maneka Gandhi (1978): Articles 14, 19 and 21 form a 'golden triangle'; procedure must be fair, just and reasonable – close to American 'due process'.
R.C. Cooper (1970) had already rejected the watertight-compartments view.

steps.title: Rights read into Article 21
steps.body:
- Livelihood: Olga Tellis (1985)
- Speedy trial: Hussainara Khatoon (1979)
- Free legal aid: M.H. Hoskot (1978), now also Art. 39A
- Against custodial violence: D.K. Basu (1997) guidelines
- Clean environment: Subhash Kumar (1991)
- Privacy: K.S. Puttaswamy (2017, nine judges) – overruling M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh on this point
- Dignity and workplace safety: Vishaka (1997)
- Live with dignity, right to die with dignity via passive euthanasia and living wills: Common Cause (2018)

steps.title: Article 21A
steps.body: 86th Amendment (2002): free and compulsory education for all children aged 6 to 14, in such manner as the State may by law determine → Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009. Earlier, Unni Krishnan (1993) had read education into Art. 21.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A city demolishes pavement dwellings overnight without notice.
1. Right: livelihood is part of life (Olga Tellis).
2. Procedure: Olga Tellis upheld the power to remove encroachments but required a fair procedure – notice and hearing.
3. Conclusion: action without notice is unfair; the dwellers can seek relief under Art. 32/226.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that India adopted 'due process' expressly: the text still says 'procedure established by law'; Maneka read fairness into it.
- Citing Kharak Singh for a privacy right: Puttaswamy overruled it to the extent it denied privacy.

activity.prompt: Put the Article 21 cases in chronological order
items: A.K. Gopalan (1950)
Kharak Singh (1963)
Maneka Gandhi (1978)
Olga Tellis (1985)
Vishaka (1997)
K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)

quiz.q: The 'golden triangle' refers to Articles
quiz.why: Maneka Gandhi linked Articles 14, 19 and 21 so that a law must satisfy all three.

quiz.q: Privacy was declared a Fundamental Right in
quiz.why: The nine-judge Bench in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) unanimously held privacy is a Fundamental Right.

quiz.q: Article 21A guarantees education for children aged
quiz.why: Article 21A covers children from six to fourteen years.

quiz.q: Right to livelihood was recognised in
quiz.why: Olga Tellis v Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) treated livelihood as part of life.

lessons.title: Article 22: arrest and preventive detention

scenes.text: Ravi is arrested at 11 pm and kept at the police station until the next evening without being told why.
Article 22 says he must be told the grounds, allowed a lawyer, and produced before a magistrate within 24 hours.

steps.title: Punitive arrest – Art. 22(1)–(2)
steps.body:
- Right to be informed of the grounds of arrest as soon as may be
- Right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of choice
- Production before the nearest magistrate within **24 hours**, excluding journey time
- No detention beyond 24 hours without a magistrate's authority
Not available to enemy aliens or to persons under preventive detention (Art. 22(3)).

steps.title: Preventive detention – Art. 22(4)–(7)
steps.body:
Detention to prevent a future act, not to punish a past one.
- No detention beyond 3 months unless an **Advisory Board** (persons qualified to be High Court judges) reports sufficient cause
- Grounds must be communicated as soon as may be and the detenu given the earliest opportunity to make a representation (22(5))
- Facts against public interest may be withheld (22(6))
- Parliament may prescribe circumstances and maximum period (22(7))
Statutes: National Security Act 1980, COFEPOSA 1974.

steps.title: Counting 24 hours
steps.body:
Arrest at 23:00 on Monday. The magistrate is 2 hours' drive away.
Deadline excluding journey = 23:00 + 24 h + 2 h travel = 01:00 Wednesday at the latest, provided the 2 hours were actually spent travelling.
Ravi produced at 18:00 Tuesday (19 hours after arrest) → within time. Not produced until 03:00 Wednesday → violation, detention unlawful from that point.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying preventive detainees get the 24-hour rule: Art. 22(3)(b) excludes them.
- Forgetting D.K. Basu guidelines (arrest memo, informing a relative) when answering custodial-rights questions.

activity.prompt: Tick the safeguards available to a person under ordinary (punitive) arrest
items: Informed of grounds of arrest
Consult a lawyer of choice
Produced before magistrate within 24 hours
No detention beyond 24 hours without magistrate's order
Arrest memo and information to a relative per D.K. Basu

quiz.q: Maximum detention without Advisory Board opinion under Art. 22(4) is
quiz.why: Detention beyond three months needs an Advisory Board report of sufficient cause.

quiz.q: The 24-hour production rule does not apply to
options: Persons held under preventive detention law
quiz.why: Art. 22(3) excludes enemy aliens and preventive detainees.

quiz.q: Arrested at 22:00 with 1 hour journey to the magistrate, the latest lawful production time is
quiz.why: 24 hours plus the 1 hour of journey brings the deadline to 23:00 the next day.

questions.q: Freedom of press is part of
questions.why: Romesh Thappar and later cases locate press freedom in 19(1)(a).

questions.q: Restrictions on freedom of trade are under
questions.why: Art. 19(6) governs restrictions on 19(1)(g).

questions.q: 'Procedure must be right, just and fair' – which case?
questions.why: Maneka Gandhi (1978) set that standard.

questions.q: Specimen signatures taken from an accused are
questions.why: Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961) held identification material is not testimony.

questions.q: Article 21A was inserted by the
questions.why: The 86th Amendment (2002) inserted Art. 21A.

questions.q: Speedy trial as part of Art. 21 was recognised in
questions.why: Hussainara Khatoon (1979) concerned undertrial prisoners.

questions.q: Custodial arrest guidelines were laid down in
questions.why: D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal (1997) laid down detailed arrest guidelines.

questions.q: Article 19 freedoms are available to
questions.why: Art. 19 opens with 'All citizens shall have the right'.

questions.q: Proportionality has four limbs. Which is NOT one of them?
questions.why: Popular support is not part of the proportionality test.

questions.q: Gopalan's 'watertight compartments' view was rejected in
questions.why: R.C. Cooper (1970) rejected it, and Maneka Gandhi built on that.

questions.q: Article 22(5) requires that a detenu
options: Be given grounds and the earliest opportunity to make a representation
questions.why: This is the core procedural safeguard for preventive detention.

questions.q: A beneficial reduction in punishment can benefit an accused per
options: Rattan Lal v State of Punjab
questions.why: Rattan Lal (1965) allowed a beneficial later law to be applied.

questions.q: Passive euthanasia with advance directives was recognised in
questions.why: Common Cause v Union of India (2018) recognised living wills under Art. 21.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Exploitation, Religion, Minorities, Writs, DPSP and Duties
courses.summary: Rights against exploitation (Articles 23–24), freedom of religion and the essential practices test (25–28), cultural and educational rights of minorities (29–30), constitutional remedies and the five writs (32, 226), public interest litigation, Directive Principles and their relationship with Fundamental Rights, and Fundamental Duties.
outcomes: Explain Articles 23–24 with Bandhua Mukti Morcha and PUDR
Apply the essential religious practices test
State the scope of minority rights under Article 30 after T.M.A. Pai
Choose the correct writ for a fact situation and compare Articles 32 and 226
Explain the FR–DPSP relationship from Champakam to Minerva Mills

lessons.title: Rights against exploitation and freedom of religion

scenes.text: Workers building Asiad 1982 venues were paid less than the minimum wage by contractors.
In PUDR v Union of India (1982) the Court held that paying less than the minimum wage is 'forced labour' under Article 23.

steps.title: Articles 23–24
steps.body:
Art. 23: traffic in human beings, begar and other similar forms of forced labour are prohibited; contravention is an offence. The State may impose compulsory service for public purposes without discrimination (e.g. conscription).
Art. 24: no child below 14 years shall be employed in any factory, mine or other hazardous employment.
Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984): bonded labour identification and rehabilitation; M.C. Mehta v State of Tamil Nadu (1996): child labour in Sivakasi, rehabilitation fund.

steps.title: Articles 25–28
steps.body:
25: freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion, subject to public order, morality, health and other Part III provisions; the State may regulate secular activities associated with religion and provide for social reform.
26: religious denominations may manage their own affairs in matters of religion and own and administer property.
27: no tax whose proceeds are appropriated for promotion of a particular religion.
28: no religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions.

steps.title: Essential religious practices test
steps.body:
Shirur Mutt (1954): only practices essential to the religion are protected; what is essential is decided with reference to the doctrines of that religion.
Rev. Stainislaus (1977): 'propagate' does not include a right to convert another person.
Indian Young Lawyers Association (Sabarimala, 2018): exclusion of women aged 10–50 was not an essential practice (the larger issues were later referred to a bigger Bench).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that Art. 25 is absolute: it is subject to public order, morality and health.
- Confusing Art. 28 (no religious instruction in wholly State-maintained institutions) with Art. 30 (minority institutions).

activity.prompt: Which Article is engaged?

items.text: A 12-year-old working in a fireworks factory
A labourer forced to work to repay a family debt
A ban on a religious procession during a riot
A special tax to fund temples of one faith

quiz.q: Paying less than minimum wage was held to be forced labour in
quiz.why: PUDR v Union of India (1982) treated sub-minimum wages as forced labour under Art. 23.

quiz.q: Article 24 prohibits employment of children below
quiz.why: Art. 24 sets the age at fourteen for hazardous employment.

quiz.q: The right to propagate does not include the right to convert – which case?
quiz.why: Rev. Stainislaus v State of MP (1977) upheld anti-conversion laws on this reasoning.

quiz.q: Article 27 bars
options: Taxes for promoting a particular religion
quiz.why: No person can be compelled to pay taxes appropriated to promote a particular religion.

lessons.title: Cultural and educational rights of minorities

scenes.text: Can a State regulate fees and admissions in a private minority college?
In T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002) eleven judges held minority status is determined State-wise and regulation is allowed only to maintain standards, not to destroy the minority character.

steps.title: Articles 29–30
steps.body:
29(1): any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture has the right to conserve it.
29(2): no citizen shall be denied admission to State-maintained or aided institutions on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language.
30(1): all minorities, religious or linguistic, have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.
30(1A): compensation on acquisition of their property.
30(2): no discrimination in State aid on the ground of minority management.

steps.title: Key holdings
steps.body:
- Kerala Education Bill (1958): regulation for standards permissible
- St. Stephen's College (1992): minority institutions receiving aid may prefer their community students up to a reasonable extent
- T.M.A. Pai (2002): minority is determined in relation to the State; aided minority institutions must admit a reasonable number of non-minority students
- P.A. Inamdar (2005): no State quota or reservation imposed on unaided minority institutions

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Art. 29 protects 'any section of citizens', not only minorities; Art. 30 is limited to minorities.

activity.prompt: Tick regulations a State may validly impose on an aided minority college
items: Qualifications for teachers
Syllabus and examination standards
Accounting and audit of grants
Admission of a reasonable share of non-minority students

quiz.q: Minority status is determined with reference to the
quiz.why: T.M.A. Pai held the unit for deciding minority status is the State.

quiz.q: No State reservation on unaided minority institutions – which case?
quiz.why: P.A. Inamdar (2005) held the State cannot impose quotas on unaided minority institutions.

quiz.q: Article 29(1) protects
options: Any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture
quiz.why: Its text extends to any section of citizens.

lessons.title: Constitutional remedies: Article 32, Article 226 and the writs

scenes.text: In the late 1970s and 1980s the Court treated letters and newspaper reports as writ petitions.
S.P. Gupta (1981) relaxed locus standi: any public-spirited person can move the Court for those who cannot.

steps.title: Article 32 vs 226
steps.body:
Art. 32 is itself a Fundamental Right – Dr Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution; it is part of the basic structure (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997).
- Art. 32: Supreme Court, only for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
- Art. 226: High Courts, for Fundamental Rights 'and for any other purpose' (legal rights too), against any person or authority – wider.
- Art. 32 can be suspended only under Art. 359 during an emergency (except Arts. 20 and 21).

steps.title: Five writs
steps.body:
**Habeas corpus** – 'produce the body'; against unlawful detention by State or private person.
**Mandamus** – 'we command'; to a public authority to perform a public duty; not against the President or Governor personally, nor against a private person.
**Prohibition** – to a lower court or tribunal to stop proceeding beyond jurisdiction (while pending).
**Certiorari** – to quash an order already made without jurisdiction or with error apparent on the record.
**Quo warranto** – 'by what authority'; to test a person's right to hold a public office.

steps.title: Choose the writ
steps.body:
1. A college principal was appointed without the statutory qualification → quo warranto.
2. A tribunal has passed an order in breach of natural justice → certiorari.
3. A municipal body refuses to decide a licence application for two years → mandamus.
4. A father illegally keeps an adult daughter confined → habeas corpus.
5. A tribunal is about to hear a matter it has no jurisdiction over → prohibition.

steps.title: PIL
steps.body: Hussainara Khatoon, S.P. Gupta, Bandhua Mukti Morcha, M.C. Mehta. Guidelines against misuse: State of Uttaranchal v Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010). Courts impose costs on frivolous PILs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying certiorari lies against legislation: it lies against judicial or quasi-judicial (and in India, administrative) action, not against a statute.
- Saying mandamus lies against a private company with no public duty.

activity.prompt: Pick the correct writ

items.text: Unqualified person holds the post of Advocate-General
Police hold a man for 4 days without production
Board refuses to issue a pension it is bound by statute to pay
Quash a tribunal order passed without hearing the affected party

quiz.q: Ambedkar called which Article the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
quiz.why: He described Article 32, the right to constitutional remedies, in those words.

quiz.q: Which writ lies even against a private person?
quiz.why: Habeas corpus tests any unlawful detention, including by private persons.

quiz.q: Article 226 is wider than Article 32 because
options: It applies only to the Union
quiz.why: High Courts can issue writs 'for any other purpose', not only Fundamental Rights.

quiz.q: Writ to stop an inferior tribunal from continuing a case beyond jurisdiction:
quiz.why: Prohibition operates while proceedings are pending; certiorari quashes a decision already made.

lessons.title: Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties

scenes.text: Article 37 says Directive Principles are not enforceable by any court but are fundamental in governance.
In Minerva Mills (1980) the Court said the harmony and balance between Parts III and IV is itself a basic feature.

steps.title: Key DPSPs (Part IV, Arts. 36–51)
steps.body:
- 38: social order with justice; minimise inequalities
- 39: adequate livelihood, distribution of resources, equal pay for equal work, protection of children; 39A free legal aid (42nd Amendment)
- 40: village panchayats
- 41–43: right to work, education, public assistance; living wage; 43A workers' participation in management
- 44: Uniform Civil Code
- 45: early childhood care and education (substituted by 86th Amendment)
- 46: educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections
- 47: nutrition, public health, prohibition of intoxicating drinks
- 48: agriculture and animal husbandry; 48A environment (42nd Amendment)
- 50: separation of judiciary from executive
- 51: international peace and security

steps.title: FR–DPSP relationship
steps.body:
1. Champakam Dorairajan (1951): DPSP must conform to and run subsidiary to Fundamental Rights.
2. Harmonious construction: Re Kerala Education Bill (1958).
3. Article 31C (25th Amendment, 1971): laws giving effect to Art. 39(b)–(c) protected from Arts. 14 and 19; upheld in Kesavananda (first part).
4. 42nd Amendment extended 31C to all DPSPs; Minerva Mills (1980) struck down that extension.
5. Courts now read DPSPs into Fundamental Rights (e.g. 39A into 21; Unni Krishnan for education).

steps.title: Fundamental Duties – Art. 51A
steps.body: Added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation; originally 10, now 11 – clause (k), duty of parents/guardians to provide education to children 6–14, was added by the 86th Amendment (2002). Examples: abide by the Constitution and respect the National Flag and Anthem; protect the environment; develop scientific temper; safeguard public property. Not directly enforceable, but courts use them to interpret laws (AIIMS Students Union, 2002).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing there are 10 Fundamental Duties: there are 11 since 2002.
- Saying DPSPs are useless because unenforceable: they guide legislation and judicial interpretation.

activity.prompt: Fundamental Right, DPSP or Fundamental Duty?

items.text: Uniform Civil Code
Free and compulsory education for 6–14 as a guaranteed right
Parents to provide opportunities for education to their child 6–14
Equal pay for equal work for men and women
To develop scientific temper
Protection against untouchability

quiz.q: Article 31C was extended to all DPSPs and that extension was struck down in
quiz.why: Minerva Mills (1980) invalidated the 42nd Amendment's extension of Art. 31C.

quiz.q: Fundamental Duties were added on the recommendation of
quiz.why: The Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended them, inserted by the 42nd Amendment.

quiz.q: The Uniform Civil Code is in Article
quiz.why: Article 44 directs the State to endeavour to secure a uniform civil code.

quiz.q: How many Fundamental Duties are there now?
quiz.why: The 86th Amendment added the eleventh duty in clause (k).

questions.q: Begar is prohibited by
questions.why: Art. 23 prohibits begar and forced labour.

questions.q: The essential practices doctrine began with
questions.why: Commissioner HRE v Shirur Mutt (1954) framed it.

questions.q: Art. 30 rights belong to
questions.why: Art. 30(1) protects all minorities based on religion or language.

questions.q: Writ to quash an order passed without jurisdiction:
questions.why: Certiorari quashes decisions already made.

questions.q: Writ that tests title to a public office:
questions.why: Quo warranto asks by what authority the office is held.

questions.q: Article 32 is part of the basic structure per
questions.why: L. Chandra Kumar (1997) treated judicial review under Arts. 32 and 226 as basic structure.

questions.q: Article 39A provides for
options: Equal justice and free legal aid
questions.why: Art. 39A was added by the 42nd Amendment.

questions.q: Article 48A concerns
questions.why: Art. 48A directs protection and improvement of the environment.

questions.q: Which case held the balance between Parts III and IV to be a basic feature?
questions.why: Minerva Mills stated harmony between FRs and DPSPs is basic structure.

questions.q: Children singing the national anthem: Jehovah's Witness students who stood respectfully but did not sing were protected in
questions.why: Bijoe Emmanuel held their expulsion violated Arts. 19(1)(a) and 25.

questions.q: Article 28 bars religious instruction in institutions
options: Wholly maintained out of State funds
questions.why: Art. 28(1) applies to institutions wholly maintained out of State funds.

questions.q: Guidelines to check misuse of PIL were laid down in
questions.why: State of Uttaranchal v Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010) issued PIL guidelines.

questions.q: T.M.A. Pai was decided by a Bench of
questions.why: It was an eleven-judge Bench.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Union and States, Centre–State Relations, Emergency and Amendment
courses.summary: The President, Prime Minister and Council of Ministers; Parliament and law-making including money bills and ordinances; the Supreme Court, High Courts and judicial appointments; legislative, administrative and financial relations between the Union and States; emergency provisions and Article 356; amendment under Article 368 and the basic structure doctrine.
outcomes: Explain the constitutional position of the President and Governor and the ordinance power
Describe ordinary, money and constitutional amendment bill procedures
Apply the Seventh Schedule, pith and substance and repugnancy rules
Explain the safeguards on Articles 352 and 356 after the 44th Amendment and Bommai
Trace the amendment cases from Shankari Prasad to Minerva Mills and NJAC

lessons.title: The Union executive and legislature

story.title: A law made while Parliament was not sitting

scenes.text: Bihar re-promulgated the same ordinances again and again for years without placing them before the Legislature.
In Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) seven judges held re-promulgation is a fraud on the Constitution, and ordinances are subject to judicial review.

steps.title: President and Council of Ministers
steps.body:
Art. 53: executive power of the Union vests in the President. Art. 74(1): Council of Ministers headed by the PM aids and advises; the President 'shall act in accordance with such advice' (42nd Amendment) but may once send it back for reconsideration (44th Amendment).
Election (Art. 54–55): by elected members of both Houses and of State Legislative Assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry), by proportional representation with single transferable vote.
Impeachment (Art. 61): for violation of the Constitution, by a 2/3 majority of the total membership of each House.
Shamsher Singh (1974): the President and Governor are constitutional heads acting on ministerial advice.

steps.title: Parliament and law-making
steps.body:
- Ordinary bill: either House; deadlock → joint sitting (Art. 108), presided by the Speaker.
- Money bill (Art. 110): only in Lok Sabha; Speaker certifies; Rajya Sabha can only recommend within 14 days; no joint sitting.
- Constitution amendment bill (Art. 368): special majority in each House separately; no joint sitting.
President's options on an ordinary bill (Art. 111): assent, withhold, or return once for reconsideration.
Art. 123: President's ordinance when either House is not in session; it lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles.

steps.title: Special majority arithmetic
steps.body:
Lok Sabha total membership 543; on voting day 500 present and voting.
Requirement: majority of total membership (more than 543/2 → at least 272) AND 2/3 of present and voting (2/3 × 500 = 333.33 → at least 334).
Binding figure = max(272, 334) = 334 votes in favour.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying money bills can go to a joint sitting: they cannot.
- Saying an ordinance lasts six months in all: its maximum life is six weeks from reassembly, so roughly six months plus six weeks at most.

activity.prompt: Order the life of a money bill
items: Introduced in Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation
Speaker certifies it as a money bill
Passed by Lok Sabha
Sent to Rajya Sabha for recommendations within 14 days
Lok Sabha accepts or rejects recommendations
Presented to the President for assent

quiz.q: Re-promulgation of ordinances was called a fraud on the Constitution in
quiz.why: D.C. Wadhwa (1987) and Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) condemned repeated re-promulgation.

quiz.q: Rajya Sabha must return a money bill within
quiz.why: Under Art. 109 it has 14 days to return it with recommendations.

quiz.q: If 500 of 543 members vote, the minimum votes needed for an amendment bill in Lok Sabha is
quiz.why: Two-thirds of 500 is 333.33, so 334 votes are needed, which also exceeds 272.

quiz.q: Joint sittings are presided over by
quiz.why: Under Art. 118(4) the Speaker presides at a joint sitting.

lessons.title: The judiciary: Supreme Court, High Courts and appointments

scenes.text: In 2014 Parliament created a National Judicial Appointments Commission through the 99th Amendment.
In 2015 a five-judge Bench struck it down as violating judicial independence, reviving the collegium.

steps.title: Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
steps.body:
- Original (Art. 131): disputes between Union and States or between States
- Writ (Art. 32)
- Appellate (Arts. 132–134, 136 special leave)
- Advisory (Art. 143): President may refer questions; opinion not binding on the President
- Review (Art. 137) and curative petition (Rupa Hurra, 2002)
- Art. 141: law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts; Art. 142: complete justice

steps.title: Judges cases
steps.body:
First Judges (S.P. Gupta, 1981): executive primacy.
Second Judges (1993): primacy to CJI's opinion – collegium created.
Third Judges (Re Presidential Reference, 1998): collegium of CJI plus four senior-most judges for SC appointments.
Fourth Judges (SCAORA, 2015): NJAC and 99th Amendment struck down.
Removal (Art. 124(4)): by order of President after an address by each House supported by a majority of total membership and 2/3 of those present and voting, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity; procedure under the Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a Supreme Court advisory opinion binding on the President.
- Saying the collegium is mentioned in the Constitution: it is a creation of judicial interpretation of 'consultation' in Arts. 124 and 217.

activity.prompt: Which jurisdiction is used?

items.text: Water dispute suit between two States on legal rights
President seeks the Court's view on a question of public importance
A litigant challenges a High Court judgment with the Court's permission

quiz.q: The NJAC was struck down in
quiz.why: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v Union of India (2015) invalidated the 99th Amendment.

quiz.q: Curative petition was evolved in
quiz.why: Rupa Ashok Hurra v Ashok Hurra (2002) created the curative petition.

lessons.title: Centre–State relations

story.title: A State law that seemed to tax trade

scenes.text: A State law on a State subject incidentally touched a Union subject.
Courts ask: what is the law's true nature and character – its pith and substance?

steps.title: Legislative relations (Arts. 245–255)
steps.body:
Seventh Schedule: List I Union, List II State, List III Concurrent (the 42nd Amendment moved education, forests, weights and measures, wildlife, administration of justice to List III).
Parliament can legislate on List II: Rajya Sabha resolution in national interest (Art. 249); during emergency (250); with consent of two or more States (252); to implement treaties (253); President's Rule (357).

steps.title: Interpretation doctrines
steps.body:
- **Pith and substance**: true nature decides the entry; incidental encroachment is allowed (Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee, 1947 PC; State of Bombay v F.N. Balsara, 1951).
- **Colourable legislation**: you cannot do indirectly what you cannot do directly (K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo, 1953).
- **Repugnancy (Art. 254)**: on a Concurrent subject, Union law prevails; a State law reserved for and receiving the President's assent prevails in that State unless Parliament later legislates otherwise.
- **Harmonious construction** of entries.

steps.title: Administrative and financial relations
steps.body:
Art. 256–257: States must comply with Union laws; Union may give directions. Art. 263: Inter-State Council. Art. 280: Finance Commission every five years. Art. 246A and 279A (101st Amendment, 2016): GST and GST Council. Mohit Minerals (2022): GST Council recommendations are persuasive, not binding.
Commissions: Sarkaria (1988), Punchhi (2010).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying Union law always prevails over State law: Art. 254 repugnancy is about the Concurrent List; on List II subjects a valid State law stands.

activity.prompt: Which List? (Seventh Schedule)

items.text: Defence
Police and public order
Education
Banking
Criminal procedure
Agriculture

quiz.q: The doctrine of pith and substance looks at
options: The law's true nature and character
quiz.why: The dominant purpose decides the List entry, and incidental overlap is ignored.

quiz.q: Finance Commission is constituted under
quiz.why: Art. 280 provides for a Finance Commission every five years or earlier.

quiz.q: GST Council recommendations were held not strictly binding in
quiz.why: Union of India v Mohit Minerals (2022) treated them as persuasive.

quiz.q: Education was moved to the Concurrent List by the
quiz.why: The 42nd Amendment (1976) transferred education to List III.

lessons.title: Emergency provisions and Article 356

scenes.text: Article 356 was used over 100 times, often to remove opposition governments.
S.R. Bommai (1994): the proclamation is judicially reviewable, and the majority must be tested on the floor of the House.

steps.title: Three emergencies
steps.body:
**National (Art. 352)**: war, external aggression or **armed rebellion** (44th Amendment replaced 'internal disturbance'). Only on written advice of the Cabinet; approval by each House within one month by special majority; continues for six months at a time.
**State emergency (Art. 356)**: failure of constitutional machinery; approval within two months by simple majority; max six months at a time and three years overall (beyond one year only if a national emergency is in force and the Election Commission certifies difficulty).
**Financial (Art. 360)**: threat to financial stability; approval within two months; never proclaimed so far.

steps.title: Effects
steps.body:
Art. 358: Art. 19 suspended automatically only for war or external aggression.
Art. 359: President may suspend enforcement of other rights, but never Arts. 20 and 21 (44th Amendment). ADM Jabalpur (1976), which held habeas corpus unavailable during emergency, was overruled in Puttaswamy (2017).

steps.title: Bommai guidelines
steps.body:
1. The proclamation is subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides or irrelevant material.
2. The floor test is the proper way to test majority.
3. The Assembly should not be dissolved before both Houses approve the proclamation; it can only be kept in suspended animation.
4. Secularism is basic structure; a State government acting against it may be dismissed.
5. Courts can restore a dismissed government.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying 'internal disturbance' is still a ground under Art. 352: since 1978 the ground is armed rebellion.

activity.prompt: Which Article fits?

items.text: Armed rebellion in part of the country
Governor reports no party can form a stable government
Credit of India threatened
External aggression

quiz.why: The 44th Amendment narrowed the ground after the 1975 emergency.

quiz.q: Rights that cannot be suspended under Art. 359:
quiz.why: After 1978, enforcement of Arts. 20 and 21 cannot be suspended.

quiz.q: Financial emergency has been proclaimed
quiz.why: Art. 360 has never been invoked.

quiz.q: Floor test as the proper test of majority was emphasised in
quiz.why: S.R. Bommai (1994) held the floor of the House decides majority.

lessons.title: Amendment and the basic structure doctrine

story.title: The case that saved the Constitution

scenes.text: Swami Kesavananda Bharati challenged Kerala land reform laws affecting his math's property.
On 24 April 1973 a 13-judge Bench by 7:6 held Parliament can amend any part but not the basic structure.

steps.title: Three procedures
steps.body:
1. Simple majority (outside Art. 368): e.g. Arts. 2, 3, 4, 169 – creation of States, Legislative Councils.
2. Special majority under Art. 368(2): majority of total membership and 2/3 of present and voting in each House.
3. Special majority plus ratification by half the State Legislatures: federal matters – election of President, Union and State executive powers, judiciary, Seventh Schedule, representation in Parliament, Art. 368 itself.

steps.title: The case chain
steps.body:
- Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965): amendment is not 'law' under Art. 13 – Parliament can amend FRs.
- Golaknath (1967, 11 judges): Parliament cannot abridge FRs (prospective overruling).
- 24th Amendment (1971): Art. 13(4), 368(3).
- Kesavananda Bharati (1973): basic structure cannot be destroyed.
- Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975): free and fair elections basic; Art. 329A(4) struck down.
- Minerva Mills (1980): limited amending power is itself basic; Art. 368(4)–(5) struck down.
- Waman Rao (1981): Ninth Schedule laws after 24 April 1973 open to basic-structure review.
- I.R. Coelho (2007): Ninth Schedule laws reviewable against basic structure including Arts. 14, 19, 21.
- SCAORA (2015): judicial independence.

steps.title: Features held basic
steps.body: Supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form, secularism, federalism, separation of powers, judicial review, rule of law, free and fair elections, harmony of FR and DPSP, limited amending power, independence of judiciary.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that Kesavananda was unanimous: it was 7:6.
- Saying there is a fixed list of basic features: the list is developed case by case.

uni-llb-contracts.title: Law of Contracts I & II
uni-llb-contracts.description: The Indian Contract Act 1872 in depth – formation, consideration, capacity, free consent, void agreements, contingent contracts, performance, discharge, breach and damages, quasi-contracts and specific relief – followed by indemnity, guarantee, bailment, pledge, agency, the Sale of Goods Act 1930 and the Indian Partnership Act 1932. General education, not legal advice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB (3-year and 5-year) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Formation: Offer, Acceptance, Consideration and Capacity
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Law of Contract I)
courses.summary: Definitions in section 2, essentials in section 10, proposal and acceptance with communication and revocation rules (sections 3–9), consideration and its exceptions (sections 2(d) and 25), privity, and capacity of minors, persons of unsound mind and disqualified persons (sections 11–12, 68).
outcomes: Use section 2 definitions to trace proposal → promise → agreement → contract
Decide when communication of offer, acceptance and revocation is complete
Distinguish offer from invitation to treat with leading cases
Apply the definition of consideration, the privity rule and section 25 exceptions
Advise on agreements with minors including Mohori Bibee and section 68

lessons.title: Proposal, acceptance and invitation to treat

story.title: The boy who did not know about the reward

scenes.text: Gauri Dutt's nephew ran away. His servant Lalman was sent to search and found the boy.
Later a reward was announced. Lalman claimed it, but in Lalman Shukla v Gauri Dutt (1913) the court said he could not accept an offer he did not know of.

steps.title: The chain in section 2
steps.body:
2(a) proposal: signifying willingness to do or abstain, with a view to obtaining assent.
2(b) acceptance: assent to the proposal → the proposal becomes a promise.
2(e) every promise and set of promises forming consideration for each other = agreement.
2(h) agreement enforceable by law = contract.
Section 10: free consent, competent parties, lawful consideration and object, not expressly declared void.
Section 9: promises may be express or implied.

steps.title: Offer vs invitation to treat
steps.body:
- Display of goods with price tags: invitation (Pharmaceutical Society v Boots, 1953)
- Quoting a lowest price in reply to an enquiry: not an offer (Harvey v Facey, 1893)
- Auction: bid is the offer; fall of the hammer is acceptance
- Tenders: a call for tenders is an invitation; each tender is an offer
- General offer to the world: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball (1893)
- Specific offer vs general offer; cross offers do not make a contract

steps.title: Rules of acceptance
steps.body:
- Absolute and unqualified (s.7); a counter-offer rejects the offer (Hyde v Wrench, 1840)
- Expressed in a usual and reasonable manner unless a manner is prescribed (s.7(2))
- Must be by the offeree and communicated; mental acceptance is not enough (Felthouse v Bindley, 1862; Brogden v Metropolitan Railway, 1877 for acceptance by conduct)
- Performance of conditions can be acceptance (s.8)

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A posts on a website: 'Used bike, ₹30,000, first come first served.' B emails 'I'll take it at ₹28,000'. A replies 'No'. B then emails 'OK, ₹30,000'.
1. A's post: arguably an invitation to treat.
2. B's ₹28,000 email: offer (or counter-offer).
3. A rejects it.
4. B's ₹30,000 email: a fresh offer; no contract until A accepts it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling every advertisement an offer.
- Ignoring knowledge: you cannot accept an offer you do not know of (Lalman Shukla).

activity.prompt: Offer or invitation to treat?

items.text: A reward notice for finding a lost dog
Goods displayed with prices in a self-service store
A call for tenders by a municipality
A bid at an auction
A catalogue of a mail-order company

quiz.q: A counter-offer
quiz.why: Hyde v Wrench shows a counter-offer destroys the original offer.

quiz.q: Lalman Shukla v Gauri Dutt held that
options: Acceptance needs knowledge of the offer
quiz.why: Lalman did not know of the reward when he found the boy, so he could not accept it.

quiz.q: In an auction, acceptance occurs
options: At the fall of the hammer
quiz.why: The auctioneer accepts the bid by the fall of the hammer.

quiz.q: Harvey v Facey decided that quoting the lowest price is
quiz.why: It was only information in reply to an enquiry, not an offer to sell.

lessons.title: Communication and revocation (sections 3–6)

scenes.text: A posts a proposal to B on 1 June; B receives it on 3 June and posts an acceptance the same day.
A's letter of revocation reaches B on 4 June. Is there a contract?

steps.title: Section 4
steps.body:
Communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made.
Communication of acceptance is complete:
- as against the **proposer**, when it is put in course of transmission to him so as to be out of the power of the acceptor;
- as against the **acceptor**, when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer.
Communication of revocation is complete against the person who makes it when put in course of transmission, and against the recipient when it comes to his knowledge.

steps.title: Section 5 – time windows
steps.body:
A proposal may be revoked any time before communication of acceptance is complete as against the proposer, not afterwards.
An acceptance may be revoked any time before communication of acceptance is complete as against the acceptor, not afterwards.
Section 6: revocation by notice, lapse of time, failure to fulfil a condition precedent, death or insanity of proposer if known to acceptor before acceptance.

steps.title: Solving the story
steps.body:
1 June: A posts offer. 3 June: B receives it and posts acceptance → acceptance complete against A on 3 June. A's revocation reaching B on 4 June is too late; contract formed.
Variant: B posts acceptance 3 June; B telegraphs revocation of acceptance that reaches A on 4 June, before the letter of acceptance arrives on 5 June → B's revocation is valid because acceptance was not yet complete against B.

steps.title: Instantaneous communication
steps.body: Telephone, telex and similar: contract is made where acceptance is heard (Bhagwandas Goverdhandas Kedia v Girdharilal, 1966). Emails and online acceptances are now also governed by the IT Act 2000 provisions on time and place of electronic records.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating the date of posting of the OFFER as the moment of contract: the key date is when the acceptance is posted (against proposer) and received (against acceptor).

activity.prompt: Order the events and pick the moment the acceptor is bound
items: Proposer posts the offer
Offer reaches acceptor – proposal communicated
Acceptor posts acceptance – proposer bound
Acceptance reaches proposer – acceptor bound
Neither side can now revoke

quiz.q: As against the proposer, acceptance is complete when
quiz.why: Section 4 makes acceptance complete against the proposer once it is put in course of transmission.

quiz.q: Place of contract on telephone acceptance was decided in
quiz.why: Bhagwandas Goverdhandas Kedia (1966) held the contract is made where acceptance is heard.

quiz.q: An acceptor can revoke acceptance
options: Before the acceptance reaches the proposer
quiz.why: Section 5 allows revocation before acceptance is complete against the acceptor.

lessons.title: Consideration and privity

story.title: A mother's gift and a promise

scenes.text: A mother gifted property to her daughter on condition that the daughter pay an annual sum to the mother's brother.
In Chinnaya v Ramayya (1882) the brother could sue: consideration may move from 'the promisee or any other person'.

steps.title: Section 2(d)
steps.body:
When, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee **or any other person** has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains, or promises to do or abstain, something – such act, abstinence or promise is consideration.
Key points:
- At the desire of the promisor (Durga Prasad v Baldeo, 1880: act at the Collector's desire was not consideration for the promisor)
- May move from a third person (Chinnaya v Ramayya)
- May be past, present or future
- Need not be adequate (Explanation 2 to s.25) but must be real and lawful

steps.title: Section 25 exceptions – no consideration needed
steps.body:
1. Written and registered agreement made on account of natural love and affection between near relations (s.25(1)) – Rajlukhy Dabee v Bhootnath (1900): the couple were quarrelling, no natural love and affection.
2. Promise to compensate a person who has voluntarily done something for the promisor (s.25(2)).
3. Written, signed promise to pay a time-barred debt (s.25(3)).
Also: gifts actually made (s.25 Explanation 1), and agency needs no consideration (s.185).

steps.title: Privity of contract
steps.body:
A stranger to the contract cannot sue (Tweddle v Atkinson, 1861; Dunlop v Selfridge, 1915; in India M.C. Chacko v State Bank of Travancore, 1970).
Exceptions: trust or charge (Khwaja Muhammad Khan v Husaini Begum, 1910), family arrangements, acknowledgement or estoppel, assignment, agency, covenants running with land.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
X promises Y, his friend, ₹10,000 'because you are a good man'. No writing. Y sues.
1. Did Y do or promise anything at X's desire? No.
2. Any s.25 exception? Not near relations in writing and registered; no past voluntary service; no time-barred debt.
3. Result: agreement without consideration, void under s.25.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Copying the English rule that consideration must move from the promisee: Indian law allows 'any other person'.
- Confusing 'stranger to consideration' (can sue in India) with 'stranger to contract' (generally cannot).

activity.prompt: Enforceable or void?

items.text: Registered written promise by a father to give land to his son out of love
Oral promise to pay a friend for no reason
Signed written promise to pay a time-barred loan
Promise to pay a finder who returned your wallet voluntarily
Oral promise to a neighbour to gift a car

quiz.q: In India consideration may move from
options: The promisee or any other person
quiz.why: Section 2(d) uses the words 'the promisee or any other person'.

quiz.q: Inadequacy of consideration
options: Does not by itself make it void, but may be evidence on free consent
quiz.why: Explanation 2 to s.25 says so.

quiz.q: Rajlukhy Dabee is an authority on
quiz.why: It held natural love and affection was absent between quarrelling spouses.

quiz.q: Durga Prasad v Baldeo shows that consideration must be given
options: At the desire of the promisor
quiz.why: The work done at the Collector's desire was not consideration for the defendant's promise.

lessons.title: Capacity: minors, unsound mind and disqualified persons

scenes.text: Dharmodas Ghose, a minor, mortgaged his house to Brahmo Dutt for ₹20,000; the lender's agent knew he was a minor.
The Privy Council in Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose (1903) held a minor's agreement void and refused to order refund of the advance.

steps.title: Section 11–12
steps.body:
Competent: age of majority by the law he is subject to (18 under the Indian Majority Act 1875; 21 where a guardian of person or property is appointed by a court – that rule was in s.3 of the 1875 Act and the 1999 amendment brought uniformity at 18 for most purposes; state carefully), sound mind, not disqualified by law.
Section 12: sound mind = capable of understanding the contract and forming a rational judgment of its effect on his interests. A person usually of unsound mind may contract in lucid intervals, and vice versa (e.g. drunk).

steps.title: Rules on minors
steps.body:
1. Agreement with a minor is void ab initio (Mohori Bibee).
2. No ratification on attaining majority.
3. No estoppel against a minor who misrepresented age (Sadiq Ali Khan v Jai Kishore, 1928 PC).
4. Restitution: s.33 Specific Relief Act 1963 lets courts order a minor to restore benefit where he is plaintiff or defendant seeking to avoid the contract (equitable relief; Khan Gul v Lakha Singh, 1928).
5. Necessaries supplied to a minor: supplier reimbursed from the minor's property (s.68), no personal liability.
6. Minor can be a promisee, beneficiary, agent (s.184), and admitted to benefits of partnership (s.30 Partnership Act).

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A 17-year-old student buys a ₹1,50,000 gaming laptop on instalments by falsely stating he is 19. He defaults.
1. Agreement: void (minor).
2. Estoppel? Not against a minor.
3. Necessaries? A luxury gaming laptop is unlikely to be a necessary suited to his condition in life.
4. Remedy for the seller: possibly restitution of the laptop if still with him (equitable relief), not price or damages.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a minor's agreement 'voidable': it is void.
- Saying the minor is personally liable for necessaries: only his estate is (s.68).

activity.prompt: Tick what a minor CAN do
items: Be a beneficiary of a contract
Act as an agent
Be admitted to the benefits of a partnership
Be the payee of a promissory note

quiz.q: A minor's agreement is
quiz.why: Mohori Bibee held it absolutely void.

quiz.q: Liability for necessaries supplied to a minor is
quiz.why: Section 68 makes only the minor's property liable.

quiz.q: A minor who lies about his age
options: Is not estopped from pleading minority
Commits no wrong at all in any law
quiz.why: There is no estoppel against a statute that protects minors.

quiz.q: A person usually of unsound mind
options: Can contract when of sound mind
quiz.why: Section 12 lets him contract during lucid intervals.

questions.why: Section 2(h) defines contract.

questions.why: The words 'has done or abstained' recognise past consideration.

questions.why: Consideration moved from the mother, a third person.

questions.why: Section 25(3).

questions.q: Revocation of offer by death of proposer is effective
options: If the acceptor knew of the death before accepting
questions.why: Section 6(4).

questions.why: Section 33 of the Specific Relief Act 1963 enables it.

options: Do not create a contract without acceptance
questions.why: There is no acceptance of either offer.

questions.q: Tenders invited by a government department are
