questions.why: Such a person is incompetent under s.11, so the agreement is void.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Free Consent, Lawful Object, Void Agreements and Contingent Contracts
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Law of Contract I)
courses.summary: Coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation and mistake (sections 13–22); unlawful object and consideration (section 23); agreements expressly declared void (sections 24–30) including restraint of marriage, trade and legal proceedings and wagers; and contingent contracts (sections 31–36).
outcomes: Distinguish coercion, undue influence, fraud and misrepresentation and their consequences
Apply the rules on mistake of fact and of law
Test an agreement for unlawful object under section 23 and public policy
Apply sections 26–30 with leading cases on restraint of trade and wagers
Decide when a contingent contract becomes enforceable or void

lessons.title: Coercion and undue influence

story.title: The widow and the adopted son

scenes.text: In Chikham Ammiraju v Chikham Seshamma (1917) a man threatened to commit suicide unless his wife and son released property to his brother.
The Madras High Court held a threat of suicide is coercion: attempted suicide was then punishable, so it was an act 'forbidden by the Penal Code'.

steps.title: Section 14 and 15
steps.body:
Consent is free when not caused by coercion (s.15), undue influence (s.16), fraud (s.17), misrepresentation (s.18) or mistake (ss.20–22).
Coercion: committing or threatening any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code (now read with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023), or unlawfully detaining or threatening to detain property, to the prejudice of any person, with intention of causing a person to enter an agreement. It can be by anyone, against anyone, and it does not matter whether the IPC is in force where it happens.

steps.title: Undue influence (s.16)
steps.body:
Where the relations are such that one party can dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage.
Presumed positions: real or apparent authority (employer–employee, police), fiduciary relations (doctor–patient, guru–disciple, solicitor–client), mental distress, age or illness.
Burden (s.16(3)): where the transaction appears unconscionable and the dominant party is in a position to dominate, he must prove absence of undue influence. Pardanashin women get special protection.

steps.title: Consequences
steps.body:
s.19: contracts caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation are voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.
s.19A: undue influence – voidable; the court may set it aside absolutely or on terms.
s.72: money paid under coercion must be repaid.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A spiritual guru persuades an elderly devotee to gift him her house worth ₹80 lakh for no return.
1. Relationship: guru–disciple → position to dominate.
2. Transaction unconscionable on its face.
3. Burden shifts to the guru to prove free consent (s.16(3)).
4. Absent independent advice, the gift is voidable at the devotee's option (Mannu Singh v Umadat Pande, 1890).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying coercion must come from the other party: s.15 covers 'any person', even a stranger.

activity.prompt: Coercion or undue influence?

items.text: Threat to burn the shop unless a lease is signed
Doctor persuades a sick patient to sell land cheaply to him
Holding someone's car until he signs
Guru obtains gift of property from a disciple

quiz.q: Threat of suicide was held to be coercion in
quiz.why: The Madras High Court treated it as an act forbidden by the Penal Code.

quiz.q: Burden of proof in undue influence shifts when
options: The dominant party gets an unconscionable bargain
quiz.why: Section 16(3) shifts the burden in that situation.

quiz.q: A contract caused by coercion is
quiz.why: Section 19 makes it voidable at the option of the coerced party.

lessons.title: Fraud, misrepresentation and mistake

scenes.text: A seller knows his horse is unsound but says nothing. The buyer is his daughter who trusts him completely.
Silence is generally not fraud, but here there was a duty to speak because of the relationship (illustration to s.17).

steps.title: Fraud (s.17)
steps.body:
Acts by a party or his agent with intent to deceive or induce a contract:
1. Suggesting as fact what is not true by one who does not believe it true
2. Active concealment
3. A promise made without intention of performing
4. Any other act fitted to deceive
5. Act or omission declared fraudulent by law
Mere silence is not fraud unless there is a duty to speak or silence is equivalent to speech.
Derry v Peek (1889): fraud requires a false statement made knowingly, without belief in its truth, or recklessly.

steps.title: Misrepresentation (s.18)
steps.body:
Innocent false statements: positive assertion not warranted by the maker's information, breach of duty without intent to deceive, or causing a mistake as to the subject matter innocently.
Remedy: rescission (voidable). Under s.19 exception, if the party could have discovered the truth with ordinary diligence, the contract is not voidable for misrepresentation or silent fraud.

steps.title: Mistake (ss.20–22)
steps.body:
s.20: both parties under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement → void (e.g. goods had perished: Couturier v Hastie, 1856).
s.21: mistake of Indian law does not make it voidable; mistake of foreign law is treated like mistake of fact.
s.22: unilateral mistake – not voidable merely because one party was mistaken. But mistake as to identity (Cundy v Lindsay, 1878) or nature of document (non est factum, Foster v Mackinnon, 1869) can make it void.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A sells B a painting both believe is by Raja Ravi Varma for ₹50 lakh. Neither knew it was a copy.
- Is it a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement? Authorship goes to the identity of what is sold → arguably bilateral mistake under s.20 → void.
If A knew it was a copy and stated otherwise → fraud → voidable plus damages in tort of deceit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a contract induced by fraud 'void'.
- Treating unilateral mistake as making a contract void in all cases.

activity.prompt: Classify the vitiating factor

items.text: Seller knowingly rolls back a car's odometer
Seller honestly but wrongly says the flat is 1,200 sq ft based on old plans
Ship carrying the sold cargo had sunk before sale, unknown to both
Promise made with no intention of performing it

quiz.q: Derry v Peek defined
quiz.why: It held fraud needs knowledge of falsity, absence of belief or recklessness.

quiz.q: Mistake of Indian law
quiz.why: Section 21 says a contract is not voidable because of a mistake as to any law in force in India.

quiz.q: Both parties mistaken about an essential fact makes the agreement
quiz.why: Section 20 declares it void.

quiz.q: Silence amounts to fraud when
options: There is a duty to speak
quiz.why: The Explanation to s.17 makes silence fraud where there is a duty to speak.

lessons.title: Unlawful object and agreements declared void

scenes.text: A software company makes engineers sign a clause not to work for any competitor in India for two years after leaving.
Under s.27 post-employment restraints are void in India (Superintendence Co. v Krishan Murgai, 1981), though restraints during employment can be valid.

steps.title: Section 23
steps.body:
Consideration or object is unlawful if it is forbidden by law, would defeat any law, is fraudulent, involves injury to person or property, or the court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy.
Examples: agreement to pay a bribe; trafficking in public offices; agreement to stifle prosecution of a non-compoundable offence; champerty in some cases. Gherulal Parakh v Mahadeodas (1959): the doctrine of public policy should be applied cautiously; heads should not be expanded easily.

steps.title: Expressly void (ss.24–30)
steps.body:
s.24 – part unlawful consideration/object
s.25 – without consideration (subject to exceptions)
s.26 – restraint of marriage of any person other than a minor
s.27 – restraint of trade, profession or business (exception: sale of goodwill within specified local limits)
s.28 – restraint of legal proceedings, or limiting the time to enforce rights (arbitration clauses saved)
s.29 – uncertain agreements
s.30 – wagering agreements (exception for horse-race prizes over ₹500 in the section)
s.56 – impossible acts

steps.title: Wagers
steps.body:
Essentials: two parties, mutual chances of gain or loss, uncertain event, neither party controls the event, no other interest than the stake.
Wagers are void but not illegal (except where a State law prohibits gambling), so collateral transactions may be enforceable in most States (Gherulal Parakh). Insurance is not a wager because of insurable interest.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A sells his chemist shop and goodwill to B and agrees not to open another chemist shop within 3 km for 5 years.
1. Restraint of trade: prima facie void (s.27).
2. Exception: seller of goodwill may agree to refrain from carrying on similar business within specified local limits, so long as the buyer carries on like business, if reasonable.
3. 3 km and 5 years look reasonable → valid.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling all void agreements illegal: every illegal agreement is void, but not every void agreement is illegal.
- Applying the English 'reasonable restraint' test to employee restraints after employment: Indian courts generally treat them as void.

activity.prompt: Which section makes it void?

items.text: Agreement that an adult will never marry
Ex-employee may not work anywhere in his field for 3 years
Clause barring any suit in any court ever
Bet on which team wins a match

quiz.q: Post-employment non-compete clauses in India are generally
quiz.why: Superintendence Co. v Krishan Murgai held them void.

quiz.q: A wagering agreement is
quiz.why: Section 30 declares wagers void.

quiz.q: Gherulal Parakh cautioned courts about
quiz.why: It said public policy is an unruly horse and should not be stretched easily.

quiz.q: An arbitration clause is
options: Saved by an exception to s.28
quiz.why: Exception 1 to s.28 protects agreements to refer disputes to arbitration.

lessons.title: Contingent contracts (sections 31–36)

scenes.text: A agrees to pay B ₹1 lakh if a certain ship returns within a year.
The ship sinks within the year. The contract becomes void.

steps.title: Definition and rules
steps.body:
s.31: a contract to do or not to do something if some event, collateral to the contract, does or does not happen.
s.32: contingent on an event happening – enforceable only when the event happens; void if it becomes impossible.
s.33: on an event not happening – enforceable when its happening becomes impossible.
s.34: event depending on future conduct of a living person – becomes impossible when that person acts so as to make it impossible.
s.35: within a fixed time – void if not happened (or certain not to happen) within time.
s.36: on an impossible event – void, whether or not parties knew of the impossibility.

steps.title: Applying s.34
steps.body: A agrees to pay B if B marries C. C marries D. Marriage of B to C is now considered impossible (although D may die and C may later marry B) → the contract is void.

steps.title: Wager vs contingent contract
steps.body: Every wager is a contingent contract, but not every contingent contract is a wager. Insurance, indemnity and guarantee are contingent contracts with genuine interests and reciprocal promises.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling an event that is part of the promise itself a 'collateral event'. The event must be collateral – e.g. a sale where delivery is the very performance is not contingent.

activity.prompt: Order the analysis of a contingent contract problem
items: Identify the collateral event
Decide whether the contract depends on happening or not happening
Check if a time limit is fixed
Check whether the event has happened or become impossible
Conclude: enforceable, not yet enforceable, or void

quiz.q: A contract contingent on an impossible event is
quiz.why: Section 36 makes it void whether or not the impossibility was known.

quiz.q: A contract contingent on a ship NOT returning becomes enforceable when
options: A year passes in all cases
quiz.why: Under s.33 it is enforceable when the happening of the event becomes impossible.

quiz.q: Every wagering agreement is
quiz.why: Wagers depend on an uncertain collateral event, but are void under s.30.

questions.q: Free consent is defined in
questions.why: Section 14 lists what makes consent free.

questions.q: Consent is defined in s.13 as agreeing upon
options: The same thing in the same sense
questions.why: Consensus ad idem.

questions.q: Undue influence makes a contract
questions.why: Section 19A.

questions.q: A promise made without any intention of performing it is
questions.why: Section 17(3).

questions.q: Agreement in restraint of marriage of a minor is
questions.why: Section 26 excludes minors from its protection.

questions.q: Couturier v Hastie concerns
questions.why: Common mistake about existence of subject matter.

questions.q: Agreement uncertain in meaning is void under
questions.why: Section 29.

questions.q: Money paid under coercion is recoverable under
questions.why: Section 72.

questions.q: Contracts contingent on an event within a fixed time are governed by
questions.why: Section 35.

questions.q: Seller of goodwill may agree not to compete within local limits – this is
questions.why: The only statutory exception in s.27.

questions.q: Non est factum relates to
options: Mistake as to nature of document signed
questions.why: The signer did not know what kind of document he signed.

questions.q: Misrepresentation cannot be pleaded where
options: The party could discover the truth with ordinary diligence
questions.why: Exception to s.19.

questions.q: Agreement to pay money to procure a government job by influence is
options: Void as opposed to public policy
questions.why: Trafficking in public offices is against public policy under s.23.

questions.q: An agreement where the object is partly unlawful and inseparable is void under
questions.why: Section 24 voids the whole agreement if the unlawful part cannot be separated.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Performance, Discharge, Breach, Damages, Quasi-Contracts and Specific Relief
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Law of Contract I)
courses.summary: Who must perform and when (sections 37–67), discharge by performance, agreement, frustration (section 56) and breach including anticipatory breach (section 39); damages under sections 73–75 with Hadley v Baxendale; quasi-contracts (sections 68–72); and the Specific Relief Act 1963 after the 2018 amendment.
outcomes: Identify who must perform, joint promisors and reciprocal promises
Apply the doctrine of frustration with Satyabrata Ghose
Calculate damages using remoteness and mitigation
Distinguish liquidated damages and penalty under section 74
Explain quasi-contractual obligations and specific performance after 2018

lessons.title: Performance and discharge by agreement

story.title: The novation that saved a deal

scenes.text: A owes B ₹5 lakh. A, B and C agree that C will owe the debt to B instead and A is released.
This is novation under section 62: a new contract replaces the old.

steps.title: Who must perform
steps.body:
s.37: parties must perform or offer to perform their promises unless excused.
s.38: a valid tender (offer of performance) that is refused discharges the promisor from further tender but not from the debt.
s.40: if personal skill is required, the promisor must perform personally.
s.42–44: joint promisors – all must perform jointly; the promisee may compel any one of them to perform the whole; contribution among them.
s.46–50: time and place; s.55: time as essence – if not essence, failure only gives damages.

steps.title: Discharge by agreement (s.62–63)
steps.body:
- **Novation**: substituting a new contract
- **Rescission**: cancelling the contract
- **Alteration**: changing terms
- **Remission** (s.63): promisee may dispense with or remit performance, wholly or partly, or accept any satisfaction he thinks fit, without consideration
- **Waiver** of rights
Also: merger, and discharge by lapse of time under the Limitation Act.

steps.title: Remission
steps.body: A owes B ₹10,000. B agrees to accept ₹6,000 in full satisfaction, and A pays it. Under s.63 the whole debt is discharged even without fresh consideration (contrast the English rule in Pinnel's case).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming time is always of the essence in commercial contracts: courts presume it is not in contracts for sale of immovable property unless clearly stated.

activity.prompt: Which mode of discharge by agreement?

items.text: Parties cancel a supply order by mutual consent
Creditor accepts ₹7,000 for a ₹10,000 debt
Delivery date changed from 1 May to 15 May
A new debtor substituted with consent of all

quiz.q: Accepting less money in full satisfaction is valid in India under
quiz.why: Section 63 allows remission without consideration.

quiz.q: Substitution of a new contract is
quiz.why: Novation replaces the original contract.

quiz.q: A promisee can compel any one of several joint promisors to perform the whole under
quiz.why: Section 43 permits that and gives contribution among promisors.

lessons.title: Frustration and breach

scenes.text: A company agreed to develop land into plots, but part was requisitioned during World War II.
In Satyabrata Ghose v Mugneeram Bangur (1954) the Supreme Court held the contract was not frustrated: the delay did not destroy its basic purpose.

steps.title: Section 56
steps.body:
Para 1: agreement to do an impossible act is void.
Para 2: a contract becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful after it is made, due to an event the promisor could not prevent (supervening impossibility).
Para 3: promisor who knew of impossibility must compensate the promisee.
Satyabrata Ghose: 'impossible' means impracticable from the point of view of the object and purpose, not literally impossible; s.56 is exhaustive in India.
Not frustration: increased cost, commercial hardship, strikes generally, self-induced frustration (Maritime National Fish, 1935). Examples: destruction of subject matter (Taylor v Caldwell, 1863), death or incapacity in personal contracts, change of law, war.

steps.title: Breach
steps.body:
- Actual breach at the time of performance
- **Anticipatory breach** (s.39): a party refuses or disables himself before the due date; the other may rescind immediately or wait. Hochster v De La Tour (1853).
If the innocent party keeps the contract alive and a frustrating event occurs before the due date, he loses the right to damages (Avery v Bowden, 1855).

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A hall is booked for a wedding on 10 Dec. On 8 Dec the hall burns down without fault. Advance of ₹50,000 paid.
1. Supervening impossibility → contract void under s.56.
2. s.65: when a contract becomes void, any person who received an advantage must restore it → hall owner refunds ₹50,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using frustration where performance just became expensive: courts refuse (e.g. Alopi Parshad v Union of India, 1960).

activity.prompt: Frustrated or not?

items.text: Singer dies before the concert she contracted to perform
Raw material price doubles
Theatre burns down before the hire date
Supplier's own factory strike he could have averted
New law bans the export contracted for

quiz.q: Satyabrata Ghose held that 'impossible' in s.56 means
options: Impracticable and useless in view of the object
quiz.why: The Court gave impossibility a practical meaning tied to purpose.

quiz.q: Anticipatory breach is dealt with in
quiz.why: Section 39 covers refusal before the time for performance.

quiz.q: Advance paid under a frustrated contract is returned under
quiz.why: Section 65 requires restoration of benefits when an agreement is discovered or becomes void.

lessons.title: Damages: sections 73–75

scenes.text: A mill's crankshaft broke; the carrier delayed returning it from repair, and the mill stood idle.
In Hadley v Baxendale (1854) lost profits were not recoverable because the carrier was not told the mill would be idle.

steps.title: Section 73
steps.body:
Compensation for loss or damage which **naturally arose in the usual course of things** from the breach, or which the parties **knew, when they made the contract, to be likely** to result. No compensation for remote and indirect loss. Explanation: the means of remedying inconvenience (mitigation) must be taken into account.
Kinds: ordinary (general), special (knowledge), nominal, exemplary (rare in contract – e.g. dishonour of a cheque in older law, breach of promise to marry).

steps.title: Section 74
steps.body:
Where a sum is named as payable on breach, or there is a penalty stipulation, the innocent party may get reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount named, whether or not actual loss is proved.
India does not apply the English penalty/liquidated damages distinction strictly: the named sum is the ceiling. Fateh Chand v Balkishan Das (1963); ONGC v Saw Pipes (2003); Kailash Nath Associates v DDA (2015) – where loss is capable of proof, it must be shown; reasonable compensation up to the cap.

steps.title: Worked numeric 1 – market rule
steps.body:
S contracts to sell 100 tonnes of steel to B at ₹50,000/tonne, delivery 1 March. S refuses on 1 March, when the market price is ₹56,000/tonne.
Damages = (market − contract) × quantity = (56,000 − 50,000) × 100 = ₹6,00,000.
If B unreasonably waited and bought at ₹60,000 in April, he still gets only ₹6,00,000 because he had to mitigate at the date of breach.

steps.title: Worked numeric 2 – section 74
steps.body:
A construction contract has a clause: 'Delay penalty ₹20,000 per week, maximum ₹2,00,000.' Contractor is 15 weeks late; owner proves actual loss of ₹1,40,000.
Clause cap: 15 × 20,000 = ₹3,00,000 but maximum ₹2,00,000.
Under s.74, reasonable compensation not exceeding ₹2,00,000; since actual loss is proved at ₹1,40,000, the court is likely to award ₹1,40,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Awarding the full penalty sum automatically.
- Forgetting mitigation in s.73 Explanation.

activity.prompt: Tick every question you must ask when computing damages under s.73
items: Did the loss arise naturally in the usual course of things?
Did the parties know of special circumstances when contracting?
What was the market price at the date of breach?
Did the claimant take reasonable steps to mitigate?
Is any loss too remote or indirect?

quiz.q: Contract price ₹400/unit, market price at breach ₹460/unit, 500 units. Damages?
Under s.74 the sum named in the contract is
options: The upper limit of reasonable compensation
quiz.why: Courts award reasonable compensation not exceeding the stipulated sum.

quiz.q: Hadley v Baxendale is the leading case on
quiz.why: It set the two limbs of recoverable loss reproduced in s.73.

quiz.q: Kailash Nath Associates v DDA (2015) said that where loss can be proved
quiz.why: Only where loss is difficult to prove can the named sum be taken as a genuine pre-estimate without proof.

lessons.title: Quasi-contracts and specific relief

story.title: Goods left at the wrong house

scenes.text: A trader delivers goods to B's house by mistake. B uses them.
Under s.70 B must pay for goods he enjoyed when they were not delivered gratuitously.

steps.title: Sections 68–72
steps.body:
Based on unjust enrichment, not agreement:
- s.68 necessaries supplied to an incapable person
- s.69 payment by an interested person of money another is bound to pay
- s.70 non-gratuitous act enjoyed by another (State of West Bengal v B.K. Mondal, 1962: government liable to pay for work it accepted, even though the contract did not comply with Art. 299)
- s.71 finder of goods – has the responsibility of a bailee
- s.72 money paid or goods delivered by mistake or under coercion (Sales Tax Officer v Kanhaiya Lal, 1959: tax paid under mistake of law recoverable)

steps.title: Specific Relief Act 1963
steps.body:
After the 2018 amendment, s.10 says specific performance **shall** be enforced by the court subject to ss.11(2), 14 and 16 – it is no longer discretionary in the old sense.
s.14: contracts not specifically enforceable – where a party has obtained substituted performance (s.20), contracts involving continuous duty the court cannot supervise, contracts dependent on personal qualifications, determinable contracts.
s.20: substituted performance by the aggrieved party at the defaulter's cost after 30 days' written notice.
Injunctions: temporary (CPC Order 39), perpetual (s.38), mandatory (s.39). s.41: cases where injunction is refused. Lumley v Wagner (1852): negative covenant enforced by injunction (s.42).

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
Seller agrees to sell a flat for ₹90 lakh; buyer is ready and willing and paid ₹10 lakh. Seller backs out because prices rose.
1. Contract for immovable property – damages not adequate as each property is unique.
2. Buyer has shown readiness and willingness (s.16(c)).
3. After 2018, the court shall decree specific performance unless barred by s.14 or s.16.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying quasi-contracts arise from agreement.
- Quoting pre-2018 law that specific performance is purely discretionary.

activity.prompt: Which section applies?

items.text: Food supplied to a person of unsound mind
Municipality uses a building a contractor built without valid contract
Person picks up a lost wallet
Bank pays a sum twice by mistake

quiz.q: State of West Bengal v B.K. Mondal applied
quiz.why: The State was liable to pay for the benefit it enjoyed.

quiz.q: After 2018, specific performance under s.10 is
options: To be enforced by the court subject to the Act's exceptions
quiz.why: The amendment made it the general rule.

quiz.q: A finder of goods is in the position of a
quiz.why: Section 71 gives him a bailee's responsibility.

questions.q: A valid tender that is refused discharges the promisor from
questions.why: Under s.38 a refused tender of goods discharges further tender; money debt remains.

questions.q: Taylor v Caldwell involved
questions.why: Destruction of subject matter frustrated the contract.

questions.q: Self-induced frustration
questions.why: A party cannot rely on an event he caused.

questions.q: Damages for 200 units, contract ₹1,000, market at breach ₹1,150:
Duty to mitigate is found in
questions.why: The Explanation to s.73.

questions.q: Fateh Chand v Balkishan Das is a leading case on
questions.why: It held the named sum is the outer limit.

questions.q: Hochster v De La Tour concerns
questions.why: Refusal before the due date.

questions.q: Money paid under mistake is recoverable under
questions.why: Section 72.

questions.q: Substituted performance requires notice of at least
questions.why: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act requires 30 days' written notice.

questions.q: An injunction to enforce a negative covenant was granted in
questions.why: The singer was restrained from singing elsewhere.

questions.q: Contract with owner's clause 'maximum ₹1,00,000 delay damages'; proved loss ₹1,50,000. Under s.74 the maximum award is
questions.why: Compensation cannot exceed the stipulated sum.

questions.q: Time is generally not of the essence in
options: Contracts for sale of immovable property
questions.why: Courts presume so unless parties clearly intended otherwise.

questions.q: Kanhaiya Lal (1959) allowed recovery of tax paid under
questions.why: 'Mistake' in s.72 includes mistake of law.

questions.q: Performance requiring personal skill must be done by
questions.why: Section 40.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Indemnity, Guarantee, Bailment, Pledge and Agency
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Law of Contract II)
courses.summary: Contracts of indemnity (sections 124–125) and guarantee (126–147) with the surety's rights and discharge; bailment (148–171) including duties, lien and finder of goods; pledge (172–181); and agency (182–238): creation, ratification, authority, duties, liability to third parties and termination.
outcomes: Distinguish indemnity and guarantee and state the rights of an indemnity-holder
Explain co-extensive liability of the surety and modes of discharge
State duties of bailor and bailee and the rule on lien
Identify who may pledge goods validly
Explain kinds of agents, ratification, and the principal's liability

lessons.title: Indemnity and guarantee

story.title: The bank loan and the friend

scenes.text: Meena takes a ₹10 lakh loan; her friend Kabir signs as guarantor.
Meena defaults. The bank sues Kabir first, without suing Meena. Can it?

steps.title: Indemnity (ss.124–125)
steps.body:
s.124: a contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused by the conduct of the promisor himself or of any other person. Two parties: indemnifier and indemnity-holder.
s.125 rights of the indemnity-holder: all damages he is compelled to pay in any suit, all costs, and sums paid under a compromise, if he acted prudently.
Gajanan Moreshwar v Moreshwar Madan (1942): the indemnity-holder can call on the indemnifier once liability becomes absolute, even before paying.

steps.title: Guarantee (ss.126–129)
steps.body:
Three parties: creditor, principal debtor, surety. Three contracts (creditor–debtor, creditor–surety, surety–debtor implied indemnity).
s.127: anything done for the benefit of the principal debtor is sufficient consideration for the surety.
s.128: surety's liability is **co-extensive** with that of the principal debtor unless otherwise provided. The creditor may sue the surety without first suing the debtor (Bank of Bihar v Damodar Prasad, 1969).
s.129: continuing guarantee; s.130 revocation by notice for future transactions; s.131 death of surety revokes as to future transactions.

steps.title: Discharge of surety and rights
steps.body:
Discharge: variance in terms without consent (s.133), release or discharge of principal debtor (s.134), compounding or giving time to the debtor (s.135), creditor's act or omission impairing surety's remedy (s.139), loss of security (s.141).
Rights: subrogation (s.140), indemnity from debtor (s.145), contribution among co-sureties equally (s.146) or in proportion to limits (s.147).

steps.title: Co-sureties
steps.body:
A, B and C guarantee a ₹3,00,000 debt with limits ₹50,000, ₹1,00,000 and ₹2,00,000. Debtor defaults on ₹2,10,000.
s.147: each pays equally up to their limits.
Equal share = 2,10,000 / 3 = 70,000. A's limit is 50,000 → A pays 50,000. Remaining 1,60,000 split between B and C = 80,000 each (within limits).
A ₹50,000, B ₹80,000, C ₹80,000 = ₹2,10,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the bank must sue the debtor first: liability is co-extensive and immediate.
- Treating indemnity as having three parties: it has two.

activity.prompt: Does this discharge the surety?

items.text: Creditor and debtor change loan interest without surety's consent
Creditor merely delays suing the debtor
Creditor gives the debtor extra time by binding contract
Creditor releases the debtor

quiz.q: Surety's liability is
options: Secondary and only after suing debtor
quiz.why: Section 128 makes it co-extensive.

quiz.q: Indemnity-holder may claim before paying once liability is absolute – case?
quiz.why: The Bombay High Court so held in 1942.

quiz.q: Creditor's mere forbearance to sue
quiz.why: Section 137 says forbearance does not discharge the surety.

quiz.q: Debt ₹1,80,000; two co-sureties with equal unlimited guarantees each pay
quiz.why: Co-sureties contribute equally under s.146: 1,80,000 ÷ 2 = ₹90,000.

lessons.title: Bailment

story.title: The lost bag at the cloakroom

scenes.text: A traveller leaves a bag at a railway cloakroom and gets a token; the bag is stolen through the staff's negligence.
The bailee must take the care a person of ordinary prudence would take of his own goods (s.151).

steps.title: Definition (s.148)
steps.body:
Delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, on a contract that they shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or disposed of according to the bailor's directions.
Essentials: delivery (actual or constructive), purpose, return of the same goods. Money deposited in a bank is not bailment (the same notes are not returned).
Ultzen v Nicols (1894) and in India the 'possession' test: a car parked in a self-park lot may not be bailment if keys are kept by the owner.

steps.title: Duties
steps.body:
Bailor: disclose known faults (s.150), bear necessary expenses in gratuitous bailment (s.158).
Bailee: reasonable care (s.151), not liable for loss despite such care absent special contract (s.152), no unauthorised use (s.154), not to mix goods (ss.155–157), return goods on time (s.160), liable if not returned in time (s.161), return accretions (s.163).
Rights: lien – particular lien for services involving skill and labour (s.170); general lien for bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of High Court, policy brokers (s.171).

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A gives his car to a garage for repairs costing ₹18,000. He refuses to pay.
1. Bailment for reward.
2. Garage applied skill and labour → particular lien under s.170.
3. It can retain the car until ₹18,000 is paid, but not sell it without a court order or statutory power.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying a bailee is an insurer: under s.152 he is liable only for want of reasonable care unless the contract says otherwise.

activity.prompt: Particular or general lien?

items.text: Tailor who stitched a suit
Banker over securities for a general balance
Jeweller who reset a ring
Wharfinger over goods for general dues

quiz.q: Standard of care for a bailee is
options: Ordinary prudence regarding own goods of the same kind
quiz.why: Section 151 sets the ordinary prudence standard.

quiz.q: General lien is available to
quiz.why: Section 171 lists bankers among those with general lien.

quiz.q: A bank deposit of cash is
quiz.why: The identical notes are not returned, so it is a debtor–creditor relation.

lessons.title: Pledge

scenes.text: Asha pledges gold ornaments with a lender for a ₹1,00,000 loan.
She defaults. The lender gives reasonable notice and sells the ornaments.

steps.title: Definition and rights
steps.body:
s.172: bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise. Pawnor and pawnee.
Pawnee may retain goods for the debt, interest and necessary expenses (s.173). On default (s.176) he may sue on the debt and retain goods as collateral, or sell after **reasonable notice**; deficiency recoverable from pawnor, surplus to be paid to pawnor.
Pawnor may redeem before actual sale (s.177).

steps.body:
- Mercantile agent in possession with owner's consent, acting in ordinary course (s.178)
- Person in possession under a voidable contract not yet rescinded (s.178A)

Lallan Prasad v Rahmat Ali (1967): pawnee who has sold or lost the goods cannot sue for the debt without being able to return them.

steps.body:

After notice, the gold sells for ₹1,30,000 → surplus ₹15,000 to Asha.
If it had sold for ₹1,05,000 → deficit ₹10,000 recoverable from Asha.

lessons.title: Agency

scenes.text: A company's sales manager signs a contract at a 20% discount; his authority was only 10%.
If the buyer had no notice of the limit and the act was within apparent authority, the company may still be bound (s.237).

steps.title: Creation
steps.body:
s.182: agent is a person employed to do any act for another or represent another in dealings with third persons.
Modes: express or implied authority (s.187), by estoppel/holding out (s.237), by necessity (s.189), by ratification (ss.196–200).
Ratification conditions: agent purported to act for the principal; principal existed and was competent at the time; full knowledge; whole transaction ratified; cannot injure a third person (s.200).

steps.title: Duties and rights
steps.body:
Agent's duties: follow directions and customs (s.211), skill and diligence (s.212), render accounts (s.213), not deal on own account without consent (s.215–216), not delegate except as allowed (s.190).
Agent's rights: remuneration (s.219), lien (s.221), indemnity (ss.222–223).
Sub-agent (s.191) vs substituted agent (s.194).

steps.title: Liability and termination
steps.body:
Principal is bound by acts of agent within authority (s.226), including torts and frauds in the course of business (Lloyd v Grace Smith, 1912).
Agent personally liable: foreign principal, undisclosed principal, principal cannot be sued (s.230); breach of warranty of authority (s.235).
Termination (s.201): revocation, renunciation, completion, death or insanity, insolvency of principal. Agency coupled with interest cannot be terminated to the agent's prejudice (s.202).

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
Without authority, X buys rice for Y on Monday at ₹40/kg. On Wednesday Y, knowing all facts, says 'I accept the purchase'.
Ratification: X acted in Y's name; Y existed and was competent; full knowledge; whole transaction adopted → Y bound as if he had authorised it from Monday (s.196).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying consideration is needed to create agency: s.185 says it is not.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Sale of Goods Act 1930 and Indian Partnership Act 1932
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Law of Contract II)
courses.summary: Sale and agreement to sell, conditions and warranties with implied terms and caveat emptor, passing of property and risk, transfer of title by non-owners, rights of the unpaid seller; then partnership: definition and tests, rights and duties of partners, implied authority, liability to third parties, registration effects and dissolution.
outcomes: Distinguish sale from agreement to sell and conditions from warranties
Apply implied conditions in sections 14–17 and exceptions to caveat emptor
Apply rules for passing of property in section 20–24
Explain unpaid seller's lien, stoppage in transit and resale
Apply section 4 and the effects of non-registration under section 69

lessons.title: Sale, conditions, warranties and caveat emptor

scenes.text: A buyer asked a chemist for a hot-water bottle; it burst and injured his wife.
In Priest v Last (1903) the purpose was obvious, so the implied condition of fitness for purpose was breached.

steps.title: Sale vs agreement to sell (s.4)
steps.body:
Contract of sale: seller transfers or agrees to transfer property in goods to the buyer for a price.
- **Sale**: property passes now; seller can sue for price; risk with buyer.
- **Agreement to sell**: property passes in future or on a condition; remedy usually damages; becomes a sale when the time elapses or conditions are fulfilled.
Goods (s.2(7)): every kind of movable property other than actionable claims and money; includes stock and shares, growing crops.

steps.title: Condition vs warranty (ss.12–13)
steps.body:
Condition: stipulation essential to the main purpose; breach gives right to repudiate.
Warranty: collateral to the main purpose; breach gives only damages.
s.13: buyer may waive a condition or elect to treat it as a warranty; where goods are accepted, breach of condition can only be treated as breach of warranty.

steps.title: Implied terms (ss.14–17)
steps.body:
s.14: title, quiet possession, freedom from encumbrances.
s.15: sale by description – goods must correspond with description (Varley v Whipp, 1900).
s.16(1): fitness for purpose where buyer makes purpose known and relies on seller's skill (Priest v Last); s.16(2): merchantable quality where goods bought by description from a dealer.
s.17: sale by sample.
**Caveat emptor** (s.16 opening) – buyer beware, subject to exceptions: fitness for purpose, merchantability, usage of trade, seller's fraud.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
B tells a dealer he needs a pump to lift water to the 10th floor and relies on the dealer's choice. The pump works but only to the 4th floor.
1. Purpose made known, reliance on skill, dealer in such goods → implied condition of fitness (s.16(1)).
2. Breach → B may reject the pump and recover the price, unless he has accepted it, in which case damages only.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling every breach of an implied term a warranty: ss.14(a), 15, 16 and 17 create conditions.

activity.prompt: Condition or warranty?

items.text: Seller has a right to sell
Buyer shall enjoy quiet possession
Goods correspond with description
Goods free from undisclosed charge or encumbrance
Goods reasonably fit for buyer's known purpose

quiz.why: A warranty is collateral, so breach gives only a claim for damages.

quiz.why: The buyer's purpose was obvious and he relied on the seller.

quiz.q: 'Goods' under the Act exclude
quiz.why: Section 2(7) excludes money and actionable claims.

quiz.why: A reaping machine did not match its description.

lessons.title: Passing of property and transfer of title

scenes.text: A thief sells a stolen car to an innocent buyer for full value.
Nemo dat quod non habet: no one gives what he does not have – the owner can recover the car.

steps.title: Rules for passing of property
steps.body:
Property passes when intended (s.19). Presumptive rules:
- s.20: specific goods in deliverable state – when the contract is made, even if payment or delivery is postponed
- s.21: specific goods to be put into deliverable state – when done and buyer has notice
- s.22: specific goods to be weighed or measured to fix price – when done and buyer notified
- s.23: unascertained goods – on unconditional appropriation of goods of description in deliverable state with assent
- s.24: goods on approval or sale or return – on acceptance, act adopting, or retention beyond the time fixed or a reasonable time
s.26: risk prima facie passes with property.

steps.title: Exceptions to nemo dat
steps.body:
- s.27: estoppel; mercantile agent in possession with owner's consent
- s.28: joint owner in sole possession
- s.29: possession under a voidable contract not rescinded
- s.30: seller or buyer in possession after sale
- s.169 Contract Act (finder's sale) and pawnee's sale

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
On 1 June A agrees to sell a specific, ready-to-use TV to B for ₹40,000, payment on 5 June, delivery on 7 June. On 3 June the TV is destroyed by fire at A's shop without A's fault.
Property passed on 1 June (s.20) → risk with B (s.26) → B must pay ₹40,000, unless the parties agreed otherwise.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming property passes only on payment or delivery: for specific goods in a deliverable state it passes on making the contract.

activity.prompt: Order the transfer of unascertained goods
items: Contract for 50 bags of rice of a description
Seller separates 50 bags matching description
Goods are in deliverable state
Seller appropriates them unconditionally with buyer's assent
Property passes to buyer

quiz.why: Section 20 is the default rule.

quiz.why: Section 26 links risk with ownership.

options: Keeps them beyond the fixed time
quiz.why: Section 24 treats retention beyond the time as acceptance.

lessons.title: Rights of the unpaid seller

story.title: Goods on a truck, buyer insolvent

scenes.text: A seller dispatches goods by truck; on the way he learns the buyer is insolvent.
He instructs the carrier to stop and return the goods – stoppage in transit.

steps.title: Who is an unpaid seller (s.45)
steps.body: When the whole price has not been paid or tendered, or a bill of exchange given as payment has been dishonoured.

steps.title: Rights against goods
steps.body:
- **Lien** (ss.47–49): retain goods in possession until paid; lost on delivery to carrier without reserving right, buyer obtaining possession, or waiver
- **Stoppage in transit** (ss.50–52): on buyer's insolvency, while goods are with a carrier
- **Resale** (s.54): perishable goods, or after notice of intention to resell if buyer does not pay in a reasonable time; seller may recover loss
Rights against the buyer personally: suit for price (s.55), damages for non-acceptance (s.56), interest (s.61).

steps.title: Resale numeric
steps.body:
Price ₹2,00,000 unpaid. After notice, seller resells for ₹1,70,000, incurring ₹5,000 resale costs.
Loss = 2,00,000 − 1,70,000 + 5,000 = ₹35,000 recoverable from buyer. If resale had fetched ₹2,10,000 after notice, the seller keeps the profit (s.54(2)).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Stoppage in transit requires buyer's insolvency; lien does not.

activity.prompt: Which right is used?

Goods on a ship, buyer declared insolvent
Perishable fruit, buyer not paying

Stoppage in transit requires the buyer to be

quiz.why: Section 49 lists this as a mode of losing lien.

lessons.title: Partnership: nature, relations and dissolution

scenes.text: A lender to a restaurant takes a share of profits as interest. Is he a partner?
Cox v Hickman (1860) and s.6: the real test is mutual agency, not mere sharing of profits.

steps.title: Definition (s.4) and tests
steps.body:
Relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all.
Elements: agreement, business, sharing profits, **mutual agency** (the 'acting for all' limb). Partnership does not arise from status (s.5) – e.g. a Hindu Undivided Family business is not partnership.
Firm is not a legal person separate from partners (contrast LLP Act 2008).

steps.title: Relations
steps.body:
Partners' rights (s.12–13): take part in business, be consulted, access books, equal share of profits by default, interest on advances at 6% p.a. (s.13(d)), indemnity.
Implied authority (s.19): act done in the usual way of business binds the firm; restrictions listed in s.19(2) (e.g. submit to arbitration, open bank account in own name, compromise claims, acquire immovable property).
Liability (s.25): every partner is jointly and severally liable for acts of the firm. Holding out (s.28).
Minor admitted to benefits (s.30).

steps.title: Registration and dissolution
steps.body:
Registration is not compulsory, but s.69: an unregistered firm or its partners cannot sue third parties or each other to enforce rights arising from a contract (third parties can still sue the firm).
Dissolution: by agreement (s.40), compulsory (s.41: insolvency, unlawful business), on notice in partnership at will (s.43), by court (s.44: insanity, misconduct, perpetual losses, just and equitable).
Settlement of accounts (s.48): losses paid first from profits, then capital, then partners individually; assets applied to outside debts, then advances, then capital, then residue.

steps.title: Profit sharing numeric
steps.body:
A, B, C have no agreement on profit share. A advanced ₹1,00,000 beyond capital for a full year. Profit before interest ₹96,000.
Interest on A's advance at 6% (s.13(d)) = ₹6,000.
Distributable = 96,000 − 6,000 = 90,000 → equal shares ₹30,000 each.
A gets 30,000 + 6,000 = ₹36,000; B ₹30,000; C ₹30,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying an unregistered firm cannot be sued: it can be.
- Treating profit-sharing alone as conclusive proof of partnership.

uni-llb-core.description: A study companion for LLB students in India: the law of contract, the law of torts, and criminal law under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, BNSS and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (in force from 1 July 2024). courses.title: Law of Contract (Indian Contract Act, 1872)
courses.summary: Offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity, free consent, void and voidable agreements, performance, breach and damages, worked through real commercial disputes.
outcomes: Learners can test whether an agreement is a valid contract using section 10
Learners can distinguish void, voidable and unenforceable agreements
Learners can apply coercion, undue influence, fraud and misrepresentation to facts
Learners can explain remedies for breach, including damages

lessons.title: Lab: Is there a valid contract? Section 10 checklist

scenes.text: Arjun messages a seller: I will buy your laptop for 40,000 rupees. The seller replies: Done, collect it tomorrow.
The next day the seller says he got a better offer and refuses. Arjun wonders whether he can sue.

steps.title: Section 10 in one line
steps.body:
All agreements are contracts if made by the **free consent** of parties **competent to contract**, for a **lawful consideration** and with a **lawful object**, and are not expressly declared void. Writing is not always needed; many contracts are valid orally or by messages.

Section 2(h) defines a contract as an agreement enforceable by law.

steps.title: Applying it to Arjun
steps.body:
- Offer: Arjun's message with a price
- Acceptance: the seller's unqualified reply, Done
- Consideration: 40,000 rupees for the laptop
- Capacity: both adults of sound mind
- Object lawful, consent free

So a binding contract likely exists and the seller's refusal is a breach.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a written, stamped document is always necessary
- Confusing an invitation to treat (a shop display, a price list) with an offer
- Forgetting that a social promise like dinner at my house usually lacks intention to create legal relations

activity.prompt: Tick each element you would verify before advising a client that a contract exists
items: A proposal (offer) was communicated
It was accepted absolutely and unconditionally
There was consideration from both sides
Parties were competent: adults, sound mind, not disqualified by law
Consent was free of coercion, fraud, mistake and the rest
Object and consideration are lawful

quiz.q: Which section lists the essentials of a valid contract?
quiz.why: Section 10 states when agreements become contracts.

quiz.why: It invites customers to make offers.

quiz.why: Section 2(h) definition.

lessons.title: Lab: Offer, acceptance and the smoke ball

scenes.text: A company advertises that it will pay 100 pounds to anyone who catches influenza after using its smoke ball as directed, and says it has deposited money in a bank to show sincerity.
Mrs Carlill uses it, catches influenza and claims. The company says an advertisement cannot be an offer.

steps.title: General offers
steps.body:
In Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co (1893) the English court held that an advertisement with a definite promise can be a **general offer** to the whole world, accepted by performing the stated conditions. This reasoning is followed in Indian law.

Acceptance must be absolute, communicated (or by conduct as the offer allows) and match the terms of the offer.

steps.title: Counter-offer and revocation
steps.body:
- A counter-offer (I will pay 38,000) rejects the original offer
- An offer can be revoked before acceptance is complete (section 5)
- Silence cannot be imposed as acceptance by the offeror
- Postal acceptance is complete against the proposer when the letter is posted (section 4)

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Always list the facts in time order: offer, any change, acceptance, then ask whether each step was communicated.

activity.prompt: Put the formation of a contract by post in order

B receives the letter and decides to accept
B posts an unconditional acceptance

quiz.why: It destroys the original offer.

lessons.title: Lab: Free consent and void agreements

scenes.text: Rekha, a widow with little education, signs a loan document at the lender's office after the lender's manager threatens to complain to her employer unless she signs.
Later she asks a lawyer whether the agreement binds her.

steps.title: Consent is free when it is not caused by
steps.body:
- **Coercion** (section 15): committing or threatening an act forbidden by the Indian Penal law, now the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, or unlawful detention of property
- **Undue influence** (section 16): a dominant position used to gain unfair advantage
- **Fraud** (section 17): deliberate deceit
- **Misrepresentation** (section 18): innocent false statement
- **Mistake** (sections 20 to 22)

A contract made without free consent is **voidable** at the option of the aggrieved party, except for mutual mistake of fact going to the root, which makes it void.

steps.title: Void and voidable
steps.body:
- **Void**: no legal effect, for example a wagering agreement (section 30), an agreement in restraint of trade (section 27) or with a minor
- **Voidable**: valid until the innocent party rescinds it
- A minor's agreement is void from the start (Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose, 1903)

steps.title: Relief
steps.body: The aggrieved party may rescind and may also claim compensation. Delay and affirmation can lose the right to rescind.

quiz.why: Mohori Bibee: void from the beginning.

quiz.q: Section 27 deals with
quiz.why: Agreements in restraint of trade are void to that extent.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – breach and damages

scenes.text: A bakery orders an oven from a supplier for delivery on 1 March. The supplier delivers it on 30 March and the bakery loses a large festival order.
The bakery claims lost profits; the supplier says it did not know about the festival order.

steps.title: Remedies
steps.body:
Under section 73, the party who suffers breach is entitled to compensation for loss that naturally arose in the usual course of things or that the parties knew, when they made the contract, would be likely to result. **Remote** or indirect loss is not recoverable. This follows Hadley v Baxendale.

Section 74 allows reasonable compensation up to the stipulated sum where a contract names a penalty or liquidated damages. The injured party must still prove loss in many cases. Specific performance and injunction come under the Specific Relief Act, 1963.

steps.title: Mitigation
steps.body: The innocent party must take reasonable steps to reduce loss, for example by hiring a replacement oven. Loss that could have been avoided is not recoverable.

steps.title: Frustration
steps.body: Section 56: a contract to do an act that becomes impossible or unlawful afterwards becomes void when the act becomes impossible.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

a.text: As the bakery's lawyer, what loss do you claim under section 73?

choices.label: All the profits from the festival, even though the supplier was never told
choices.feedback: Remote loss unknown to the supplier is risky to claim.

choices.label: Direct loss from the delay and any special loss only if the supplier knew of it
choices.feedback: Matches the two limbs of section 73.

b.text: The court refuses the festival profit. What would have helped?

choices.label: Informing the supplier of the festival deadline when ordering
choices.feedback: Knowledge brings special loss within section 73.

c.text: The bakery could have rented an oven for a week. What should it have done?

choices.label: Mitigate by renting and claim the cost

end2.text: The claim succeeds in a reasonable amount.

quiz.q: Frustration of contract is under section
quiz.why: Section 56 deals with impossible acts.

quiz.q: A duty to mitigate means
quiz.why: The innocent party should limit the loss.

lessons.title: Lab: Negligence – the snail in the bottle

story.title: A cafe, a bottle and a bad surprise

scenes.text: In 1928 a woman drank ginger beer from an opaque bottle bought by a friend and later found a decomposed snail, becoming ill.
She had no contract with the shopkeeper. Could she sue the manufacturer?

steps.title: The elements
steps.body: Negligence needs: (1) a **duty of care** owed to the claimant, (2) **breach** of that duty by falling below the standard of a reasonable person, and (3) **damage** caused by the breach, not too remote. Donoghue v Stevenson (1932) created the neighbour principle: take reasonable care to avoid acts you can reasonably foresee would injure your neighbour.

steps.title: Indian practice
steps.body: Courts apply the same elements. Medical negligence, road accidents and defective products are common cases; consumers may also use the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

steps.title: Res ipsa loquitur
steps.body: Where the thing speaks for itself, for example a surgical instrument left inside a patient, the burden shifts to the defendant to explain.

lessons.title: Lab: Strict and absolute liability

scenes.text: A chemical plant in a crowded city leaks oleum gas. Many nearby residents are injured.
The plant says it took every reasonable precaution. Does that save it?

steps.title: From Rylands to M.C. Mehta
steps.body:
Rylands v Fletcher (1868): a person who brings onto land something likely to do mischief if it escapes is liable for the damage, subject to exceptions such as act of God or the claimant's consent.

In M.C. Mehta v Union of India (1987), the Supreme Court of India evolved **absolute liability**: an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity is liable for harm, with **no exceptions**, and the compensation should relate to the size and capacity of the enterprise.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Do not say the Indian rule is the same as Rylands. India removed the exceptions for hazardous industries.

steps.title: Two torts
steps.body:
**Defamation**: a false statement that lowers a person's reputation in the eyes of right-thinking people, published to a third party. Libel is in permanent form; slander is spoken. Defences include truth (justification), fair comment on a matter of public interest and privilege.

**Nuisance**: unlawful interference with use or enjoyment of land. Private nuisance affects individuals; public nuisance affects the community. Remedies: damages and injunction.

steps.title: Vicarious liability
steps.body: An employer is liable for torts committed by an employee **in the course of employment**. The test asks whether the act was authorised or an unauthorised mode of doing an authorised act. An independent contractor's torts generally do not make the principal liable, with exceptions. Remedies include compensation and, for road accidents, claims before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal.

courses.summary: General principles of crime, key offences and the procedure and evidence laws that replaced the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act on 1 July 2024, explained in general terms.

lessons.title: Lab: Three new laws – which one answers which question?

scenes.text: Nisha finds old notes quoting IPC and CrPC. Her professor says those codes were replaced from 1 July 2024.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: The three replacements
steps.body:
- **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023** replaced the Indian Penal Code (substantive offences and punishments)
- **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023** replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure
- **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023** replaced the Indian Evidence Act

They apply to offences committed on or after 1 July 2024; older offences are dealt with under the earlier laws.

steps.title: Old cases
steps.body: Judgments citing IPC sections remain important for principles. Always map the old section to the new one using the official correspondence tables.

steps.title: Do not say
steps.body: Do not present IPC or CrPC as the current law for new offences.

lessons.title: Lab: Actus reus, mens rea and stages of a crime

scenes.text: Dev buys a knife intending to harm a rival, waits outside his house, then walks away without acting.
At what stage did Dev cross into criminal liability, if at all?

steps.title: General principles
steps.body:
A crime usually needs a guilty act (**actus reus**) and a guilty mind (**mens rea**). The stages are: intention, preparation, attempt, commission. Intention and mere preparation are generally not punishable, but an attempt, which comes close to the completed act, usually is. Some serious preparations (for example to wage war or make counterfeit tools) are separately offences.

Chapter III of the BNS lists general exceptions such as acts of a child below the age fixed by law, unsoundness of mind, accident, necessity and private defence.

steps.title: Murder and culpable homicide
steps.body: BNS section 103 prescribes punishment for murder and section 105 for culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Both turn on intention and knowledge; the difference is the degree of likelihood of death and the circumstances.

steps.title: Sections
steps.body: Check the Act text and an official correspondence table for exact section numbers before citing.

steps.title: Process under the BNSS
steps.body:
- **Information** about a cognizable offence is recorded as an FIR (section 173). A **zero FIR** can be registered at any police station and transferred. Information may also be given electronically and then signed within the prescribed time.
- **Investigation**: statements, evidence collection, forensic examination for serious offences, arrest following the rules, and a police report on completion.
- **Bail and remand**: bailable offences give bail as of right; for others a court decides. Production before a magistrate within 24 hours of arrest.
- **Trial**: cognizance, charges, evidence, arguments, judgment, and appeal.

steps.title: Theft and cheating
steps.body: Theft is defined in BNS section 303 and cheating in section 318, with snatching as a separate offence.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – is the electronic record admissible?

scenes.text: A complainant produces a printout of chat messages as proof of a threat. The defence says it is easily edited.

steps.title: Evidence under the BSA
steps.body:
The BSA treats **electronic records** as documents. Section 63 requires a certificate, in the prescribed form, from the person in charge of the device and an expert, so that the court can trust the record's origin and integrity. Primary evidence is the original; secondary evidence is allowed only in defined cases.

A confession made to a police officer is generally not admissible against the accused, subject to the discovery rule. The burden of proof in criminal cases is on the prosecution, beyond reasonable doubt.

uni-llb-cpc-limitation.title: Civil Procedure Code & Limitation Act
uni-llb-cpc-limitation.description: Jurisdiction, res sub judice and res judicata, pleadings, summons and trial, interim orders, judgment, decree and execution, appeals, review and revision, special suits, and the Limitation Act, 1963 with worked computations. General education, not legal advice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Basic concepts, jurisdiction, res sub judice and res judicata
courses.summary: Key definitions in s.2 CPC, civil nature of suits under s.9, stay of suits (s.10), res judicata (s.11), bar on further suit and place of suing (ss.15–20), and objections to jurisdiction (s.21).
outcomes: Define decree, order, judgment and decree-holder under s.2
Apply s.9 to decide if a suit is of a civil nature
Distinguish res sub judice (s.10) and res judicata (s.11)
Determine the court in which to file a suit under ss.15–20

lessons.title: Key definitions and s.9 jurisdiction

scenes.text: A priest sues the temple committee, claiming he was wrongly removed from the office of chief priest which carries a fixed salary.
The committee says religious matters cannot go to civil courts.

steps.title: Section 2 definitions
steps.body:
- **Decree** (s.2(2)): formal expression of an adjudication which, so far as the court expressing it is concerned, **conclusively determines the rights of the parties** with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy. May be preliminary, final or partly both. Includes rejection of a plaint and determination of questions under s.144; excludes appealable orders and dismissal for default.
- **Order** (s.2(14)): formal expression of any decision of a civil court which is not a decree.
- **Judgment** (s.2(9)): statement given by the judge of the grounds of a decree or order.
- **Decree-holder** (s.2(3)) and **judgment-debtor** (s.2(10)).
- **Mesne profits** (s.2(12)): profits the person in wrongful possession actually received or might with ordinary diligence have received, with interest, excluding profits due to improvements by him.

steps.title: Section 9
steps.body: Courts shall try **all suits of a civil nature** except those whose cognizance is **expressly or impliedly barred**. Explanation I: a suit in which the right to property or an office is contested is of a civil nature even if it depends on questions of religious rites or ceremonies. Explanation II: it does not matter whether fees are attached to the office.

steps.title: Solving the priest case
steps.body:
1. Dispute: right to an office (chief priest).
2. Explanation I: right to an office is civil though it involves religious ceremonies.
3. Any statutory bar? If a State religious endowments law gives exclusive jurisdiction to a tribunal, that would bar the civil court; otherwise none.
4. Conclusion: civil court has jurisdiction. A suit purely about the correct way to perform a ritual, with no right to property or office, would not be civil.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling an order rejecting a plaint an 'order' – it is a decree by definition.
- Assuming implied bars easily – exclusion of civil court jurisdiction is not readily inferred (Dhulabhai v State of MP, SC 1968).

activity.prompt: Tick the elements of a 'decree' under s.2(2)
items: Formal expression of an adjudication
Adjudication by the court in a suit
Conclusive determination of rights of parties

quiz.q: Rejection of a plaint is
quiz.why: Section 2(2) expressly deems the rejection of a plaint to be a decree.

quiz.q: A suit for right to an office involving religious rites is
quiz.why: Explanation I says such a suit is civil even if it depends on religious questions.

quiz.q: Leading case on exclusion of civil court jurisdiction
quiz.why: Dhulabhai laid down principles for when a statute excludes civil court jurisdiction.

lessons.title: Res sub judice (s.10) and res judicata (s.11)

scenes.text: Asha's suit claiming ownership of a house against her brother was dismissed on merits in 2019; the decree became final.
In 2024 she sues again for possession of the same house claiming title on the same basis.

steps.title: Section 10 – stay of suit
steps.body: No court shall proceed with the trial of a suit in which the **matter in issue is directly and substantially in issue in a previously instituted suit** between the **same parties** (or those under whom they claim), litigating under the same title, pending in the same or any other court in India competent to grant the relief. The later suit is **stayed**, not dismissed. Courts can still pass interim orders.

steps.title: Section 11 – res judicata
steps.body:
Conditions:
1. Matter directly and substantially in issue in the later suit was directly and substantially in issue in the former suit.
2. Former suit between the **same parties** or their privies.
3. Parties litigated under the **same title**.
4. Former court was **competent** to try the later suit.
5. The issue was **heard and finally decided**.
Explanation IV – **constructive res judicata**: any matter which might and ought to have been made a ground of attack or defence is deemed to have been in issue.

steps.title: Solving Asha's case
steps.body:
1. Title was directly and substantially in issue in 2019 and now.
2. Same parties, same title.
3. Former court competent.
4. Heard and finally decided on merits.
→ Barred by res judicata. Even a new ground of title she could have raised earlier is barred by Explanation IV.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing the stages: s.10 applies to **pending** suits; s.11 to **decided** ones.
- Saying dismissal for default is res judicata – it was not 'heard and finally decided' on merits (though O9 R9 may bar a fresh suit).

activity.prompt: Order the res judicata test
items: Identify the issue in the present suit
Check it was directly and substantially in issue in the former suit
Check same parties and same title
Check competence of the former court
Check the issue was heard and finally decided

quiz.why: Section 10 directs the court not to proceed with the trial, so the later suit is stayed.

quiz.q: Constructive res judicata is in
quiz.why: Explanation IV treats matters that might and ought to have been raised as decided.

quiz.q: Res judicata requires the former decision to be
quiz.why: Only a matter heard and finally decided by a competent court attracts s.11.

lessons.title: Place of suing (ss.15–20) and objections (s.21)

scenes.text: A Pune supplier delivers goods worth ₹8 lakh to a buyer in Nagpur; the contract was signed in Mumbai and payment was to be made in Pune.
The buyer does not pay. In which city can the supplier sue?

steps.title: The scheme
steps.body:
- **s.15**: every suit shall be instituted in the **court of lowest grade** competent to try it (pecuniary jurisdiction).
- **s.16**: suits for recovery, partition, foreclosure, determination of rights in, or compensation for wrong to immovable property → where the **property is situate**.
- **s.17**: property in jurisdiction of different courts → any of them.
- **s.19**: compensation for wrongs to person or movables → where the wrong was done **or** where defendant resides/carries on business, at plaintiff's option.
- **s.20**: other suits → where defendant resides/carries on business/personally works for gain, or where the **cause of action wholly or in part arises**.

steps.title: Solving the supplier case
steps.body:
Contract suit for price → s.20.
Options: Nagpur (defendant resides/business; delivery), Mumbai (contract concluded – part of cause of action), Pune (place of payment – part of cause of action).
If the contract has an exclusive jurisdiction clause choosing one of these courts that otherwise has jurisdiction, it is generally upheld (A.B.C. Laminart v A.P. Agencies, SC 1989); parties cannot confer jurisdiction on a court that has none.

steps.title: Section 21
steps.body: Objections to **territorial** and **pecuniary** jurisdiction are not allowed in appeal or revision unless taken at the earliest opportunity in the court of first instance and there has been a **consequent failure of justice**. Lack of **subject-matter** jurisdiction makes a decree a nullity and can be raised at any stage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying s.20 to immovable property suits – use s.16.
- Treating territorial objections like subject-matter ones.

activity.prompt: Tick each place where a suit under s.20 can be filed
items: Where the defendant resides
Where the defendant carries on business
Where the cause of action wholly arises
Where any part of the cause of action arises

quiz.q: Parties can by contract
options: Confer jurisdiction on a court that has none
Choose one of several competent courts
quiz.why: A.B.C. Laminart allows parties to limit jurisdiction to one of several courts already competent.

quiz.q: A decree without subject-matter jurisdiction is
quiz.why: Inherent lack of jurisdiction goes to the root, and s.21 saves only territorial and pecuniary objections.

lessons.title: Bar on suits, s.80 notice and institution of suits

scenes.text: A trader's goods are damaged in Railway custody and he wants to sue the Union of India.
His lawyer insists on sending a notice before filing. Why?

steps.title: Section 80
steps.body: No suit shall be instituted against the **Government** or a **public officer** (for acts in official capacity) until **two months** after notice in writing has been delivered stating the cause of action, name, description and residence of the plaintiff and relief claimed. s.80(2): with **leave of the court**, a suit for urgent or immediate relief may be filed without notice, but the court will not grant relief without giving the Government a reasonable opportunity to show cause.

steps.title: Other bars and rules
steps.body:
- **Order 2 Rule 2**: a suit must include the whole claim arising from the cause of action; omitted portions cannot later be sued for without leave.
- **s.12**: where a plaintiff is precluded by rules from suing on a cause, he cannot sue again in the same court.
- **s.26 & Order 4**: suit is instituted by presentation of a plaint, verified by affidavit (2002 amendment).

steps.title: Applying to the trader
steps.body:
1. Defendant: Union of India (Railways) → s.80 applies.
2. Send notice to the General Manager of the zonal Railway as specified in s.80(1)(b).
3. Wait two months; then file the suit.
4. Limitation: time during which notice period runs is excluded (s.15(2) Limitation Act).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that s.80 notice can be waived by the Government.
- Splitting claims: suing for rent of one month while three months were due bars the rest (O2 R2).
