lessons.title: Parties to suits (Order 1) and joinder of causes (Order 2)

scenes.text: Three co-owners of a building want to evict a tenant; only one of them files the suit.
200 residents of a colony want to sue a builder for the same defect in common amenities.

steps.title: Necessary vs proper parties
steps.body:
- **Necessary party**: one against whom relief is sought and **without whom no effective decree** can be passed. Non-joinder of a necessary party is fatal (O1 R9 proviso).
- **Proper party**: one whose presence enables the court to adjudicate completely, though no relief is claimed against him.
- **O1 R9**: no suit fails merely for misjoinder or non-joinder (save necessary parties).
- **O1 R10**: court may add, strike out or substitute parties at any stage.

steps.title: Representative suit (O1 R8)
steps.body: Where there are numerous persons having the **same interest** in one suit, one or more may sue or be sued on behalf of all, with **permission of the court** and **notice to all interested** persons (by public advertisement where personal service is impracticable). Any person interested may apply to be joined. Decree binds all represented. No abandonment, compromise or withdrawal without notice to all.

steps.title: Applying to the two cases
steps.body:
1. Co-owners: generally one co-owner can sue to evict a tenant, as the others are presumed to consent (Supreme Court has so held in several cases), but joining all is safer.
2. 200 residents: same interest in common amenities → seek court permission under O1 R8, publish notice, sue in a representative capacity; the decree binds all.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating 'same cause of action' as required in O1 R8 – what is required is the **same interest**.
- Forgetting the notice requirement in representative suits.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of a representative suit
items: Identify numerous persons with the same interest
Apply to the court for permission under O1 R8
Give notice to all interested persons (personal or public advertisement)
Allow any interested person to be joined
Proceed to trial; decree binds all represented persons

quiz.q: Without a necessary party
options: No effective decree can be passed
quiz.why: A necessary party is one without whom an effective decree cannot be passed.

quiz.q: O1 R8 requires persons to have
quiz.why: Rule 8 permits representative suits where numerous persons have the same interest in one suit.

quiz.q: Parties may be added
options: At any stage under O1 R10
quiz.why: Order 1 Rule 10(2) lets the court add or strike out parties at any stage of the proceedings.

lessons.title: Pleadings and amendment (Order 6)

scenes.text: After evidence has begun, a defendant wants to add a plea that the suit agreement was signed under fraud.
The plaintiff objects that it is too late.

steps.title: Fundamental rules (O6 R2)
steps.body:
Pleadings shall contain **material facts only**, **not evidence** or **law**, in a **concise form**. Facts must be stated, not the evidence by which they are proved.
- Particulars must be given of fraud, misrepresentation, breach of trust, wilful default, undue influence (O6 R4).
- Pleadings must be signed (R14) and **verified** (R15), with an affidavit (R15(4)).

steps.title: Amendment (O6 R17)
steps.body: The court may at any stage allow amendment necessary to determine the **real questions in controversy**. **Proviso (2002)**: no amendment after **commencement of trial** unless the court concludes that, in spite of **due diligence**, the party could not have raised the matter before. Courts are liberal before trial; amendments that change the nature of the suit, or withdraw admissions, or introduce time-barred claims are usually refused.

steps.title: Solving the fraud plea
steps.body:
1. Trial commenced (evidence started) → proviso applies.
2. Defendant must show due diligence – e.g., he discovered the forged signature only on seeing the original produced at trial.
3. If shown, the court may allow amendment with costs; fraud must be pleaded with particulars (O6 R4).
4. If he always knew the facts, amendment will likely be refused.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Pleading law or arguments instead of facts.
- Pleading 'fraud' generally without particulars.

activity.prompt: Tick what a good pleading must do
items: State material facts
Omit the evidence by which facts are proved
Be concise and in numbered paragraphs
Give particulars of fraud or undue influence if alleged
Be signed and verified by affidavit

quiz.q: Pleadings must contain
quiz.why: Order 6 Rule 2 requires a statement of material facts but not evidence or law.

quiz.q: Amendment after trial begins needs
quiz.why: The 2002 proviso to O6 R17 allows it only if despite due diligence the matter could not be raised earlier.

quiz.q: Particulars are mandatory for
quiz.why: Order 6 Rule 4 requires particulars of fraud, misrepresentation and similar allegations.

lessons.title: Plaint (Order 7), written statement, set-off and counter-claim (Order 8)

scenes.text: A defendant served summons on 1 March in an ordinary money suit files his written statement on 15 May.
In a separate commercial suit of specified value, another defendant files on day 125.

steps.title: Rejection of plaint (O7 R11)
Written statement (O8 R1)
steps.body:
Filed within **30 days** of service of summons; court may extend up to **90 days** for reasons recorded. In ordinary suits this limit is held directory (Kailash v Nanhku, SC 2005). In **commercial disputes** (Commercial Courts Act, 2015 amendments) the outer limit is **120 days** and the right is forfeited thereafter (SCG Contracts v K.S. Chamankar, SC 2019).
- Denial must be **specific**; evasive denial = admission (O8 R3–R5).
- **Set-off** (R6): ascertained sum legally recoverable, within pecuniary jurisdiction.
- **Counter-claim** (R6A): any right or claim against the plaintiff, treated as a cross-suit.

steps.title: Computing the two cases
steps.body:
Ordinary suit: served 1 March. Day 30 = 31 March (March has 31 days: 1 Mar + 30 days = 31 Mar). Filed 15 May = 75 days after service → within the 90-day extendable limit if the court grants extension for recorded reasons.
Commercial suit: day 125 > 120 → the defendant forfeits the right; the court cannot take the WS on record.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the defendant's defence to reject a plaint under O7 R11.
- Treating counter-claim and set-off as the same: set-off must be an ascertained money sum; counter-claim can be any claim.

activity.prompt: Tick the grounds for rejection of a plaint under O7 R11
items: No cause of action disclosed
Relief undervalued and not corrected
Insufficiently stamped and not made good
Suit barred by law on the face of the plaint
Not filed in duplicate

quiz.q: Outer limit for written statement in a commercial suit
quiz.why: The commercial-court proviso to O8 R1 fixes 120 days, after which the right is forfeited.

quiz.q: To decide O7 R11 the court looks at
quiz.why: Rejection is decided on the plaint's own averments, read with documents filed with it.

quiz.q: An evasive denial in a written statement is
quiz.why: Order 8 Rule 5 treats allegations not specifically denied as admitted.

lessons.title: Summons, ex parte decrees, issues and trial (Orders 5, 9, 14, 17, 18)

scenes.text: Vivek was abroad when summons was allegedly served by affixing on his door. An ex parte decree followed.
He returns and learns of it. What should he file?

steps.title: Summons and appearance
steps.body: Summons is served personally, by post/courier/email as permitted, or by **affixation** and substituted service (O5 R17, R20) if the defendant cannot be found. Under O9: if the plaintiff is absent – suit dismissed (R8); if the defendant is absent though duly served – court may proceed **ex parte** (R6).

steps.title: Remedies against ex parte decree
steps.body:
1. **O9 R13** application to the same court to set aside: show summons was **not duly served** or he was prevented by **sufficient cause** from appearing. Limitation: 30 days (Art 123) from decree, or from knowledge where summons not duly served.
2. **Appeal** under s.96(2).
3. **Review** in limited cases.
O9 R13 proviso: no setting aside merely for irregular service if the defendant had notice of the hearing in time.

steps.title: Trial stages
steps.body: Issues are framed from material propositions of fact or law affirmed by one party and denied by the other (**O14 R1**). Discovery and inspection: O11. Admissions: O12. **Adjournments (O17 R1)**: no more than **three** adjournments to a party, with costs. Evidence: O18 – examination-in-chief may be on **affidavit**; cross-examination before court or a commissioner.

steps.title: Advice to Vivek
steps.body:
1. File O9 R13 application within 30 days of knowing the decree, pleading he was abroad and service by affixation was improper (with passport stamps as proof).
2. Seek stay of execution meanwhile.
3. Alternatively, file a first appeal under s.96(2) within 30/90 days as applicable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Filing a fresh suit to challenge an ex parte decree – the remedy lies in O9 R13 or appeal.

Defendant's evidence

questions.why: The Supreme Court read O8 R1 as procedural and directory for ordinary suits.

questions.why: Order 8 Rule 6A lets a defendant set up a counter-claim with the effect of a cross-suit.

questions.why: Legal set-off under O8 R6 is limited to an ascertained sum legally recoverable.

questions.why: Clause (d) mandates rejection where the suit appears barred from the plaint's statements.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Interim orders, judgment, decree and execution
courses.summary: Temporary injunctions, attachment before judgment, receivers and commissions, inherent powers; judgment, decree, interest and costs; execution: courts, s.47 questions, modes of execution, attachment of salary, arrest and detention.
outcomes: Apply the three-part test for a temporary injunction under O39
Explain attachment before judgment under O38
Identify the executing court and questions under s.47
Compute the attachable part of a judgment-debtor's salary under s.60
State limits on civil detention under s.58

lessons.title: Temporary injunctions (Order 39) and inherent powers (s.151)

scenes.text: A tenant's shop is about to be demolished by the landlord while the tenant's suit for declaration of tenancy is pending.
Demolition is scheduled for tomorrow morning.

steps.title: Grounds (O39 R1 & R2)
steps.body: A temporary injunction may be granted where property in dispute is in danger of being **wasted, damaged or alienated**, or wrongfully sold in execution; where the defendant threatens to **remove or dispose** of property to defraud creditors; or threatens to **dispossess** the plaintiff or otherwise cause injury (R1); or to restrain breach of contract or other injury (R2).

steps.title: The three tests
steps.body:
1. **Prima facie case** – a bona fide dispute raising a serious question to be tried.
2. **Balance of convenience** – comparative hardship if injunction is granted or refused.
3. **Irreparable injury** – injury that cannot be adequately compensated by damages.
(Dalpat Kumar v Prahlad Singh, SC 1992.) Equitable considerations: clean hands, delay, conduct.
**O39 R3**: ex parte injunction only with reasons recorded; applicant must send copies to the opposite party; court should try to dispose of application within 30 days.
**O39 R2A**: disobedience may lead to attachment of property and civil detention up to 3 months.

steps.title: Applying to the tenant
steps.body:
1. Prima facie case: rent receipts, possession → serious question of tenancy.
2. Balance of convenience: demolition is irreversible; landlord suffers only delay.
3. Irreparable injury: loss of shop and business cannot be undone.
4. Urgency justifies ex parte ad-interim injunction under O39 R3 with reasons; tenant must serve copies immediately.

steps.title: Section 151
steps.body: Nothing in the CPC limits the **inherent power** of the court to make orders necessary for the **ends of justice** or to prevent **abuse of process**. It cannot be used where the Code expressly provides a remedy, or contrary to its provisions (Manohar Lal Chopra v Seth Hiralal, SC 1962).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating prima facie case as proof of the whole case. It only needs a serious triable issue.

activity.prompt: Tick what the applicant must show for a temporary injunction
items: Prima facie case
Balance of convenience in his favour
Irreparable injury if refused
No undue delay or unclean conduct

quiz.q: The three tests for injunction were explained in
quiz.why: Dalpat Kumar set out prima facie case, balance of convenience and irreparable injury.

quiz.q: Disobedience of an injunction is dealt with under
quiz.why: Rule 2A provides for attachment of property and civil detention for disobedience.

quiz.q: s.151 cannot be used
options: Where the Code expressly provides a remedy
quiz.why: Inherent powers supplement, but cannot override, express provisions of the Code.

lessons.title: Attachment before judgment, receivers and commissions (Orders 38, 40, 26)

scenes.text: A creditor suing for ₹30 lakh learns the defendant is loading machinery onto trucks to move it out of the State.
What interim protection can the creditor seek?

steps.title: Order 38
steps.body:
- **R1**: arrest before judgment if the defendant, with intent to delay or obstruct, is about to abscond or leave the jurisdiction.
- **R5**: **attachment before judgment** if the defendant, with intent to obstruct or delay execution of any decree, is about to dispose of or **remove property** from the court's jurisdiction. The court may direct him to furnish security or produce the property; if he fails, the property may be attached. It is a drastic remedy granted only on specific allegations.

steps.title: Order 40 and Order 26
steps.body:
- **O40 R1**: where just and convenient, the court may appoint a **receiver** of any property and give him powers to manage, collect rents, preserve property.
- **O26**: **commissions** to examine witnesses (R1-R8), make **local investigations** (R9), examine accounts (R11), make partition (R13), scientific investigation (R10A).

steps.title: Applying to the creditor
steps.body:
1. Evidence: photographs of trucks, transport bookings.
2. Allegation: intent to obstruct execution by removing property.
3. Apply under O38 R5 → court calls upon defendant to furnish security of ₹30 lakh or show cause.
4. On failure, conditional attachment of the machinery.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Seeking O38 R5 merely because the defendant is in debt – intent to obstruct execution must be shown.

activity.prompt: Order the procedure under O38 R5
items: Plaintiff files affidavit showing defendant is removing property to obstruct execution
Court directs defendant to furnish security or show cause
Defendant fails to furnish security or show cause
Court orders attachment of specified property
Attachment continues till decree or release

quiz.q: Attachment before judgment is under
quiz.why: Order 38 Rule 5 deals with attachment before judgment.

quiz.q: A local investigation by commissioner is under
quiz.why: Rule 9 of Order 26 allows commissions for local investigations.

quiz.q: A receiver is appointed when
quiz.why: Order 40 Rule 1 allows appointment where it appears just and convenient.

lessons.title: Judgment, decree, interest and costs (Order 20, ss.33–35)

scenes.text: A court decrees ₹10 lakh principal in a commercial loan suit.
The plaintiff asks for interest from the date of suit till payment.

steps.title: Order 20 and s.33
steps.body: After hearing, the court pronounces **judgment**, followed by a **decree** (s.33). Judgment contains a concise statement of the case, points for determination, decision and reasons (O20 R4). The decree must agree with the judgment and specify the relief (R6). Judgment is ordinarily pronounced within 30 days of hearing, and not later than 60 days save exceptional cases (R1).

steps.title: Interest (s.34)
steps.body: Where the decree is for payment of money, the court may order **reasonable interest** on the principal from the date of suit to the date of decree, and further interest from decree to payment at not exceeding **6% per annum** – but where the liability arose out of a **commercial transaction** the further interest may exceed 6%, not exceeding the contractual rate or, absent that, the rate at which nationalised banks lend for commercial transactions.

steps.title: A worked interest computation
steps.body:
Principal ₹10,00,000. Pendente lite interest awarded at 9% p.a. simple for 2 years from suit to decree: 10,00,000 × 0.09 × 2 = ₹1,80,000.
Future interest at 9% (commercial transaction, contractual rate 9%) for 6 months after decree: 10,00,000 × 0.09 × 0.5 = ₹45,000.
Total payable after 6 months = 10,00,000 + 1,80,000 + 45,000 = ₹12,25,000 (plus costs).

steps.title: Costs (ss.35, 35A, 35B)
steps.body: Costs follow the event at the court's discretion (s.35); reasons are recorded if not. s.35A: compensatory costs for false or vexatious claims. s.35B: costs for causing delay, payment a condition precedent to further prosecution.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Capping all post-decree interest at 6% even for commercial transactions.
- Computing interest on interest when only simple interest is awarded.

activity.prompt: Order the contents of a judgment under O20 R4(2)
items: Concise statement of the case
Points for determination
Decision on each point
Reasons for the decision

quiz.q: Post-decree interest in a non-commercial money decree is capped at
quiz.why: Section 34 limits further interest to six per cent per annum except for commercial transactions.

quiz.q: ₹5,00,000 at 8% simple interest for 3 years =
quiz.why: Simple interest is 5,00,000 × 0.08 × 3 which equals ₹1,20,000.

quiz.why: Section 35B provides for costs for causing delay.

lessons.title: Execution (ss.36–74, Order 21)

story.title: Winning is only half the battle

scenes.text: Rina got a money decree of ₹6 lakh from a Delhi court; the judgment-debtor, a salaried employee earning ₹40,000 a month, lives in Jaipur.
She wants to recover through his salary and his car.

steps.title: Courts and questions
steps.body:
- **s.38**: decree executed by the court which passed it or the court to which it is sent.
- **s.39**: transfer for execution where the judgment-debtor resides/carries on business or has property within another court's jurisdiction.
- **s.47**: all questions between the parties to the suit relating to **execution, discharge or satisfaction** of the decree are decided by the executing court, not by a separate suit.
- Executing court cannot go behind the decree, except where it is a **nullity**.

steps.title: Modes (s.51) and exemptions (s.60)
steps.body:
Execution by delivery of property, **attachment and sale**, **arrest and detention** (only after giving the debtor a chance to show cause and recording that he has means but refuses or neglects to pay), appointment of a receiver, or other modes.
**s.60(1)(i)**: in salary attachment, the **first ₹1,000 and two-thirds of the remainder** are exempt (for most employees). Also exempt: necessary clothing, tools of artisans, agriculturists' implements, etc.
**s.58** detention limits: decree > ₹5,000 → up to **3 months**; > ₹2,000 to ₹5,000 → up to **6 weeks**; ≤ ₹2,000 → no detention.

steps.title: Computing the attachable salary
steps.body:
Monthly salary = ₹40,000.
Exempt = 1,000 + (2/3)(40,000 − 1,000) = 1,000 + (2/3)(39,000) = 1,000 + 26,000 = ₹27,000.
Attachable = 40,000 − 27,000 = **₹13,000 per month**.
Months needed for ₹6,00,000 (ignoring interest and costs) = 6,00,000 ÷ 13,000 ≈ 46.15 → **47 months**. Rina should also attach and sell the car (s.51(b)) after transferring the decree to the Jaipur court (s.39).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Filing a separate suit on questions of satisfaction – barred by s.47.
- Asking for arrest merely because the debt is unpaid; inability to pay is not wilful refusal (Jolly George Varghese v Bank of Cochin, SC 1980).

activity.prompt: Order the steps in executing Rina's decree
items: Apply to the decree court for transfer under s.39
Decree court sends the decree to the Jaipur court
File execution application under O21 R11 in Jaipur
Seek attachment of salary (limited by s.60) and of the car
Car sold by court auction; proceeds and salary credited to Rina
Record satisfaction of decree

quiz.why: Exempt is 1,000 plus two-thirds of 30,000, i.e. 21,000, so 31,000 minus 21,000 leaves ₹10,000 attachable.
