courses.title: Unit 4 · Appeals, reference, review, revision and special suits
courses.summary: First and second appeals, appeals from orders, stay and additional evidence in appeal, reference, review and revision; suits by indigent persons, minors, summary suits under Order 37 and suits by or against the Government.
outcomes: Distinguish first appeal (s.96) and second appeal (s.100)
Identify appealable orders under s.104 and Order 43
State the grounds of review under Order 47
Apply the conditions for revision under s.115
Explain leave to defend in a summary suit under Order 37

lessons.title: First appeals (s.96, Order 41)

scenes.text: A civil judge dismisses Harish's suit for recovery of ₹12 lakh, disbelieving his witnesses.
Harish wants the District Court to look at the evidence afresh.

steps.title: Section 96
steps.body:
An appeal lies from every **original decree** to the court authorised to hear appeals. An appeal lies from an **ex parte decree** (s.96(2)). **No appeal** lies from a decree passed with the **consent** of parties (s.96(3)). No appeal on facts lies in suits of the nature cognizable by Small Causes Courts where the amount does not exceed **₹10,000**, except on a question of law (s.96(4)).
A first appeal is a **rehearing on facts and law**: the appellate court must address all issues with reasons (Santosh Hazari v Purushottam Tiwari, SC 2001).

steps.title: Order 41 essentials
steps.body:
- **R1**: memorandum of appeal with grounds, accompanied by a copy of the decree (judgment copy as required).
- **R5**: appeal does not operate as a **stay**; the appellate court may stay execution for sufficient cause, on security.
- **R22**: respondent may support the decree on any ground or file **cross-objection**.
- **R27**: **additional evidence** only if the trial court wrongly refused it, or despite due diligence it was not available, or the appellate court requires it.
- **R33**: appellate court may pass any decree that ought to have been passed.

steps.title: Harish's appeal
steps.body:
1. Original decree of dismissal → first appeal under s.96 to the District Court (pecuniary limits permitting).
2. Limitation: 30 days from decree (Art 116(b)), excluding time to obtain certified copy (s.12(2) Limitation Act).
3. Grounds: misappreciation of evidence, failure to consider documents.
4. The appellate court may reappreciate evidence fully; it gives weight to the trial judge's view on witness credibility.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking filing an appeal stays execution automatically.
- Thinking a consent decree is appealable.

activity.prompt: Tick the grounds on which additional evidence may be admitted under O41 R27
items: Trial court wrongly refused to admit it
Despite due diligence it was not within the party's knowledge or could not be produced
Appellate court requires it to pronounce judgment or for other substantial cause

quiz.q: Does filing an appeal stay execution?
options: No, unless ordered under O41 R5
quiz.why: Order 41 Rule 5 states an appeal does not operate as a stay unless the appellate court orders it.

quiz.q: No appeal lies from
quiz.why: Section 96(3) bars appeals from decrees passed with the consent of parties.

quiz.q: A first appeal is
options: A rehearing on facts and law
quiz.why: Santosh Hazari emphasises the first appellate court reviews both fact and law with reasons.

lessons.title: Second appeals and appeals from orders (ss.100, 104, Order 43)

scenes.text: The District Court affirms the decree against Harish. He wants to go to the High Court.
His senior asks: 'What is the substantial question of law?'

steps.title: Section 100
steps.body:
A second appeal lies to the **High Court** from a decree passed in appeal by a subordinate court only if the case involves a **substantial question of law**. The memorandum must precisely state it; the High Court must **formulate** it at admission and hear the appeal on it. Pure findings of fact cannot be reopened unless perverse or based on no evidence.
**s.100A**: no further appeal (e.g., Letters Patent) from a single judge's decision in such an appeal.
**s.102**: no second appeal in money suits where the amount does not exceed ₹25,000.

steps.title: Appeals from orders
steps.body: **s.104 and O43 R1** list appealable orders, e.g.: return of plaint (O7 R10), refusal to set aside dismissal or ex parte decree (O9 R9, R13), orders under O39 R1, R2, R2A (injunctions), O40 R1 (receiver), O21 orders on obstruction, etc. No second appeal from orders under s.104 (s.104(2)). Other orders can be challenged in an appeal against the final decree (s.105).

steps.title: What is substantial?
steps.body: Test from Sir Chunilal V. Mehta v Century Spinning (SC 1962) and later cases: whether the question is of general public importance, or directly and substantially affects the rights of parties, and is not finally settled or is debatable. 'Did the courts misread the registered sale deed by ignoring a binding presumption under the Evidence law?' may qualify; 'Was witness A believable?' does not.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Filing a second appeal on facts alone; it will be dismissed at admission.

activity.prompt: Tick the orders appealable under Order 43 Rule 1
items: Order returning a plaint under O7 R10
Order rejecting an application to set aside an ex parte decree under O9 R13
Order granting or refusing a temporary injunction under O39 R1
Order appointing a receiver under O40 R1

quiz.q: Second appeal requires
quiz.why: Section 100 restricts second appeals to cases involving a substantial question of law.

quiz.q: Injunction orders under O39 R1 are
quiz.why: Order 43 Rule 1(r) makes such orders appealable.

quiz.q: No Letters Patent appeal from a single judge in a second appeal under
quiz.why: Section 100A bars further appeal from a single judge's decision in an appeal from an original or appellate decree.

lessons.title: Reference, review and revision (ss.113–115, Order 47)

scenes.text: After a decree, the losing party finds an original receipt that was lost in a flood during trial.
No appeal is filed. Can the same judge reconsider?

steps.title: Review (s.114, O47 R1)
Revision (s.115)
steps.body:
The High Court may call for the record of any case **decided** by a subordinate court **in which no appeal lies** to it, if the subordinate court:
(a) exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it; (b) failed to exercise a jurisdiction vested; or (c) acted illegally or with **material irregularity** in exercise of jurisdiction.
**Proviso (1999)**: no variation or reversal of an interlocutory order unless the order, if made in favour of the revisionist, would have **finally disposed** of the suit. Revision does not stay proceedings unless ordered.

steps.title: Reference (s.113, O46)
steps.body: A subordinate court may refer a case to the High Court where it entertains reasonable doubt on a question of law, especially on the validity of an Act, Ordinance or Regulation that must be decided to dispose of the case.

steps.title: The flood receipt
steps.body:
1. New and important evidence ✔; due diligence shown (it was lost in a flood) ✔.
2. No appeal filed ✔.
3. File review before the same judge within 30 days of decree; attach proof of the flood and the receipt.
If an appeal had already been filed by him, review on that ground is generally unavailable for him.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing revision with appeal – revision corrects jurisdictional errors, not mere errors of fact.

activity.prompt: Order the remedies a party should consider in sequence after an adverse decree
items: Check whether a first appeal lies under s.96
If the error is apparent on record or new evidence exists, consider review
If no appeal lies, consider revision under s.115 for jurisdictional error
After first appeal, check for a substantial question of law for s.100

quiz.q: Review lies to
quiz.why: Section 114 and O47 provide for review by the court which passed the decree or order.

quiz.q: Revision lies where
options: No appeal lies to the High Court
quiz.why: Section 115 applies to cases decided by subordinate courts in which no appeal lies.

quiz.q: Reference under s.113 is made by
options: A subordinate court to the High Court
quiz.why: Section 113 allows a subordinate court in doubt on a question of law to refer the case to the High Court.

lessons.title: Special suits: indigent persons, minors, summary suits (Orders 32, 33, 37)

scenes.text: A distributor holds three dishonoured cheques of ₹4 lakh each from a retailer and wants quick recovery.
His lawyer suggests a summary suit.

steps.title: Order 37 – summary suits
steps.body:
Applies to suits on **bills of exchange, hundis, promissory notes**, or for a **liquidated debt** under a written contract, enactment or guarantee. The defendant cannot defend unless he enters appearance within **10 days** of service and then obtains **leave to defend** (applying within 10 days of service of summons for judgment).
Leave principles (IDBI Trusteeship v Hubtown, SC 2016): substantial defence → unconditional leave; triable issue showing fair/bona fide defence → unconditional; plausible but improbable → conditional (deposit); frivolous or vexatious → leave refused and decree follows; if any part of the amount is admitted, leave only on deposit of that part.

steps.title: Order 33 – indigent persons
steps.body: A person **without sufficient means** to pay court fee (and not entitled to property worth the fee) may sue as an indigent person, applying with a schedule of his property. The court inquires; if allowed, no court fee is paid initially; if he succeeds, the fee becomes a first charge on the subject matter (O33 R10).

steps.title: Order 32 – minors
steps.body: A minor sues through a **next friend** and is defended by a **guardian ad litem** appointed by the court. A decree against a minor without a guardian is void as to him; compromise on his behalf needs **leave of the court** (O32 R7), otherwise voidable against the minor.

steps.title: The distributor's suit
steps.body:
1. Claim on negotiable instruments (cheques are bills of exchange) of ₹12 lakh → O37 suit.
2. Retailer appears within 10 days and seeks leave, claiming goods were defective.
3. If he shows credible documents (complaint emails), court may give conditional or unconditional leave; a bare denial → leave refused, decree for ₹12 lakh + interest.
(Criminal liability under s.138 Negotiable Instruments Act is separate.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking the defendant in a summary suit can file a written statement as of right – he needs leave.

activity.prompt: Order the stages of a summary suit
items: Plaintiff files plaint under O37 with required endorsement
Defendant served; enters appearance within 10 days
Plaintiff serves summons for judgment
Defendant applies for leave to defend within 10 days
Court grants leave (with or without conditions) or refuses it
If refused, decree is passed forthwith

quiz.q: Summary suits are under
quiz.why: Order 37 governs summary procedure for negotiable instruments and liquidated debts.

quiz.q: A minor defendant is represented by
quiz.why: Order 32 requires the court to appoint a guardian ad litem for a minor defendant.

quiz.q: Leave to defend principles were restated in
quiz.why: In IDBI Trusteeship v Hubtown the Supreme Court restated the tests after the 1976 amendment.

questions.q: First appeal lies under
questions.why: Section 96 provides appeals from original decrees.

questions.q: Limitation for appeal to the High Court from a decree
questions.why: Article 116(a) gives ninety days for appeals to a High Court.

questions.q: Cross-objection is filed under
questions.why: Order 41 Rule 22 allows the respondent to file a cross-objection.

questions.q: Second appeal in money suits up to ₹25,000 is
questions.why: Section 102 bars second appeals in money recovery suits not exceeding ₹25,000.

questions.q: Error apparent on the face of record is a ground for
questions.why: Order 47 Rule 1 lists error apparent on the record as a review ground.

questions.q: Revision proviso bars interference with interlocutory orders unless
options: The order would have finally disposed of the suit if made for the revisionist
questions.why: The 1999 proviso to s.115 so restricts revision of interlocutory orders.

questions.q: Limitation for review
questions.why: Article 124 prescribes thirty days for review applications in courts other than the Supreme Court.

questions.q: A compromise on behalf of a minor without leave is
questions.why: Order 32 Rule 7(2) makes it voidable against all parties other than the minor.

questions.q: Court fee of a successful indigent plaintiff becomes
options: First charge on the subject matter
questions.why: Order 33 Rule 10 makes the court fee a first charge on the subject-matter of the suit.

questions.q: In a summary suit, a frivolous defence leads to
questions.why: Leave is refused where the defence is frivolous or vexatious.

questions.q: Validity of an Act doubted by a subordinate court — remedy
questions.why: Section 113 proviso requires reference when the validity of an Act is in doubt and necessary to decide.

questions.q: Appeal against ex parte decree lies under
questions.why: Section 96(2) expressly allows appeal from an original decree passed ex parte.

courses.title: Unit 5 · The Limitation Act, 1963
courses.summary: Bar of limitation and its policy, computation rules, condonation of delay, legal disability, exclusion of time, acknowledgment and part-payment, adverse possession and key articles of the Schedule, with dated worked computations.
outcomes: Apply s.3 and explain why limitation bars the remedy, not (generally) the right
Apply s.5 condonation of delay and its limits
Compute limitation with legal disability (ss.6–8) and exclusions (ss.12–15)
Compute a fresh period after acknowledgment (s.18) or part-payment (s.19)
Apply Articles 65 and 64 and s.27 to adverse possession

lessons.title: Bar of limitation (s.3), court closure (s.4) and condonation (s.5)

scenes.text: An appellant's 30-day appeal period ends on a Sunday; he files on Monday.
Another appellant files 40 days late, after being hospitalised with documented illness.

steps.title: Section 3
steps.body: Every suit instituted, appeal preferred and application made **after the prescribed period shall be dismissed**, although limitation has not been set up as a defence. The court must examine limitation **on its own**. Limitation generally bars the **remedy**, not the right – except s.27 (extinction of title to property after the period for possession) and similar cases. Policy: *interest reipublicae ut sit finis litium* – there must be an end to litigation; *vigilantibus non dormientibus jura subveniunt* – the law helps the vigilant.

steps.title: Sections 4 and 5
steps.body:
**s.4**: if the prescribed period expires on a day the court is **closed**, the proceeding may be filed on the day it reopens.
**s.5**: an **appeal or application** (other than an application under Order 21 CPC) may be admitted after the period if the appellant or applicant shows **sufficient cause**. It does **not apply to suits**. Courts take a liberal, justice-oriented approach (Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v Mst. Katiji, SC 1987), but delay must be explained, and negligence or lack of bona fides defeats it.

steps.title: Solving both
steps.body:
1. Last day Sunday (court closed) → filing on Monday is within time under s.4; no condonation needed.
2. 40 days' delay with medical records → apply under s.5 with affidavit explaining each period of delay; documented hospitalisation is typically sufficient cause.
3. Had it been a **suit** filed late, s.5 could not help: the plaint would be rejected/dismissed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying s.5 to suits.
- Assuming the defendant must plead limitation – s.3 obliges the court to apply it anyway.

activity.prompt: Tick statements that are TRUE
items: s.3 applies even if limitation is not pleaded
s.5 can condone delay in appeals
s.4 helps when the last day falls on a court holiday
Limitation usually bars the remedy rather than the right

quiz.q: Section 5 does NOT apply to
quiz.why: Section 5 covers only appeals and applications, never suits.

quiz.q: Leading liberal case on condonation
quiz.why: Katiji held that a justice-oriented approach should be taken to sufficient cause.

quiz.q: If the last day is a court holiday
options: File on reopening day under s.4
quiz.why: Section 4 allows filing on the day the court reopens.

lessons.title: Legal disability and continuous running of time (ss.6–9)

scenes.text: Kavya, born 1 June 2010, has a claim (3-year limitation) that accrued on 1 June 2025 when she was 15.
When must she sue?

steps.title: Section 6
steps.body:
If the person entitled is, **at the time from which the period is to be reckoned**, a **minor, insane or an idiot**, he may institute the suit or make the application within the same period **after the disability ceases**, as would otherwise have been allowed from the time specified in the Schedule.
**s.7**: where one of several joint claimants is under disability and a discharge can be given without his concurrence, time runs against all.
**s.8**: s.6 and s.7 do not extend the period beyond **three years from cessation** of disability (and do not apply to pre-emption suits).
**s.9**: once time **begins to run**, no subsequent disability or inability stops it.

steps.title: Computing Kavya's deadline
steps.body:
1. Cause of action: 1 June 2025, Kavya aged 15 → disability exists at the start.
2. Majority (18): 1 June 2028 → disability ceases.
3. Period of 3 years runs from 1 June 2028 → deadline **1 June 2031**.
4. s.8 cap: not beyond 3 years from cessation → 1 June 2031, same result.

Contrast: had she turned insane in 2026 **after** a claim accrued when she was an adult, s.9 would keep time running.

steps.title: A 12-year claim
steps.body: A minor aged 10 at accrual of a 12-year possession claim on 1 Jan 2020 (born 1 Jan 2010) attains majority on 1 Jan 2028. Normal period from accrual: till 1 Jan 2032. s.6 would give 12 years after majority, but s.8 caps the extension at 3 years from cessation → 1 Jan 2031. Since the ordinary period (1 Jan 2032) is longer, he simply uses the ordinary period: **1 Jan 2032**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying s.6 to a disability that arises **after** time has begun (s.9 forbids).
- Forgetting the s.8 three-year cap and that the ordinary period still applies if longer.

activity.prompt: Order the steps for computing limitation with disability
items: Find the Article and the starting point in the Schedule
Check if the claimant was under disability on that date
Find the date the disability ceases
Apply the full period from cessation (s.6)
Apply the s.8 cap of three years from cessation
Compare with the ordinary period and take the later date

quiz.q: Disabilities recognised by s.6
quiz.why: Section 6 recognises only minority, insanity and idiocy.

quiz.q: Once time begins to run, a later disability
quiz.why: Section 9 provides that subsequent disability or inability does not stop time running.

quiz.q: Born 1 Mar 2009, 3-year claim accrued 1 Mar 2023 — last date
quiz.why: She turns 18 on 1 Mar 2027, and three years from then gives 1 Mar 2030, within the s.8 cap.

lessons.title: Exclusion of time (ss.12–15), acknowledgment (s.18) and part-payment (s.19)

scenes.text: Sameer lent ₹3 lakh to a friend on 10 January 2023; the loan is repayable on demand and no demand was made.
On 2 December 2025 the friend writes and signs: 'I owe you ₹3 lakh, will repay soon.'

steps.title: Exclusions
steps.body:
- **s.12(1)**: the day from which the period is reckoned is **excluded**.
- **s.12(2)**: for appeals/revision/review, time to obtain a **certified copy** of the decree/order is excluded (and the day of pronouncement).
- **s.13**: time spent in applying for leave to sue as an indigent person, where refused.
- **s.14**: time spent **bona fide with due diligence** prosecuting a proceeding in a court **without jurisdiction** (or other cause of like nature).
- **s.15**: periods of stay/injunction and of statutory notice (e.g., s.80 CPC) are excluded.

steps.title: Sections 18 and 19
steps.body:
**s.18**: an **acknowledgment of liability** in writing, signed by the party against whom the right is claimed, made **before expiry** of the period, gives a **fresh period** from the date of signing. It need not specify the exact amount or contain a promise to pay.
**s.19**: a **payment on account** of a debt or interest made before expiry by the person liable gives a fresh period from the date of payment; except for payment of interest before 1 Jan 1928, the acknowledgment of the payment must appear in the **handwriting of, or a writing signed by**, the payer.

steps.title: Computing Sameer's deadline
steps.body:
Article 19 (money payable for money lent): 3 years from when the loan is made.
1. Loan 10 Jan 2023 → period ends **10 Jan 2026** (day of loan excluded under s.12(1)).
2. Acknowledgment signed 2 Dec 2025 → before expiry ✔ → fresh 3 years from 2 Dec 2025 → **2 Dec 2028**.
3. If the friend pays ₹20,000 on 1 Nov 2028 with a signed receipt note in his writing → fresh period from 1 Nov 2028 → **1 Nov 2031** (s.19).
Assumption: no special exclusion orders apply.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- An acknowledgment made **after** expiry does not revive the claim under s.18 (though it may be a fresh promise under s.25(3) Contract Act if it meets that section).
- An oral acknowledgment does not count.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to test an acknowledgment
items: Identify the Article and original expiry date
Confirm the acknowledgment is in writing
Confirm it is signed by the party liable or his authorised agent
Confirm it was made before the original expiry
Compute the fresh period from the date of signing

quiz.q: Loan given 15 Feb 2024, Article 19 — original expiry
quiz.why: Article 19 gives three years from the date of the loan, so 15 Feb 2024 plus three years is 15 Feb 2027.

quiz.q: An acknowledgment under s.18 must be
options: In writing and signed, before expiry
quiz.why: Section 18 requires a signed written acknowledgment made before the period expires.

quiz.q: Time spent bona fide in a court without jurisdiction is excluded under
quiz.why: Section 14 excludes such time if the proceeding was prosecuted with due diligence and good faith.

lessons.title: Adverse possession (s.27, Arts 64–65) and key Articles

scenes.text: Sohan has openly occupied a vacant plot owned by an absent NRI since 5 March 2012, fenced it, and denied the owner's title in a 2013 letter.
The owner returns in 2025 and sues for possession.

steps.title: Adverse possession
steps.body:
**Article 65**: suit for possession of immovable property **based on title** – **12 years** from when the defendant's possession becomes **adverse** to the plaintiff. (30 years where the Government is the owner – Article 112.)
**Article 64**: suit for possession based on **previous possession** (not title) – 12 years from dispossession.
**s.27**: at the end of the period, the owner's **right itself is extinguished**.
Possession must be **nec vi, nec clam, nec precario** – without force, without secrecy, without permission; open, continuous, hostile, with **animus possidendi**. Ravinder Kaur Grewal v Manjit Kaur (SC 2019): the adverse possessor can also sue as plaintiff to protect his title.

steps.title: Solving Sohan's case
steps.body:
1. Possession open and continuous since 5 March 2012; hostility clear at least from the 2013 letter denying title.
2. Taking adverse possession from 2013 (say 1 June 2013), 12 years end on **1 June 2025**.
3. If the owner's suit is filed after that date, it is time-barred and his title is extinguished (s.27).
4. If filed before, Sohan's plea fails. Exact dates of hostility therefore decide the case – the burden is on the person claiming adverse possession.

steps.title: Key Articles to remember
steps.body:
| Art | Subject | Period | From |
|---|---|---|---|
| 19 | Money lent | 3 yrs | Loan made |
| 54 | Specific performance | 3 yrs | Date fixed, or notice of refusal |
| 58 | Declaration | 3 yrs | Right to sue first accrues |
| 113 | Residuary suits | 3 yrs | Right to sue accrues |
| 116 | Appeal under CPC | 90 days HC / 30 days other | Decree/order |
| 123 | Set aside ex parte decree | 30 days | Decree / knowledge |
| 136 | Execution of decree | 12 yrs | Decree enforceable |
| 137 | Residuary applications | 3 yrs | Right to apply accrues |

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting 12 years from entry when the possession was initially permissive (e.g., a tenant or licensee) – permissive possession is not adverse.
- Forgetting the 30-year period for Government land.

activity.prompt: Tick the elements an adverse possessor must prove
items: Actual physical possession
Open and known possession (not secret)
Possession without permission of the owner
Hostile intention to possess against the owner
Continuous and uninterrupted for 12 years

quiz.q: Suit for possession based on title — limitation
quiz.why: Article 65 gives twelve years from when the defendant's possession becomes adverse.

quiz.q: Period for execution of a decree (other than mandatory injunction)
quiz.why: Article 136 prescribes twelve years from when the decree becomes enforceable.

quiz.q: Permissive possession by a licensee is
quiz.why: Possession with the owner's permission is not hostile and so cannot ripen into adverse possession.

questions.q: s.3 requires a court to
options: Dismiss time-barred proceedings even if limitation is not pleaded
questions.why: Section 3 imposes the bar irrespective of whether it is set up as a defence.

questions.q: Condonation of delay in filing a suit
questions.why: Section 5 does not extend to suits.

questions.q: Born 10 Oct 2012, 3-year claim accrued 10 Oct 2024 — last date
questions.why: Majority on 10 Oct 2030 and three years thereafter is 10 Oct 2033, within the s.8 cap.

questions.q: Time to obtain a certified copy for appeal is
questions.why: Section 12(2) excludes the time requisite for obtaining a copy of the decree or order.

questions.q: Loan on 1 Apr 2023, acknowledgment signed 1 Mar 2026 — new last date
questions.why: The acknowledgment was before expiry on 1 Apr 2026, so a fresh three years runs from 1 Mar 2026.

questions.q: An acknowledgment after expiry
questions.why: Section 18 requires the acknowledgment to be made before the expiry of the prescribed period.

questions.q: Part payment must be evidenced by
options: Writing or handwriting of the payer
questions.why: Section 19 proviso requires an acknowledgment of payment in the payer's handwriting or a writing signed by him.

questions.q: Extinction of right to property after limitation is under
questions.why: Section 27 extinguishes the right to property when the period for a possession suit expires.

questions.q: Adverse possession against Government land requires
questions.why: Article 112 prescribes thirty years for suits by or on behalf of the Government.

questions.q: Specific performance limitation
questions.why: Article 54 prescribes three years from the date fixed for performance or from notice of refusal.

questions.q: Residuary period for applications
questions.why: Article 137 governs applications for which no period is provided elsewhere.

questions.q: Who can sue to protect title by adverse possession per Ravinder Kaur Grewal?
questions.why: The Supreme Court held a person who has perfected title by adverse possession may sue as plaintiff.

uni-llb-criminal-law-bns.title: Criminal Law under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
uni-llb-criminal-law-bns.description: Substantive criminal law under the BNS 2023 (in force from 1 July 2024): elements of crime, general exceptions, private defence, inchoate and group liability, offences against the body, women, children and property. General education, not legal advice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB / BA LLB programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Nature of crime and general principles
courses.summary: What a crime is, the elements of actus reus and mens rea, the scheme and territorial reach of the BNS 2023, joint liability and the kinds of punishment, including the new community service.
outcomes: Define crime and distinguish it from a civil wrong
Identify actus reus, mens rea, causation and harm in a fact pattern
Explain the structure, commencement and extent of the BNS 2023
Apply common intention under section 3(5) to group offences
List the punishments in section 4 including community service

lessons.title: Crime, its elements and the maxim actus non facit reum

scenes.text: Leaving a library, Neha takes a black umbrella from the stand, honestly believing it is her own identical one.
The owner calls the police. Has Neha committed theft, when the act of taking clearly happened?

steps.title: What is a crime?
steps.body:
A crime is an act or omission that the State prohibits on pain of punishment, prosecuted in the name of the State because it harms society, not merely the victim. A civil wrong (tort, breach of contract) is pursued by the injured person for compensation.

Four classic elements: (1) a **human being** under a legal duty, (2) **mens rea** – a guilty mind, (3) **actus reus** – a prohibited act or omission, (4) **injury/harm** to a person or society.

steps.title: Actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea
steps.body:
The act does not make one guilty unless the mind is also guilty. Mens rea in the BNS appears through words like **intentionally, knowingly, voluntarily, dishonestly, fraudulently, rashly, negligently**. 'Dishonestly' means intending wrongful gain or wrongful loss; 'fraudulently' means with intent to defraud.

In Neha's case there is no dishonest intention, so theft (which needs a dishonest taking) is not made out.

steps.title: Strict liability
steps.body: Some regulatory and public-welfare offences dispense with mens rea (food adulteration, certain revenue offences). Courts presume mens rea is required unless the statute clearly excludes it, as explained in Nathulal v State of MP (1966).

steps.title: Stages of a crime
steps.body:
1. Intention – not punishable alone
2. Preparation – generally not punishable, except special cases (e.g. preparation to wage war, making preparation for dacoity)
3. Attempt – punishable
4. Accomplishment – the complete offence

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating motive as the same as intention: motive is the reason, intention is the aim of the act
- Saying preparation is always punishable
- Forgetting that an omission is an 'act' when there is a legal duty to act

activity.prompt: Arrange the stages of a crime in the order they occur
items: Intention formed
Preparation of means
Attempt directed towards commission
Commission of the offence

quiz.q: Which element refers to the guilty mind?
quiz.why: Mens rea is the mental element such as intention, knowledge or negligence that must accompany the prohibited act.

quiz.q: Which stage of crime is generally NOT punishable?
quiz.why: Mere preparation is usually not punished because the person may still abandon the plan, with a few statutory exceptions.

quiz.q: 'Dishonestly' in criminal law means doing something with intent to cause
quiz.why: The statutory definition of dishonestly is acting with intention of causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another.

lessons.title: The BNS 2023: scheme, commencement and extent

scenes.text: A cheating offence was committed in May 2024; the FIR is filed in August 2024.
A student asks whether the IPC or the BNS governs the offence.

steps.title: Background
steps.body: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and came into force on **1 July 2024**, alongside the BNSS (procedure) and BSA (evidence). It has 358 sections in 20 chapters, compared with 511 sections in the IPC, mainly by merging and reorganising provisions.

steps.title: Substantive law is not retrospective
steps.body: Article 20(1) of the Constitution forbids conviction under an ex post facto law and a heavier penalty than the law in force at the time of the act. So an offence committed before 1 July 2024 is charged under the IPC, even if the FIR is registered later. Only procedure (BNSS) may apply to pending matters as the saving clauses provide.

steps.title: Extent
steps.body: The Sanhita applies to offences committed within India, and to Indian citizens for offences committed outside India, to persons on Indian ships or aircraft, and to persons committing offences outside India targeting computer resources located in India.

steps.title: Notable new or reworked provisions
steps.body:
- Organised crime and petty organised crime
- Terrorist act defined in the general penal law
- Murder by a group of five or more on grounds such as race, caste, community (mob lynching) in section 103(2)
- Snatching as a separate offence
- Community service as a punishment
- Acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India (section 152) in place of the old sedition offence
- Gender-neutral wording in several offences relating to children

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying BNS to acts done before 1 July 2024
- Quoting IPC section numbers as if unchanged: murder is punished under BNS section 103, not 302

activity.prompt: Before choosing IPC or BNS for an offence, verify each of these
items: Date on which the act or omission occurred
Whether the act was before or after 1 July 2024
Whether the provision is substantive (offence/penalty) or procedural
Corresponding section in the new code for citations
Any saving clause for pending proceedings

quiz.q: The BNS came into force on
quiz.why: The three new criminal laws were brought into force together on 1 July 2024.

quiz.q: An offence committed in May 2024 is charged under
quiz.why: Article 20(1) bars applying a later penal law to earlier acts, so the IPC in force at the time governs.

quiz.q: Punishment for murder under the BNS is in section
quiz.why: Section 101 defines murder while section 103 prescribes its punishment in the BNS.

lessons.title: Joint liability: common intention and common object

scenes.text: Three friends plan to beat a rival. One stands guard at the gate while two attack; the rival dies.
Can the lookout, who never touched the victim, be held liable for the same offence?

steps.title: Section 3(5) – common intention
steps.body:
When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each is liable as if he had done it alone. This replaces IPC section 34. It is a rule of evidence/liability, not a separate offence.

Ingredients: (1) a criminal act by several persons, (2) a common intention (a prior meeting of minds, which may form on the spot), (3) the act done in furtherance of it, (4) participation of the accused.

steps.title: Barendra Kumar Ghosh (1925)
steps.body: The accused stood outside a post office while others shot the postmaster. The Privy Council held that 'they also serve who only stand and wait' – presence and participation as a guard in furtherance of the common intention made him liable for murder.

steps.title: Common object – unlawful assembly
steps.body: An assembly of **five or more** persons with a common object listed in the law (e.g. to commit an offence, to resist the execution of law) is an unlawful assembly. Every member is guilty of an offence committed by any member in prosecution of the common object, or which members knew was likely. Common object needs no prior meeting of minds; common intention does.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Tabulate: number of persons (2+ vs 5+), mental element (shared intention vs shared object), participation needed (yes vs mere membership), nature (liability rule vs substantive offence).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating similar intention as common intention (Mahbub Shah v Emperor, 1945: a pre-arranged plan is needed)
- Forgetting that some participation is required for common intention

activity.prompt: Tick what the prosecution must prove to use common intention against the lookout
items: A criminal act was done by several persons
All shared a common intention formed before or at the spot
The act was done in furtherance of that intention
The lookout participated in some way, e.g. guarding

quiz.q: Common intention under the BNS is in
quiz.why: Section 3(5) of the BNS restates the old IPC section 34 rule of joint liability.

quiz.q: Minimum number of persons for an unlawful assembly
quiz.why: An unlawful assembly requires an assembly of five or more persons with a specified common object.

quiz.q: Mahbub Shah v Emperor stresses that common intention requires
options: A pre-arranged plan or meeting of minds
quiz.why: The Privy Council distinguished similar intention from common intention, which requires a prior meeting of minds.

lessons.title: Punishments and sentencing

scenes.text: A young man steals goods worth a small amount and returns the property.
The magistrate considers ordering him to do unpaid work in a public hospital instead of jail.

steps.title: Section 4 – punishments
steps.body: Offenders are liable to: (a) death, (b) imprisonment for life, (c) imprisonment – rigorous (with hard labour) or simple, (d) forfeiture of property, (e) fine, (f) **community service**. Imprisonment for life means imprisonment for the remainder of natural life unless remitted or commuted.

steps.title: Community service
steps.body: Community service is new in the BNS and is provided for some petty offences, for example theft of property below a small value where the property is returned (first-time offender), a public servant unlawfully engaging in trade, and misconduct in public by a drunken person. It means unpaid work that benefits the community as ordered by the court.

steps.title: Death penalty – rarest of rare
steps.body: Bachan Singh v State of Punjab (1980) upheld the death penalty but limited it to the 'rarest of rare' cases where life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed, weighing aggravating and mitigating circumstances. Machhi Singh (1983) gave guiding categories.

steps.title: Fractions of terms
steps.body: For computing fractions of terms of punishment, imprisonment for life is reckoned as equivalent to imprisonment for twenty years. So half of life imprisonment for that calculation is 10 years; one-fourth is 5 years.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying life imprisonment means 14 or 20 years – it means the rest of natural life, subject to remission
- Listing transportation for life: it was abolished long ago

activity.prompt: Tick each punishment recognised by section 4 of the BNS
items: Death
Imprisonment for life
Rigorous or simple imprisonment
Forfeiture of property
Fine
Community service

quiz.q: Which punishment was newly added in the BNS?
quiz.why: Community service did not exist in the IPC and was added to section 4 of the BNS for specified petty offences.

quiz.q: For calculating fractions of terms, life imprisonment is treated as
quiz.why: The Sanhita deems life imprisonment equal to twenty years only for computing fractions of terms.

quiz.q: The 'rarest of rare' doctrine comes from
quiz.why: Bachan Singh v State of Punjab (1980) laid down the rarest of rare test for imposing death.

questions.q: The maxim actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea means
options: An act is not guilty unless the mind is guilty
questions.why: It requires both a prohibited act and a guilty mind for criminal liability.

questions.q: A crime differs from a tort mainly because it is
options: Prosecuted by the State as a wrong against society
questions.why: Crimes are public wrongs prosecuted by the State, while torts are private wrongs sued by victims.

questions.q: The BNS replaced which law?
questions.why: The BNS replaced the Indian Penal Code; the BNSS and BSA replaced the CrPC and Evidence Act.

questions.q: Motive differs from intention because motive is
questions.why: Motive explains why a person acted, whereas intention is the purpose with which the act is done.

questions.q: In Barendra Kumar Ghosh the accused was liable although he
questions.why: Standing guard in furtherance of the common intention was sufficient participation.

questions.q: Common intention differs from common object in that common intention requires
questions.why: Common intention needs a pre-arranged plan, while common object only needs shared object among five or more.

questions.q: Article 20(1) of the Constitution prevents
questions.why: Article 20(1) bars ex post facto criminal laws and heavier retrospective penalties.

questions.q: Strict liability offences
questions.why: In strict liability offences the statute removes the need to prove a guilty mind.

questions.q: Which provision deals with mob lynching style murder by five or more on grounds like caste?
questions.why: Section 103(2) prescribes punishment for murder by a group of five or more on specified grounds.

questions.q: Rigorous imprisonment involves
questions.why: Rigorous imprisonment is imprisonment with hard labour, unlike simple imprisonment.

questions.q: Half of imprisonment for life for computing fractions equals
questions.why: Life is counted as 20 years for fractions, so half is 10 years.

questions.q: An omission is punishable when
options: There is a legal duty to act
questions.why: Criminal liability for omission arises where the law imposes a duty to act and it is illegally omitted.

questions.q: Section 152 BNS deals with
options: Acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
questions.why: Section 152 replaced the old sedition offence with acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity.

courses.title: Unit 2 · General exceptions and private defence
courses.summary: Chapter III of the BNS: mistake of fact, judicial acts, accident, necessity, infancy, unsoundness of mind, intoxication, consent, and the right of private defence of body and property.
outcomes: Classify general exceptions as excusable or justifiable
Apply mistake of fact and accident to facts
Apply the M'Naghten-based test of unsoundness of mind
State the limits of private defence and when it extends to causing death

lessons.title: Mistake, judicial acts, accident and necessity

scenes.text: A constable arrests a man he reasonably and in good faith believes is the person named in a warrant. It turns out to be the wrong man.
Is the constable guilty of wrongful confinement?

steps.title: Burden and scheme
steps.body:
Chapter III (sections 14 to 44) lists acts that are not offences. Under the evidence law the burden of proving that a case falls within a general exception is on the accused, on a preponderance of probability, while the prosecution must still prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

Excusable: mistake of fact, accident, infancy, insanity, intoxication. Justifiable: judicial acts, necessity, consent, private defence.

steps.title: Mistake of fact (sections 14 and 17)
steps.body:
Nothing is an offence done by a person who is, or who by reason of a mistake of **fact** (not law) in good faith believes himself to be, bound or justified by law to do it. Ignorantia juris non excusat – mistake of law is no defence.

State of Orissa v Bhagaban Barik (1987) and the classic R v Tolson illustrate honest and reasonable mistakes of fact.

steps.title: Accident (section 18) and necessity (section 19)
steps.body:
Accident: an act done by accident or misfortune, without criminal intention or knowledge, in doing a lawful act in a lawful manner by lawful means with proper care.

Necessity: an act done with knowledge it is likely to cause harm, but without criminal intention, in good faith to prevent or avoid other harm to person or property – e.g. pulling down houses to stop a spreading fire.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body:
1. A shoots at a target in a lawful range with care; a bullet ricochets and injures B – accident.
2. A ship captain changes course risking a few boats to save many – necessity.
3. A seizes Z's goods believing, as a mistake of law, that a debtor's goods may be taken without a court order – no defence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating mistake of law as a defence
- Ignoring 'good faith' – the law defines it as done with due care and attention
- Claiming accident when the act itself was unlawful

activity.prompt: Tick the conditions required for the defence of accident
items: No criminal intention or knowledge
Doing a lawful act
In a lawful manner by lawful means
With proper care and caution

quiz.q: Which mistake can be a defence?
options: Mistake of fact in good faith
quiz.why: Only a good-faith mistake of fact excuses; ignorance of law is no excuse.

quiz.q: Pulling down houses to stop a fire spreading illustrates
quiz.why: Necessity protects acts done in good faith, without criminal intent, to prevent greater harm.

quiz.q: The burden of proving a general exception lies on
quiz.why: The evidence law places the burden of proving circumstances bringing a case within an exception on the accused.

lessons.title: Infancy and unsoundness of mind

scenes.text: A man with a long history of schizophrenia kills his father, believing him to be a demon about to attack the family.
Doctors confirm he had no understanding of what he was doing at the time.

steps.title: Infancy (sections 20 and 21)
steps.body:
- Below **7 years**: nothing is an offence – absolute immunity (doli incapax).
- Above 7 and below **12 years**: not an offence if the child has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the nature and consequences of the conduct – qualified immunity; the prosecution must show maturity.
Children in conflict with law are dealt with under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015.

steps.title: Unsoundness of mind (section 22)
steps.body: Nothing is an offence done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law. This is based on the M'Naghten Rules (1843). Only **legal** insanity counts, not every medical abnormality.

steps.title: Key cases
steps.body:
- Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar v State of Gujarat (1964): the accused must prove legal insanity at the time of the act on a preponderance of probability; conduct before and after is relevant.
- Ratan Lal v State of MP (1971): setting fire to grass and saying 'I burnt it' with no motive – insanity accepted on evidence.

steps.title: Intoxication (sections 23 and 24)
steps.body: Involuntary intoxication (administered without knowledge or against will) is a defence on the same test as insanity. Voluntary intoxication is no defence, but where an offence needs specific intent, the person is treated as having the same knowledge as a sober person (Basdev v State of PEPSU, 1956).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing medical insanity with legal insanity
- Forgetting that insanity must exist at the time of the act
- Claiming voluntary drunkenness as a full defence

activity.prompt: Order the steps a court follows in assessing an insanity plea
items: Prosecution proves the act and ordinary mens rea
Accused raises unsoundness of mind
Evidence of mental condition before, during and after the act examined
Court applies the cognitive test of section 22
Court decides on a preponderance of probability whether the exception applies

quiz.q: A child of 6 who causes harm is
quiz.why: Section 20 gives absolute immunity to a child under seven years.

quiz.q: Section 22 is based on
quiz.why: The cognitive test of incapacity to know the nature or wrongness of the act derives from M'Naghten's case.

quiz.q: Voluntary intoxication
options: Is no defence; knowledge is presumed as if sober
quiz.why: A voluntarily intoxicated person is treated as having the knowledge he would have had if sober.

lessons.title: Consent and acts in good faith

scenes.text: A surgeon, with the patient's consent, performs a risky operation in good faith; the patient dies.
Is the surgeon guilty of culpable homicide?

steps.title: Consent – the scheme
steps.body:
- Act not intended and not known likely to cause death or grievous hurt, done with consent of a person above 18: protected.
- Act not intended to cause death, done in good faith for a person's benefit with consent: protected even if it risks death (medical treatment).
- Act in good faith for the benefit of a child or person of unsound mind with consent of the guardian.
- Act in good faith for benefit without consent where consent cannot be obtained (emergency).

steps.title: When consent is not valid
steps.body: Consent is not valid if given under fear of injury or misconception of fact known to the doer, by a person of unsound mind or intoxicated who cannot understand, or by a child under 12 (in the consent provision). Consent never justifies intentionally causing death.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body:
1. Boxing match with rules: injuries are covered by consent.
2. A doctor operates on an unconscious accident victim to save life: protected as an emergency good-faith act.
3. A man kills a friend who asks to be killed: no protection; at most an exception reducing murder may arise.

steps.title: Communication in good faith
steps.body: Communication made in good faith to a person for his benefit is not an offence because of harm caused by it – e.g. a doctor telling a patient of a grave diagnosis, though the shock causes harm.

activity.prompt: Tick situations where consent is NOT valid
items: Given under fear of injury
Given under a misconception of fact known to the accused
Given by a person too intoxicated to understand
Given by a child under twelve

quiz.q: Consent can justify
quiz.why: Good-faith acts for a person's benefit with consent, like surgery, are protected even if death results.

quiz.q: Consent given under fear of injury is
quiz.why: The law expressly provides that consent obtained under fear of injury is not consent.

quiz.q: A doctor operating on an unconscious emergency patient relies on
quiz.why: Acts done in good faith for a person's benefit when consent cannot be obtained are protected.

lessons.title: Right of private defence (sections 34 to 44)

scenes.text: At 2 a.m. an armed man breaks into Ramesh's house and lunges at him with a knife.
Ramesh strikes him with an iron rod; the intruder dies. Can Ramesh claim private defence?

steps.title: The right
steps.body: Nothing is an offence done in the exercise of the right of private defence. Every person may defend (1) his own or another's body against an offence affecting the human body, and (2) his own or another's property against theft, robbery, mischief, criminal trespass or attempts of them.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body:
- No right where there is time to have recourse to public authorities
- No right against acts of a public servant acting in good faith under colour of office (unless reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt)
- Harm must not exceed what is necessary
- Right begins with reasonable apprehension of danger and continues as long as it lasts

steps.title: Extends to causing death – body
steps.body: Assault causing reasonable apprehension of death; of grievous hurt; with intention of rape; of gratifying unnatural lust; of kidnapping or abducting; of wrongful confinement with apprehension of no access to authorities; throwing or attempting to throw acid causing apprehension of grievous hurt.

steps.title: Extends to causing death – property
steps.body: Robbery; house-breaking by night; mischief by fire or explosive on a building, tent or vessel used as human dwelling or custody of property; theft, mischief or house-trespass causing apprehension of death or grievous hurt.

steps.title: Cases
steps.body:
- Darshan Singh v State of Punjab (2010): a person under attack is not expected to weigh force with golden scales; the Court summarised principles of private defence.
- Deo Narain (1973): reasonable apprehension, not actual injury, triggers the right.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the attacker must first injure you
- Forgetting that the right does not include revenge or retaliation after the danger ends

activity.prompt: Order the analysis of a private defence claim
items: Identify the offence threatened against body or property
Check whether there was time to seek public authorities
Assess reasonable apprehension and when it began
Compare the harm caused with the harm necessary
Check whether the case falls in the list where death may be caused

quiz.q: House-breaking by night allows private defence of property extending to
quiz.why: House-breaking by night is one of the cases where the right of private defence of property extends to causing death.

quiz.q: Private defence is not available when
options: There is time to approach public authorities
quiz.why: The right does not arise where there is time to have recourse to the protection of public authorities.

quiz.q: Darshan Singh (2010) said force need not be weighed
quiz.why: The Supreme Court held that a person facing attack cannot be expected to calibrate force precisely.

questions.q: Chapter III of the BNS deals with
questions.why: Chapter III (sections 14–44) lists general exceptions including private defence.

questions.q: Absolute immunity applies below age
questions.why: Section 20 gives complete immunity to a child below seven.

questions.q: Between 7 and 12, a child is exempt if
options: He lacks sufficient maturity of understanding
questions.why: Section 21 gives qualified immunity based on immaturity of understanding.

questions.q: Legal insanity must exist
options: At the time of the act
questions.why: Section 22 looks at the accused's mental state at the time of doing the act.

questions.q: Basdev v State of PEPSU concerns
questions.why: Basdev dealt with voluntary intoxication and the presumption of knowledge.

questions.q: Which is a justifiable exception?
questions.why: Private defence justifies the act, whereas infancy and insanity excuse the actor.

questions.q: Acid attack apprehension allows private defence extending to
questions.why: Throwing or attempting to throw acid causing apprehension of grievous hurt is a listed case.

questions.q: Mistake of law
questions.why: Ignorantia juris non excusat: ignorance of law is not a defence.

questions.q: Good faith in the BNS requires
questions.why: Nothing is said to be done in good faith which is done without due care and attention.

questions.q: Private defence continues
options: Until the attacker flees and is caught
As long as reasonable apprehension of danger lasts
questions.why: The right commences and continues as long as the reasonable apprehension of danger continues.

questions.q: Dahyabhai Thakkar held that insanity is proved
questions.why: The accused discharges the burden on a balance of probabilities.

questions.q: Consent of a child under 12 for consent provisions is
questions.why: The law treats consent given by a person under twelve as no consent unless context indicates otherwise.

questions.q: Private defence of property is available against
questions.why: These are the property offences against which private defence is permitted.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Abetment, conspiracy, attempt and organised crime
courses.summary: Liability for incomplete and group crimes: abetment, criminal conspiracy, attempt, and the new offences of organised crime, petty organised crime and terrorist act.
outcomes: State the three modes of abetment and when an abettor is liable
Distinguish conspiracy from abetment by conspiracy
Apply the proximity and impossibility tests for attempt
Identify ingredients of organised crime and terrorist act under the BNS

lessons.title: Abetment

scenes.text: Kiran repeatedly urges her brother to burn down a rival's shop and hands him a can of kerosene.
The brother changes his mind and never acts. Has Kiran committed any offence?

steps.title: Section 45 – who abets
steps.body: A person abets the doing of a thing who (1) **instigates** any person to do it, (2) engages with others in a **conspiracy** for doing it, if an act or illegal omission takes place in pursuance of it, or (3) intentionally **aids**, by act or illegal omission, the doing of it.

steps.title: Abettor's liability
steps.body: Abetment is a distinct offence. The abettor may be liable even if the act abetted is not committed, or the person abetted is not capable of committing an offence (a child, an insane person), or lacks the same guilty intention. Where the act is committed in consequence of abetment and no express punishment exists, the abettor gets the punishment for the offence.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body:
1. Kiran instigated and supplied kerosene – abetment by instigation and aid is complete, even though no fire was set.
2. A asks a 6-year-old to put poison in food; the child does so – A is liable as abettor though the child commits no offence.
3. Mere silence or presence without intention to aid is not abetment.

steps.title: Abetment of suicide
steps.body: Abetment of suicide requires a positive act of instigation or aid with intent; words uttered in anger or a quarrel are generally not enough (as held in Sanju v State of MP, 2002, under the IPC equivalent).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the main offence must be committed for abetment
- Treating advice given in good faith as instigation

activity.prompt: Tick each mode by which abetment can be committed
items: Instigating a person to do the thing
Engaging in a conspiracy followed by an act in pursuance
Intentionally aiding by an act
Intentionally aiding by an illegal omission

quiz.q: Abetment is defined in BNS section
quiz.why: Section 45 of the BNS defines abetment of a thing.

quiz.q: Is abetment complete if the abetted act is not committed?
options: Yes, abetment is a distinct offence
quiz.why: The law makes abetment punishable even if the abetted act is not done.

quiz.q: Using a child under 7 to commit a crime makes the user
quiz.why: The abettor is liable even though the person abetted cannot legally commit an offence.

lessons.title: Criminal conspiracy

scenes.text: Four employees agree over chats to transfer bank funds to fake accounts. Police intercept them before any transfer.
Can they be prosecuted when no money moved?

steps.title: Section 61 – definition
steps.body: When two or more persons agree to do, or cause to be done, (a) an illegal act, or (b) an act which is not illegal by illegal means, the agreement is a criminal conspiracy. For an agreement to commit an **offence**, the agreement itself is enough; for other agreements, some act besides the agreement must be done in pursuance.

steps.title: Proof
steps.body: Direct evidence is rare, so conspiracy is usually inferred from circumstances. Under the evidence law, anything said or done by a conspirator in reference to the common design after the intention was formed is relevant against all (the old section 10 principle, carried into the BSA). State (NCT of Delhi) v Navjot Sandhu (2005, Parliament attack) discussed these principles.

steps.title: Conspiracy vs abetment by conspiracy
steps.body:
- Criminal conspiracy: the agreement to commit an offence is itself the offence.
- Abetment by conspiracy: needs an act or illegal omission in pursuance of the conspiracy.
So the bank employees are guilty of criminal conspiracy even though no transfer occurred.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying one person can conspire with himself – at least two are needed
- Requiring all conspirators to know every detail – knowledge of the common design is enough

activity.prompt: Order how a prosecutor builds a conspiracy case
items: Show two or more persons
Prove an agreement, often from circumstances
Show the object was an offence or illegal act/means
Use acts and statements of each in furtherance against all
Prove an overt act where the object is not an offence

quiz.q: Minimum persons for criminal conspiracy
quiz.why: An agreement requires at least two persons.

quiz.q: For an agreement to commit an offence, is an overt act needed?
quiz.why: Where the object is an offence, the agreement alone constitutes criminal conspiracy.

quiz.q: Criminal conspiracy is defined in BNS section
quiz.why: Section 61 BNS replaces IPC section 120A.

lessons.title: Attempt

scenes.text: A pickpocket thrusts his hand into a commuter's pocket on a bus; the pocket is empty.
He argues he could not have stolen anything. Is he guilty of attempted theft?

steps.title: Section 62
steps.body: Whoever attempts to commit an offence punishable with imprisonment for life or imprisonment, and in such attempt does any act towards its commission, where no express provision is made, is punished with up to one-half of the longest term provided, or fine, or both (and for offences punishable with life, up to one-half of life computed as described). Specific attempts like attempt to murder (section 109) have their own punishment.

steps.title: Tests
steps.body:
- **Proximity test**: the act must be sufficiently close to the completed offence.
- **Equivocality test**: the act must unequivocally show the intent.
- Abhayanand Mishra v State of Bihar (1961): an attempt begins when preparation is complete and the accused does an act towards commission; it need not be the penultimate act.

steps.title: Impossibility
steps.body: The illustration to the attempt provision states that a person who puts his hand in an empty pocket intending to steal is guilty of attempted theft. Factual impossibility is no defence. So the pickpocket is guilty.

steps.title: Worked computation
steps.body: An offence carries maximum 10 years imprisonment and no special attempt provision applies. Maximum for attempt = 1/2 × 10 = **5 years**, or fine, or both.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Requiring the last possible act before the offence
- Treating impossibility as a defence

activity.prompt: Order the facts from intention to attempt in Abhayanand Mishra
items: Accused decides to obtain permission fraudulently to sit an exam
He collects forged certificates
He submits the application with forged documents
University issues admit card – attempt to cheat complete

quiz.q: Putting a hand in an empty pocket to steal is
quiz.why: Impossibility due to circumstances unknown to the accused does not prevent an attempt.

quiz.q: General attempt punishment is up to
quiz.why: Section 62 provides up to one-half of the longest term for the offence.

quiz.q: Attempt for an offence with max 6 years gives max
quiz.why: One-half of 6 years is 3 years under the general attempt provision.

lessons.title: Organised crime and terrorist act

scenes.text: A gang has run a vehicle-theft and extortion network across three states for years, sharing profits.
Earlier, such gangs were dealt with mainly under state laws like MCOCA. What does the BNS now provide?

steps.title: Organised crime (section 111)
steps.body: Continuing unlawful activity – including kidnapping, robbery, vehicle theft, extortion, land grabbing, contract killing, economic offences, cyber crimes, trafficking of persons, drugs, weapons – by an individual or group acting as a member of or on behalf of an organised crime syndicate, using violence, threat, intimidation, coercion or other unlawful means, to obtain direct or indirect material or financial benefit.

steps.title: Continuing unlawful activity
steps.body: An activity prohibited by law, a cognizable offence punishable with three years or more, undertaken as a member of a syndicate, in respect of which more than one charge-sheet has been filed in a competent court within the preceding ten years and cognizance taken.

steps.title: Petty organised crime (section 112)
steps.body: Crimes causing general feelings of insecurity among citizens, such as theft, snatching, cheating, unauthorised selling of tickets, public examination paper selling, committed by groups or gangs.

steps.title: Terrorist act (section 113)
steps.body: Doing any act with intent to threaten or likely to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security or economic security of India, or to strike terror in the people, using bombs, explosives, firearms, or other means causing death, injury, damage to property or disruption of essential supplies, among other listed modes. The investigating officer of a prescribed rank decides whether to register under the BNS or the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a single theft as organised crime – a continuing pattern and syndicate are required
- Assuming the BNS repeals UAPA – both coexist

activity.prompt: Tick ingredients of 'continuing unlawful activity'
items: Cognizable offence punishable with three years or more
Undertaken as a member of or on behalf of a syndicate
More than one charge-sheet in the preceding ten years
Court has taken cognizance of those charge-sheets

quiz.q: Organised crime is in BNS section
quiz.why: Section 111 defines and punishes organised crime.

quiz.q: Snatching by gangs causing public insecurity is an example of
quiz.why: Section 112 covers petty organised crimes such as theft and snatching by groups.

quiz.q: The look-back period for prior charge-sheets is
quiz.why: Continuing unlawful activity counts more than one charge-sheet filed within the preceding ten years.

questions.q: Which is NOT a mode of abetment?
questions.why: Mere presence without intention to aid is not abetment.

questions.q: Criminal conspiracy needs
options: An agreement of two or more
questions.why: Agreement between at least two persons is the essence of conspiracy.

questions.q: Abhayanand Mishra concerns
questions.why: It held that applying with forged documents to sit an exam was an attempt to cheat.

questions.q: Attempt for an offence with maximum 14 years (no special rule) carries maximum
questions.why: One-half of 14 years is 7 years.

questions.q: Statements of a co-conspirator about the common design are
questions.why: Acts and statements in reference to the common design are relevant against every conspirator.

questions.q: Abetment by conspiracy differs from criminal conspiracy because it requires
options: An act or illegal omission in pursuance
questions.why: Abetment by conspiracy needs an act in pursuance, while conspiracy to commit an offence does not.

questions.q: Attempt to murder is specifically in BNS section
questions.why: Section 109 BNS deals with attempt to murder.

questions.q: Factual impossibility in attempt
questions.why: The empty pocket illustration shows impossibility does not prevent attempt.

questions.q: The terrorist act offence in the BNS is section
questions.why: Section 113 BNS defines terrorist act.

questions.q: Organised crime requires the benefit to be
options: Material or financial, direct or indirect
questions.why: The definition requires the aim of obtaining direct or indirect material or financial benefit.

questions.q: An abettor may be liable even if the person abetted
questions.why: Liability of the abettor does not depend on the capacity of the person abetted.

questions.q: Proximity test asks whether the act is
options: Close enough to the completed offence
questions.why: The proximity test looks at how near the act comes to completing the offence.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Offences affecting the human body
courses.summary: Culpable homicide and murder, the exceptions to murder, death by negligence including hit-and-run, hurt and grievous hurt, and kidnapping and abduction.
outcomes: Distinguish culpable homicide from murder using the Reg v Govinda scheme
Apply the five exceptions to murder
Explain death by negligence and the hit-and-run provision
Classify hurt and grievous hurt and distinguish kidnapping from abduction

lessons.title: Culpable homicide and murder (sections 100, 101)

scenes.text: In a street quarrel A hits B once on the head with a cricket bat; B dies.
Is it murder or culpable homicide not amounting to murder? The answer depends on A's state of mind.

steps.title: Section 100 – culpable homicide
steps.body: Whoever causes death by doing an act (a) with the intention of causing death, (b) with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or (c) with the knowledge that he is likely by such act to cause death, commits culpable homicide.

steps.title: Section 101 – murder
steps.body: Culpable homicide is murder, except in the excepted cases, if the act is done (a) with intention of causing death; (b) with intention of causing bodily injury the offender knows to be likely to cause the death of the particular person; (c) with intention of causing bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death; or (d) with knowledge that the act is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death, without any excuse for the risk.

steps.title: Reg v Govinda (1876) and Virsa Singh (1958)
steps.body:
Melvill J compared the clauses: 'likely to cause death' (culpable homicide) vs 'sufficient in the ordinary course of nature' (murder) – a difference of degree of probability.
Virsa Singh v State of Punjab: for clause (c) the prosecution proves (1) bodily injury present, (2) its nature, (3) intention to inflict that particular injury, (4) that injury is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. Then it is murder regardless of intention to kill.

steps.title: Punishment
steps.body: Murder: death or imprisonment for life, and fine (section 103(1)). Culpable homicide not amounting to murder: section 105 (intention – life or up to 10 years with fine; knowledge only – up to 10 years or fine or both).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking intention to kill is always required for murder
- Ignoring the degree of probability of death
- Citing IPC sections 299/300 for post-July 2024 offences

activity.prompt: Order the Virsa Singh steps for clause (c) murder
items: Prove a bodily injury is present
Prove the nature of the injury objectively
Prove intention to inflict that particular injury
Prove the injury is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death

quiz.why: Section 101 defines murder; section 100 defines culpable homicide.

options: Injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature
quiz.why: Virsa Singh laid the four-step test for the 'sufficient in the ordinary course of nature' clause.

quiz.q: 'Likely to cause death' vs 'sufficient in the ordinary course of nature' differ in
quiz.why: Reg v Govinda explains that the difference lies in the degree of probability of death.

lessons.title: Exceptions to murder

scenes.text: A naval officer learns of his wife's affair, drops her at a cinema, collects a pistol from his ship and shoots the man hours later.
Can he claim grave and sudden provocation?

steps.title: The five exceptions
steps.body:
Culpable homicide is not murder if done:
1. Under **grave and sudden provocation**, depriving self-control
2. In exceeding the right of **private defence** in good faith
3. By a **public servant** exceeding lawful powers in good faith
4. In a **sudden fight**, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, without premeditation or undue advantage or cruel manner
5. With the **consent** of a person above 18 who suffers death or takes the risk

steps.title: K.M. Nanavati v State of Maharashtra (1962)
steps.body: The Supreme Court held the test is whether a reasonable man of the same class of society placed in the accused's situation would be so provoked as to lose self-control. The interval of time and the planned collection of a pistol showed he had cooled down – the provocation exception did not apply; conviction for murder.

steps.title: Sudden fight checklist
steps.body: No premeditation; heat of passion; sudden quarrel; no undue advantage; no cruel or unusual acts. It does not matter which party offered provocation first.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring the 'cooling time' in provocation
- Applying exception 4 where the accused used a weapon against an unarmed person cruelly

activity.prompt: Tick each requirement for the sudden fight exception
items: No premeditation
Heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel
No undue advantage taken
Offender did not act in a cruel or unusual manner

quiz.q: Nanavati's plea of provocation failed because
options: There was time to cool down
quiz.why: The time gap and deliberate fetching of a pistol showed the loss of self-control had passed.

quiz.q: Consent to death as an exception requires the victim to be above
quiz.why: The consent exception applies where the person who dies is above eighteen.

quiz.q: Exceeding private defence in good faith reduces murder to
options: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder
quiz.why: Exception 2 reduces the offence to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

lessons.title: Death by negligence (section 106)

scenes.text: A driver speeding at night hits a pedestrian, then drives away without informing police.
What offence, and does fleeing change the punishment?

steps.title: Section 106(1)
steps.body: Whoever causes death by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide is punished with imprisonment up to **five years** and fine. If committed by a registered medical practitioner while performing a medical procedure, up to two years and fine.

steps.title: Section 106(2) – hit and run
steps.body: Whoever causes death by rash and negligent driving not amounting to culpable homicide and escapes without reporting to a police officer or magistrate soon after the incident is punished with up to **ten years** and fine. (Its enforcement was kept in abeyance by the Government after transporters' protests in early 2024; check the current status before citing.)

steps.title: Medical negligence
steps.body: Jacob Mathew v State of Punjab (2005): a doctor is criminally liable only for gross negligence or recklessness, not a mere error of judgement, applying the Bolam standard of a reasonable professional.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating every road death as murder
- Forgetting the higher threshold of gross negligence for doctors

activity.prompt: Order the duties of a driver after an accident to avoid the hit-and-run provision
items: Stop the vehicle
Help the injured and arrange medical aid
Report to a police officer or magistrate soon after
Cooperate with the investigation

quiz.why: Section 106(1) prescribes imprisonment up to five years and fine.

quiz.q: Jacob Mathew requires for doctors
quiz.why: Criminal liability for doctors requires a high degree of negligence, not mere error.

quiz.q: Fleeing without reporting after a fatal negligent driving accident attracts up to
quiz.why: Section 106(2) prescribes up to ten years for hit and run.

lessons.title: Hurt, grievous hurt, kidnapping and abduction

scenes.text: A man persuades a 15-year-old girl to leave her parents' home and go with him, without force.
Her parents never consented. Is it kidnapping, even though she went willingly?

steps.title: Hurt and grievous hurt
steps.body: Hurt (section 114): causing bodily pain, disease or infirmity. Grievous hurt (section 116) includes: emasculation; permanent privation of sight of either eye; of hearing of either ear; privation of any member or joint; destruction or permanent impairing of a member or joint; permanent disfiguration of head or face; fracture or dislocation of bone or tooth; hurt endangering life or causing severe bodily pain or inability to follow ordinary pursuits for **fifteen days** (reduced from 20 days in the IPC).

steps.title: Kidnapping from lawful guardianship
steps.body:
Taking or enticing a **child** (a person below 18 under the BNS definition, now gender-neutral) or a person of unsound mind out of the keeping of the lawful guardian without the guardian's consent. The child's own consent is irrelevant.
S. Varadarajan v State of Madras (1965): where a minor near majority voluntarily leaves and joins the accused without his active persuasion, 'taking' may not be proved.

steps.title: Abduction
steps.body: Compelling a person by force, or inducing by deceitful means, to go from any place. Abduction is not an offence by itself; it is punishable when done with a specified intent (e.g. to murder, to confine).

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body:
- Victim: kidnapping – child/unsound mind; abduction – any person
- Means: kidnapping – taking/enticing, force not needed; abduction – force or deceit
- Consent of victim: irrelevant in kidnapping; relevant in abduction
- Nature: kidnapping is complete on taking; abduction is a continuing offence

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 20 days for grievous hurt under the BNS
- Treating a minor's consent as a defence to kidnapping

activity.prompt: Tick categories of grievous hurt
items: Permanent privation of sight of either eye
Fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth
Permanent disfiguration of head or face
Severe bodily pain or inability for fifteen days

quiz.why: The BNS reduced the period from twenty to fifteen days.

quiz.why: The guardian's consent, not the child's, is what matters.

quiz.q: Abduction requires
quiz.why: Abduction is compelling by force or inducing by deceit to go from a place.
