courses.title: Unit 5 · Offences against women, property and reputation
courses.summary: Sexual offences, cruelty and dowry death; theft, snatching, extortion, robbery and dacoity; criminal misappropriation, criminal breach of trust and cheating; and defamation.
outcomes: State the ingredients of rape and of cruelty and dowry death
Distinguish theft, extortion, robbery and dacoity
Distinguish criminal breach of trust from cheating
Apply the exceptions to defamation

lessons.title: Sexual offences, cruelty and dowry death

scenes.text: Two years after marriage, Priya dies of burns at her matrimonial home. Her parents say she was harassed for a car soon before her death.
Which offences can be charged against the husband and in-laws?

steps.title: Rape (sections 63 and 64)
steps.body: Section 63 defines rape broadly (penetrative acts listed) against a woman against her will, without consent, with consent obtained by fear or by impersonation, when she is of unsound mind or intoxicated, when she is under 18 (with or without consent), or when she cannot communicate consent. Consent means unequivocal voluntary agreement; absence of physical resistance is not consent. Section 64 prescribes rigorous imprisonment not less than ten years, extendable to life, and fine. Marital exception: sexual acts by a man with his own wife, not under 18, are not rape under this section (a question under constitutional challenge).

steps.title: Deceitful means (section 69)
steps.body: Sexual intercourse by deceitful means or on a false promise to marry without intention of fulfilling it, not amounting to rape, is a separate offence (up to ten years). Deceitful means include false promise of employment or promotion, or marrying after suppressing identity.

steps.title: Dowry death (section 80) and cruelty (sections 85, 86)
steps.body:
Dowry death: death of a woman by burns, bodily injury or otherwise than in normal circumstances within **seven years of marriage**, where it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or his relatives in connection with a dowry demand. Punishment: not less than seven years, up to life.
Cruelty (section 85, earlier IPC 498A): wilful conduct likely to drive her to suicide or cause grave injury to life, limb or health (mental or physical), or harassment to coerce her or her relatives to meet unlawful demands. Up to three years and fine.

steps.title: Presumption
steps.body: The evidence law raises a presumption that the husband or relative caused the dowry death once the ingredients are shown. Kans Raj v State of Punjab (2000) explained 'soon before' as a proximate and live link, not a fixed period.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating seven years as relevant for cruelty – it applies to dowry death
- Thinking passive submission equals consent

activity.prompt: Tick each ingredient the prosecution must establish for dowry death
items: Death by burns, bodily injury or otherwise than in normal circumstances
Within seven years of marriage
Cruelty or harassment by husband or his relative
Soon before death
In connection with a demand for dowry

quiz.q: Dowry death is in BNS section
quiz.why: Section 80 BNS replaces IPC section 304B on dowry death.

quiz.q: Minimum punishment for rape under section 64
quiz.why: Section 64 prescribes rigorous imprisonment of at least ten years, extendable to life.

quiz.q: Cruelty by husband or relatives is in BNS section
quiz.why: Section 85 corresponds to the old IPC section 498A.

lessons.title: Theft, snatching, extortion, robbery and dacoity

story.title: The chain at the bus stop

scenes.text: A rider on a scooter suddenly grabs a gold chain from a woman's neck and speeds away.
Is it theft, snatching or robbery?

steps.title: Theft (section 303)
steps.body: Intending to take dishonestly any **movable** property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moving that property in order to such taking. Ingredients: dishonest intention, movable property, out of possession of another, without consent, moving the property.

steps.title: Snatching (section 304)
steps.body: Theft is snatching if, to commit theft, the offender suddenly or quickly or forcibly seizes, secures, grabs or takes away movable property from any person or from his possession. Up to three years and fine.

steps.title: Extortion, robbery, dacoity
steps.body:
- Extortion (308): intentionally putting a person in fear of injury and thereby dishonestly inducing delivery of property.
- Robbery (309): theft or extortion aggravated by causing or attempting to cause death, hurt or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death, hurt or restraint, in order to commit or carry away.
- Dacoity (310): robbery committed or attempted conjointly by **five or more** persons.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body:
1. Grabbing the chain quickly – snatching.
2. If the rider had slapped the woman to take the chain – robbery.
3. Threatening to publish photos unless paid – extortion.
4. Six armed men looting a shop – dacoity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying theft to immovable property like land
- Saying extortion needs force – fear of injury inducing delivery is enough, and consent is present though vitiated

activity.prompt: Order from least to most aggravated property offence
items: Theft
Snatching
Robbery
Dacoity

quiz.q: Theft applies to
quiz.why: Theft requires movable property moved out of another's possession.

quiz.q: Dacoity requires at least
quiz.why: Robbery by five or more persons conjointly is dacoity.

quiz.q: Extortion differs from theft because
options: Property is delivered by the victim under fear
quiz.why: In extortion the victim delivers property, induced by fear of injury.

lessons.title: Misappropriation, criminal breach of trust and cheating

scenes.text: An accountant entrusted with company funds diverts ₹8 lakh to his personal account.
Separately, a seller takes advance payment by showing fake stock photos and never delivers.

steps.title: Dishonest misappropriation (section 314)
steps.body: Dishonestly misappropriating or converting to one's own use movable property, e.g. keeping a lost purse found on the road without trying to find the owner. Initial possession may be innocent.

steps.title: Criminal breach of trust (section 316)
steps.body: Being **entrusted** with property or dominion over it, dishonestly misappropriating or converting it, or dishonestly using or disposing of it in violation of a direction of law or a contract. Aggravated forms for carriers, clerks/servants, public servants, bankers, agents.

steps.title: Cheating (section 318)
steps.body: Deceiving a person and fraudulently or dishonestly inducing him to deliver property or consent to retention, or intentionally inducing him to do or omit something he would not otherwise do, causing or likely to cause damage or harm. The dishonest intention must exist **at the time of inducement** – Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v State of Bihar (2000).

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body:
- CBT: lawful entrustment, later dishonest misuse (the accountant).
- Cheating: deception from the start induces delivery (the fake seller).
- A mere breach of contract is not cheating unless fraudulent intent existed at inception.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Converting every civil dispute into cheating
- Forgetting entrustment as the core of CBT

activity.prompt: Tick ingredients of criminal breach of trust
items: Entrustment of property or dominion over it
Dishonest misappropriation or conversion
Or dishonest use or disposal in violation of law or contract
By the person entrusted

quiz.q: Core of criminal breach of trust is
quiz.why: CBT requires property to be entrusted and then dishonestly misappropriated.

quiz.q: For cheating, dishonest intention must exist
quiz.why: Hridaya Ranjan held intention must exist at the inception of the transaction.

quiz.q: Cheating is in BNS section
quiz.why: Section 318 BNS defines and punishes cheating.

lessons.title: Defamation (section 356)

scenes.text: A customer posts that a restaurant serves rotten meat. The post goes viral and the owner sues.
The customer says it is true and was in public interest.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: By words spoken or intended to be read, signs or visible representations, making or publishing an imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe it will harm, his reputation. Imputation on a deceased person, a company or a collection of persons can also defame.

steps.title: Exceptions
steps.body:
1. Truth for public good
2. Public conduct of public servants in good faith
3. Conduct of any person touching a public question
4. Reports of proceedings of courts
5. Merits of decided cases and conduct of witnesses
6. Merits of public performance
7. Censure by a person in lawful authority
8. Accusation in good faith to authorised persons
9. Imputation in good faith for protection of interests
10. Caution intended for good of the person or public

steps.title: Punishment
steps.body: Simple imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both, or **community service**. Subramanian Swamy v Union of India (2016) upheld criminal defamation as a reasonable restriction on free speech.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Truth alone is not enough; it must also be for public good
- Forgetting that defamation is non-cognizable and complaint-based

activity.prompt: Order the analysis of a defamation claim
items: Identify the imputation and its medium
Show publication to a third person

Decide liability and punishment

quiz.why: The Court upheld it as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(2).

quiz.why: Section 356 allows community service as a punishment.

lessons.title: Key-section sheet: IPC to BNS

scenes.text: Aman keeps writing 302 and 420 from habit in mock tests.
He builds a one-page map of the new numbers.

steps.title: General part
steps.body:
- Common intention: IPC 34 → BNS 3(5)
- Punishments: IPC 53 → BNS 4 (adds community service)
- General exceptions: IPC 76–106 → BNS 14–44
- Insanity: IPC 84 → BNS 22
- Abetment: IPC 107 → BNS 45
- Criminal conspiracy: IPC 120A → BNS 61
- Attempt: IPC 511 → BNS 62

steps.title: Body
steps.body:
- Culpable homicide: IPC 299 → BNS 100
- Murder: IPC 300 → BNS 101; punishment IPC 302 → BNS 103
- Culpable homicide not murder punishment: IPC 304 → BNS 105
- Death by negligence: IPC 304A → BNS 106
- Attempt to murder: IPC 307 → BNS 109
- Dowry death: IPC 304B → BNS 80
- Rape: IPC 375/376 → BNS 63/64

steps.title: Property and others
steps.body:
- Theft: IPC 378 → BNS 303
- Extortion: IPC 383 → BNS 308
- Robbery: IPC 390 → BNS 309
- Dacoity: IPC 391 → BNS 310
- CBT: IPC 405 → BNS 316
- Cheating: IPC 415/420 → BNS 318
- Cruelty: IPC 498A → BNS 85
- Defamation: IPC 499/500 → BNS 356
- New: snatching 304, organised crime 111, petty organised crime 112, terrorist act 113

steps.title: How to cite
steps.body: In answers write 'section 101 BNS (formerly section 300 IPC)' – examiners reward the mapping, and older case law is still good authority on unchanged text.

lessons.title: Lab: Solving a problem question with IRAC

scenes.text: Problem: A and B agree to beat C. A holds C while B stabs C in the chest with a knife. C dies. Discuss liability.
You have 25 minutes. Use IRAC.

steps.title: Issue
steps.body: (1) Is B guilty of murder? (2) Is A jointly liable through common intention under section 3(5)? (3) Does any exception apply?

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: Section 100 and 101 BNS; Virsa Singh four-step test for clause (c); section 3(5) common intention; Mahbub Shah and Barendra Kumar Ghosh on prior meeting of minds and participation.

steps.title: Application
steps.body: A stab in the chest with a knife is an intentional injury likely sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death – B commits murder (clause c). A and B planned a beating; did they share an intention to cause such an injury? If the plan was only a beating, A may be liable for the offence within the common intention (grievous hurt) unless the stabbing was within contemplation. Facts like A holding C while B drew the knife may show the intention developed on the spot.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: B: murder under section 101, punishable under section 103(1). A: liable for murder if common intention to cause fatal injury is proved, otherwise for voluntarily causing grievous hurt with common intention. No exception applies on the facts: no sudden quarrel or provocation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Jumping to a conclusion without stating rules
- Ignoring alternative outcomes on uncertain facts

items: State the issues

quiz.why: Under section 3(5) A is liable for acts within the common intention shared with B.

lessons.title: Lab: Briefing a leading case

scenes.text: Your moot coach asks for a one-page brief of K.M. Nanavati v State of Maharashtra.
You follow a standard case-brief template.

steps.title: Template
steps.body: Citation and court → Facts → Procedural history → Issues → Holding → Reasoning → Significance.

steps.title: Nanavati brief
steps.body:
- Court: Supreme Court of India, 1962
- Facts: Naval officer shot his wife's lover after learning of the affair, having fetched a pistol from his ship.
- History: Jury acquitted; Sessions Judge referred; High Court convicted for murder.
- Issue: Did grave and sudden provocation apply?
- Holding: No; murder conviction upheld.
- Reasoning: Reasonable man test; time to cool down; conduct showed deliberation.
- Significance: Leading authority on provocation; often cited in discussions on the end of jury trials in India.

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- What is the reasonable man test?
- Can words alone amount to provocation? (Yes, in Indian law, in appropriate circumstances.)
- Why is cooling time relevant?
